root.title: Derivative-Free Optimization
root.top_down_role: Optimization using function-value, comparison, simulation, or related black-box information, covering local and global methods, structural regimes, stochastic evaluations, constraints, and zeroth-order complexity.

children.title: Black-Box Regime Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Oracle information, objective regularity, evaluation cost, and applicability boundaries that determine which derivative-free families are appropriate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Derivative-Free Search over Continuous Policy Parameters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Application-specific characterization of a derivative-free search regime; it does not define a particular algorithm or give a convergence guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a policy parameterized by a continuous vector \(\theta\), derivative-free policy search may generate a population \(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_K\) and search among these parameters for the best candidate. The continuity and dimensionality of \(\theta\) affect which derivative-free methods are appropriate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Derivative-free policy search may generate a population of continuous policy-parameter vectors and search for the best candidate. The parameter vector's continuity and dimensionality influence method choice.
assumptions_latex: A population of candidate parameters \(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_K\) is generated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Search among the candidate policy parameters using derivative-free methods selected with regard to the continuity and dimensionality of }\theta.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Black-Box Optimizer in the Generic Stochastic-Search Framework
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition of black-box optimization for the source's generic stochastic-search framework; the algorithm may still use search-space, neighborhood, and problem-type information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the generic stochastic-search framework, if the functions \(g\) and \(h\) do not depend on the particular problem instance and the algorithm \(A\) obtains fitness values for queried solutions \(x\) from a black-box procedure without knowing how those values are determined, then \(A\) is called a black-box optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the stated generic stochastic-search framework, an algorithm is called a black-box optimizer when its functions g and h are independent of the particular problem instance and it queries a procedure for fitness values without knowing how those values are determined.
assumptions_latex: g\text{ and }h\text{ do not depend on the particular problem instance}
A\text{ obtains fitness values for queried solutions }x\text{ from a black-box procedure}
A\text{ does not know how the returned fitness values are determined}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\text{ is called a black-box optimizer}

assumptions_latex: The objective is a deterministic function \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) on a nonempty query set \(X\).

notation.meaning: Exact function-value oracle for the objective

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic, noiseless scalar objective evaluations.

source_refs.locator: 1.1 Why derivative-free optimization p. 1

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\neq\varnothing\) and let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be deterministic. An exact function-value oracle for \(f\) is a mapping \(\mathcal{O}_f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \[\mathcal{O}_f(x)=f(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in X.\] Thus a query reveals the objective value without error, randomness, derivative information, or auxiliary constraint information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact function-value oracle returns the true deterministic objective value at every permitted query point.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Function-Value Oracles

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1 Why derivative-free optimization p. 1

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information ordering between deterministic exact-value and ordinal interfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given exact values \(f(x_1),\ldots,f(x_m)\), one can compute every pairwise comparison and any batch ranking without additional objective queries. The converse fails in general: if \(\phi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is strictly increasing, then \(f\) and \(\phi\circ f\) have identical ordinal responses but generally different exact values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact values simulate pairwise comparisons and rankings, while ordinal feedback cannot generally recover exact values.
assumptions_latex: Ordinal responses depend only on order and equality relations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{exact values}\succeq\text{pairwise comparisons}\) and \(\text{exact values}\succeq\text{rankings}\), with both reverse reductions failing in general.

notation.meaning: Strictly increasing transformation of objective values

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Values Dominate Ordinal Oracles
Inexact Function-Value Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministically bounded additive evaluation error represented by a fixed response map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\neq\varnothing\), let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\), and let \(\delta:X\to[0,\infty)\). A deterministically inexact function-value oracle is a mapping \(\mathcal{O}_{f,\delta}:X\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \[\mathcal{O}_{f,\delta}(x)=f(x)+e(x),\qquad |e(x)|\leq\delta(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in X.\] The exact-oracle model is recovered when \(\delta(x)=0\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministically inexact oracle returns the objective plus a fixed unknown error whose magnitude is bounded by a prescribed pointwise tolerance.
assumptions_latex: The objective is \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\), and the error tolerance is a known function \(\delta:X\to[0,\infty)\).

notation.meaning: Fixed evaluation error at query x

source_refs.locator: 1.3 Limitations of derivative-free optimization p. 5

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3 Limitations of derivative-free optimization p. 5

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Certified Ordering under Bounded Evaluation Error
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp pairwise comparison certificate from deterministic pointwise error bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y_u=\mathcal O_{f,\delta}(u)\) and \(I_u=[y_u-\delta(u),y_u+\delta(u)]\) for \(u\in\{x,z\}\). Every compatible objective satisfies \(f(u)\in I_u\). Hence \(y_x+\delta(x)<y_z-\delta(z)\) certifies \(f(x)<f(z)\). If \(I_x\cap I_z\neq\varnothing\), the observations and bounds alone certify neither strict ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disjoint uncertainty intervals certify strict ordering; overlapping intervals leave the ordering unidentified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup I_x<\inf I_z\Rightarrow f(x)<f(z)\); overlap precludes a strict-order certificate from these data alone.

notation.meaning: Objective values at u compatible with its response and error bound

knowledge_statements.title: Certified Ordering under Bounded Evaluation Error

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample behavior of independent simulator replication under a variance bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(Y_1(x),\ldots,Y_m(x)\) are independent responses with \(\mathbb E[Y_i(x)]=f(x)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Y_i(x))\leq\sigma^2(x)\). For \(\bar Y_m(x)=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^mY_i(x)\), \[\mathbb E[\bar Y_m(x)]=f(x),\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_m(x))\leq\frac{\sigma^2(x)}m,\qquad \Pr\{|\bar Y_m(x)-f(x)|\geq\varepsilon\}\leq\frac{\sigma^2(x)}{m\varepsilon^2}.\] Thus \(m\geq\sigma^2(x)/(\alpha\varepsilon^2)\) ensures error less than \(\varepsilon\) with probability at least \(1-\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent averaging preserves unbiasedness, reduces variance inversely with replication count, and yields a Chebyshev sample bound.
assumptions_latex: The responses are independent and each has mean \(f(x)\).
Each response has variance at most \(\sigma^2(x)<\infty\).

notation.meaning: Mean of m independent simulator responses at x

knowledge_statements.title: Independent-Replication Mean and Confidence Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence can prevent variance reduction across repeated simulator calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_m\) have common variance \(\sigma^2\) and common pairwise covariance \(\gamma\), then \[\operatorname{Var}\!\left(m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^mY_i\right)=\frac{\sigma^2}{m}+\frac{m-1}{m}\gamma.\] In particular, if \(Y_i=Y_1\) almost surely for every \(i\), the variance remains \(\sigma^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Correlated simulator calls need not yield inverse-sample variance reduction; identical calls yield none.
knowledge_statements.title: Correlation Boundary for Replication Averaging

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates integrability, conditional unbiasedness, finite variance, and independent replication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a mean-response oracle, integrability \(\mathbb E|Y(x)|<\infty\) makes \(f(x)=\mathbb E[Y(x)]\) well defined. If \(\mathcal H_{k-1}\) is the pre-query history and \(x_k\) is \(\mathcal H_{k-1}\)-measurable, conditional unbiasedness requires \(\mathbb E[Y_k\mid\mathcal H_{k-1}]=f(x_k)\). A finite-variance clause additionally requires \(\mathbb E[(Y_k-f(x_k))^2\mid\mathcal H_{k-1}]\le\sigma^2(x_k)<\infty\). Access to fresh independent replication is a separate interface property requiring repeated calls at fixed \(x\) to use conditionally independent draws from \(P_x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integrability, conditional unbiasedness, finite variance, and access to independent fresh draws are distinct oracle assumptions.
assumptions_latex: The target is the mean response whenever unbiasedness is asserted.
x_k\text{ is measurable with respect to the pre-query history }\mathcal H_{k-1}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Integrability, unbiasedness, finite variance, and fresh-draw independence are logically separate clauses.}
knowledge_statements.title: Distinct Moment and Fresh-Sampling Clauses

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates the simulator response law from the scalar functional selected as the optimization objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A stochastic simulation oracle associates each query \(x\in X\) with a response law \(P_x\) and returns a random response \(Y\sim P_x\). A separately declared functional \(T\) defines the optimized quantity by \(f(x)=T(P_x)\). Mean-response optimization is the specialization \(T(P)=\int y\,P(dy)\) whenever this integral exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The simulator supplies a response distribution, while a separately specified functional of that distribution defines the objective.
assumptions_latex: P_x\text{ is a probability law for every }x\in X
T(P_x)\text{ is well defined for every admissible }x

notation.meaning: Functional defining the scalar optimization target

knowledge_statements.title: Distributional Simulation-Oracle Interface

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of replication-based mean estimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\mathbb E[Y_i(x)]=f(x)+b(x)\) for every replication, then \(\mathbb E[\bar Y_m(x)]-f(x)=b(x)\); replication does not remove systematic bias. If \(Y(x)\) is integrable but \(\operatorname{Var}(Y(x))=\infty\), the mean objective remains defined, but variance and Chebyshev bounds requiring a finite \(\sigma^2(x)\) do not apply.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Averaging preserves systematic bias, and an integrable heavy-tailed response need not admit variance-based confidence bounds.
assumptions_latex: Repeated responses have the displayed finite mean when the bias assertion is used.

notation.meaning: Pointwise bias relative to the declared target

knowledge_statements.title: Bias and Infinite-Variance Boundaries

assumptions_latex: For each \(x\in X\), the simulator output \(Y(x,\xi)\) is integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{O}(x;\xi)]=f(x)\), with independent replications available under fresh draws of \(\xi\).

notation.meaning: Random simulator output at a query

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbiased simulation output with repeatable random sampling.

source_refs.locator: 7 Stochastic optimization p. 161
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\neq\varnothing\), and for each \(x\in X\) let \(Y(x,\xi)\) be an integrable random variable. A stochastic simulation oracle returns \(\mathcal{O}(x;\xi)=Y(x,\xi)\), where fresh calls may use independent realizations of \(\xi\), and the optimized mean response is \[f(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y(x,\xi)].\] Consequently, each response is unbiased for \(f(x)\). A finite-variance model additionally assumes \(\mathbb{E}[(Y(x,\xi)-f(x))^2]\leq\sigma^2(x)<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stochastic simulation oracle returns a random integrable response whose expectation equals the objective; fresh calls can provide independent replications.
knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Simulation Oracles

source_witnesses.locator: 7 Stochastic optimization p. 161
source_witnesses.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited general stochastic-optimization section does not clearly support this simulation-oracle definition or the availability of independent replications. A simulation-optimization or stochastic-oracle source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Pairwise Comparison Oracles
children.top_down_role: Black-box feedback limited to relative outcomes for pairs of evaluated alternatives.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Observational equivalence under access restricted to exact pairwise comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f,g:X\to\mathbb R\), using the same comparison convention. Then \(\mathcal C_f=\mathcal C_g\) on \(X^2\) if and only if, for every \(x,y\in X\), \[f(x)<f(y)\iff g(x)<g(y),\qquad f(x)=f(y)\iff g(x)=g(y).\] Thus exact pairwise access identifies the induced total preorder, not objective-value magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two objectives give identical exact pairwise feedback exactly when they induce the same ordering and tie classes.
assumptions_latex: Both oracles report strict preference and equality exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal C_f=\mathcal C_g\iff f\text{ and }g\text{ induce the same total preorder on }X\).
knowledge_statements.title: Order-Type Characterization of Exact Comparisons

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Consistency Identities for Exact Pairwise Responses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic consistency forced by a single deterministic scalar objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mathcal C_f(x,y)=\operatorname{sgn}(f(y)-f(x))\), \[\mathcal C_f(x,x)=0,\qquad \mathcal C_f(y,x)=-\mathcal C_f(x,y).\] If \(\mathcal C_f(x,y),\mathcal C_f(y,z)\in\{0,1\}\), then \(\mathcal C_f(x,z)\in\{0,1\}\); if either premise is strict, then \(\mathcal C_f(x,z)=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact pairwise comparisons are reflexive at ties, antisymmetric under reversal, and transitively consistent.
assumptions_latex: All responses are generated by one deterministic scalar objective \(f\).
A positive response means that the first argument has smaller objective value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal C_f\) satisfies reversal antisymmetry and the transitivity laws of the total preorder induced by \(f\).
knowledge_statements.title: Consistency Identities for Exact Pairwise Responses

assumptions_latex: The latent objective is \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\), and smaller values are preferred.

notation.meaning: Sign function with zero representing a tie

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact ordinal feedback for minimization, including ties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\), with smaller values preferred. An exact pairwise comparison oracle is the map \(\mathcal{C}_f:X\times X\to\{-1,0,1\}\) defined by \[\mathcal{C}_f(x,y)=\operatorname{sgn}(f(y)-f(x)).\] Hence \(\mathcal{C}_f(x,y)=1\) means that \(x\) is preferred to \(y\), \(\mathcal{C}_f(x,y)=-1\) means that \(y\) is preferred, and \(\mathcal{C}_f(x,y)=0\) records equal objective values. The response is invariant under every strictly increasing transformation of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pairwise comparison oracle reports which of two points has the smaller latent objective value, or reports a tie.
knowledge_statements.title: Pairwise Comparison Oracles

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact ordinal definition is coherent and fits the leaf, but no citation supports the convention, tie semantics, or transformation-invariance claim.

children.title: Ranking Oracles
children.top_down_role: Ordinal feedback over sets of candidate alternatives.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Comparison Cost of Recovering an Exact Strict Ranking
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise-query burden for simulating a strict batch-ranking response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m\) alternatives having distinct objective values, every deterministic binary-comparison decision tree that reconstructs their total order has worst-case depth at least \(\lceil\log_2(m!)\rceil\). Comparison sorting reconstructs the order using \(O(m\log m)\) pairwise comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strict ranking requires order m log m pairwise comparisons in the worst case, and comparison sorting attains that order.
assumptions_latex: The batch has \(m\) distinct latent objective values.
Each pairwise query is exact and binary.

notation.meaning: Worst-case pairwise queries needed to reconstruct the strict ranking

knowledge_statements.title: Comparison Cost of Recovering an Exact Strict Ranking

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ranking–Pairwise Equivalence on a Finite Batch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information equivalence when the ranking retains objective-value tie classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(B=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\), an ordered partition into objective-value tie blocks determines \(\mathcal C_f(x_i,x_j)\) for every \(i,j\). Conversely, the complete objective-consistent pairwise table determines those ordered tie blocks. A permutation formed by arbitrary deterministic tie-breaking retains only a linear extension and need not reveal equality classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tie-preserving batch ranking and its complete consistent pairwise table contain the same ordinal information; arbitrary tie-breaking can erase equality information.
assumptions_latex: All responses are induced by one deterministic scalar objective.
The weak-ranking variant retains equality classes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{ordered tie blocks on }B\longleftrightarrow\{\mathcal C_f(x_i,x_j):1\le i<j\le m\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Ranking–Pairwise Equivalence on a Finite Batch

assumptions_latex: The latent objective is \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\), and a query is a finite tuple \((x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in X^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x_{\pi(1)})\leq\cdots\leq f(x_{\pi(m)})\), with a fixed rule resolving ties.

notation.meaning: Ranking oracle on batches of size m

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact total ranking of a finite query batch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(m\geq2\) and a latent objective \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\). An exact ranking oracle is a map \(\mathcal{R}_{f,m}:X^m\to S_m\) whose response \(\pi=\mathcal{R}_{f,m}(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\) satisfies \[f(x_{\pi(1)})\leq f(x_{\pi(2)})\leq\cdots\leq f(x_{\pi(m)}).\] A predetermined deterministic convention orders indices having equal values. The response contains ordinal information only and is unchanged when \(f\) is replaced by a strictly increasing transformation of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A ranking oracle orders a finite batch from lowest to highest latent objective value, using a fixed tie-breaking convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Ranking Oracles

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ranking-oracle definition is coherent, but its batch, permutation, and deterministic tie-breaking conventions have no cited authoritative source.

children.title: Preference-Learning Feedback
children.top_down_role: Human or automated preference signals used by derivative-free optimization.

assumptions_latex: There is a latent utility \(u:X\to\mathbb{R}\), with larger values preferred.
The link \(\psi:\mathbb{R}\to[0,1]\) is nondecreasing and satisfies \(\psi(t)+\psi(-t)=1\).

notation.meaning: Binary preference label, where one favors the first item

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary probabilistic feedback generated by latent utility differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be a latent utility and let \(\psi:\mathbb{R}\to[0,1]\) be nondecreasing with \(\psi(t)+\psi(-t)=1\). Preference-learning feedback for a queried pair \((x,y)\) is a binary random variable \(B\in\{0,1\}\) satisfying \[\mathbb{P}(B=1\mid x,y)=\psi(u(x)-u(y)),\qquad \mathbb{P}(B=0\mid x,y)=\psi(u(y)-u(x)).\] Here \(B=1\) denotes preference for \(x\). Only utility differences identifiable through \(\psi\) govern the observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Preference-learning feedback is a random binary choice whose probability depends monotonically on the difference between two latent utilities.
knowledge_statements.title: Preference-Learning Feedback

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement selects a particular latent-utility difference-link model for a broader feedback leaf. An authoritative source is needed to establish this intended model and its assumptions.

children.title: Noisy Comparison Responses
children.top_down_role: Comparison feedback subject to inconsistency, uncertainty, or response errors.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Query amplification under a uniform correctness advantage and conditional independence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an unequal pair \((x,y)\). Suppose \(m\) is odd and repeated responses are conditionally independent, each correct with probability at least \(1/2+\gamma\), where \(\gamma>0\). If \(\widehat Z_m\) is their majority vote, then \[\mathbb P\!\left(\widehat Z_m\ne\operatorname{sgn}(f(y)-f(x))\mid x,y\right)\le e^{-2m\gamma^2}.\] Thus error at most \(\delta\) is ensured by any odd \(m\ge(2\gamma^2)^{-1}\log(1/\delta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent repeated comparisons with a fixed advantage can be amplified exponentially by majority vote.
assumptions_latex: Each response is correct with probability at least \(1/2+\gamma\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb P(\widehat Z_m\text{ is incorrect}\mid x,y)\le e^{-2m\gamma^2}.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent-Repetition Majority Amplification

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure of majority amplification without a dependence assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an unequal pair and draw one Bernoulli correctness variable \(B\) with \(\mathbb P(B=1)=1/2+\gamma\). Return the same comparison outcome determined by \(B\) on every repetition. Each marginal response is correct with probability \(1/2+\gamma\), but every majority vote has error probability \(1/2-\gamma\), independent of the repetition count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perfectly correlated comparison errors keep majority-vote error constant despite arbitrarily many repetitions.
assumptions_latex: All repeated responses share one correctness variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb P(\widehat Z_m\text{ is incorrect})=\frac12-\gamma\quad\text{for every odd }m.
knowledge_statements.title: Dependence Can Defeat Repetition Amplification

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-neutral representation of a random binary response for an unequal queried pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a latent minimization objective \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), a binary noisy-comparison response is specified by a conditional kernel \(K(\cdot\mid x,y)\) on \(\{-1,1\}\). For \(f(x)\ne f(y)\), define \[p(x,y)=K\!\left(\operatorname{sgn}(f(y)-f(x))\mid x,y\right).\] The kernel alone imposes neither a uniform advantage, independence across repetitions, antisymmetry under query reversal, nor a tie convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A noisy binary comparison is a response distribution conditional on the queried pair; reliability, dependence, reversal, and tie rules are separate assumptions.
knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Noisy-Comparison Kernel

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical alternatives for specifying how comparison reliability depends on the latent objective gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For unequal pairs, common reliability specifications include: a uniform advantage \(p(x,y)\ge\tfrac12+\gamma\); a gap-dependent advantage \(p(x,y)\ge\tfrac12+\psi(|f(y)-f(x)|)\) for a declared nonnegative function \(\psi\); or a parametric link \(\mathbb P(Z=1\mid x,y)=G(f(y)-f(x))\). These are distinct models. A tie rule must specify \(K(\cdot\mid x,y)\) when \(f(x)=f(y)\), and reversal consistency must be imposed separately, for example \(K(z\mid y,x)=K(-z\mid x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform-margin, gap-dependent, and parametric-link comparison noise are distinct reliability regimes, each requiring explicit tie and reversal conventions.
assumptions_latex: \(p(x,y)\) denotes correctness probability for unequal pairs.
Any function \(\psi\) or link \(G\) is declared as part of the oracle model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Reliability, tie behavior, and reversal consistency are separate components of a noisy-comparison model}.
knowledge_statements.title: Noisy-Comparison Reliability Regimes

assumptions_latex: The latent objective is \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\), with smaller values preferred.
For unequal values, the response is correct with probability at least \(1/2+\gamma\), where \(0<\gamma\leq1/2\).

notation.meaning: Uniform comparison advantage over random guessing

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniformly reliable binary comparisons away from ties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\), and let a comparison query \((x,y)\) return \(Z\in\{-1,1\}\). The uniformly noisy comparison condition with margin \(\gamma\in(0,1/2]\) is \[\mathbb{P}\!\left(Z=\operatorname{sgn}(f(y)-f(x))\mid x,y\right)\geq\frac12+\gamma\] for every pair satisfying \(f(x)\neq f(y)\). Conditional independence between repeated responses is an additional assumption, not part of this correctness condition. Ties require a separately specified response convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A noisy comparison remains informative when every unequal pair is ordered correctly with probability uniformly greater than one half.
knowledge_statements.title: Noisy Comparison Responses

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniform advantage condition is one valid noisy-comparison model, but no source establishes that this is the intended variant for the leaf or supports its tie and dependence conventions.

children.title: Failed Evaluation Responses
children.top_down_role: Oracle outcomes in which an attempted evaluation returns no usable objective value.

assumptions_latex: The objective is defined on a query set \(X\), but evaluation may fail at some points.

notation.meaning: Set of points where evaluation succeeds

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit missing response without an objective value.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Introduction: Tools and Challenges in Derivative-Free and Blackbox Optimization p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\neq\varnothing\), let \(D\subseteq X\) be the set on which an evaluation terminates successfully, and let \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\). A failed-evaluation response oracle has codomain \(\mathbb{R}\cup\{\bot\}\) and obeys \[\mathcal{O}(x)=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in D,\\ \bot,&x\in X\setminus D.\end{cases}\] The symbol \(\bot\) is not a numerical penalty and, without additional semantics, reveals only that no objective value was returned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A failed-evaluation oracle returns the objective where evaluation succeeds and a distinguished nonnumeric failure symbol elsewhere.
knowledge_statements.title: Failed Evaluation Responses

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 1. Introduction: Tools and Challenges in Derivative-Free and Blackbox Optimization p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cause Nonidentifiability from an Untyped Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical limitation of a bare nonnumeric failure response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every unsuccessful evaluation is reported only as \(\bot\), then \(\mathcal O(x)=\bot\) cannot distinguish domain violation, simulator breakdown, timeout, numerical overflow, or any other mechanism mapped to that symbol. In particular, it does not imply infeasibility unless that implication belongs to the declared oracle contract.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bare failure symbol identifies no particular cause and does not by itself certify infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: All failure mechanisms are encoded by the same symbol \(\bot\).
No auxiliary diagnostic or semantic contract is observed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O(x)=\bot\not\Rightarrow x\notin F\) without a declared implication from failure to nonmembership in the intended feasible set \(F\).
knowledge_statements.title: Cause Nonidentifiability from an Untyped Failure

children.title: Censored Objective Responses
children.top_down_role: Partially observed, clipped, thresholded, or otherwise censored objective information.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatible-value sets for upper and lower threshold censoring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For upper censoring at known threshold \(\tau\), a tagged response \((y,c)\) determines \[I(x)=\begin{cases}\{y\},&c=0,\\[\tau,\infty),&c=1.\end{cases}\] Thus a censored response states a lower bound and must not be interpreted as \(f(x)=\tau\). Lower censoring analogously gives the compatible set \(( -\infty,\tau]\) for a censored response.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A threshold-censored observation supplies a one-sided compatible-value set rather than equality at the clipping threshold.
assumptions_latex: The censoring direction and threshold are known.
The response distinguishes censored from uncensored numerical components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)\in I(x)\), and \(I(x)\) is a singleton exactly for an uncensored response.

notation.meaning: Values compatible with the response at \(x\)

knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Semantics of Threshold Censoring

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General deterministic representation covering clipping, thresholding, interval reports, and related coarsenings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\kappa:\mathbb R\to Y\) be a declared censoring map and let the oracle report \(r(x)=\kappa(f(x))\). The exact information in response \(r\) is the fiber \[I_r=\kappa^{-1}(\{r\}).\] Hence \(f(x)\in I_{r(x)}\); the value is point-identified exactly when this fiber is a singleton. Two objective values in the same fiber are observationally indistinguishable at that query.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic censored response identifies the set of objective values mapped to the reported symbol, not generally one exact value.
assumptions_latex: The censoring map \(\kappa\) and its response semantics are known.
No auxiliary observation refines the reported response.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)\in\kappa^{-1}(\{r(x)\})\), with exact identification if and only if that fiber is a singleton.
knowledge_statements.title: Fiber Representation of Deterministic Censoring

assumptions_latex: The objective is \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\), and \(\tau\in\mathbb{R}\) is a known upper-censoring threshold.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper censoring at a known threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) and fix a known threshold \(\tau\in\mathbb{R}\). An upper-censored objective oracle returns \[\mathcal{O}_\tau(x)=(y,c),\qquad y=\min\{f(x),\tau\},\qquad c=\mathbf{1}_{\{f(x)\geq\tau\}}.\] If \(c=0\), then \(y=f(x)<\tau\); if \(c=1\), the response certifies only \(f(x)\geq\tau\), while the exact value above the threshold remains unobserved. Lower censoring is defined analogously by reversing the inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An upper-censored response gives the exact objective below a threshold and only a threshold-exceedance signal at or above it.
knowledge_statements.title: Censored Objective Responses

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The upper-censoring formula is internally coherent, including its equality convention, but the selected direction and tagged response semantics have no cited source.

children.title: Hidden-Constraint Signals
children.top_down_role: Indirect feasibility information revealed through black-box evaluation outcomes.

assumptions_latex: There is an unknown evaluable region \(D\subseteq X\).
The objective value \(f(x)\) is available only when \(x\in D\).

notation.meaning: Unknown region where simulation and objective evaluation are valid

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary revelation of an unknown evaluability constraint.

source_refs.locator: 1.1. What Are Derivative-Free and Blackbox Optimization? p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq X\) be an unknown evaluable region and let \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\). A hidden-constraint signal is \(h(x)=\mathbf{1}_D(x)\), revealed only by attempting the query. The associated oracle returns \[\mathcal{O}(x)=\begin{cases}(1,f(x)),&x\in D,\\(0,\bot),&x\notin D.\end{cases}\] Thus a failed query certifies violation of the hidden evaluability constraint but supplies no objective value. No geometric description of \(D\) is assumed available to the algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hidden-constraint oracle reveals through attempted evaluation whether a point lies in an unknown evaluable region, returning no objective outside it.
knowledge_statements.title: Hidden-Constraint Signals

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1. What Are Derivative-Free and Blackbox Optimization? p. 3

children.title: Failure-Aware Oracle Semantics
children.top_down_role: Interpretations of exceptional oracle responses within derivative-free search.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semantic Contract Boundary for Failure Tags
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes observed status codes from conclusions not licensed by their declared semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a failure-aware oracle return tag \(q\) with declared meaning \(P_q(x)\). Observing \(q\) licenses \(P_q(x)\) and its logical consequences only. If infeasibility, an objective bound, or permanent failure does not follow from \(P_q(x)\), assigning that stronger meaning changes the oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A failure tag supports exactly its declared predicate; stronger interpretations require a stronger oracle contract.
assumptions_latex: Each tag has a fixed declared predicate \(P_q\).
No information beyond the response and its contract is available.
knowledge_statements.title: Semantic Contract Boundary for Failure Tags

assumptions_latex: Each query produces exactly one tagged outcome from a prescribed response space.
Every success tag carries a valid objective value; failure tags carry no value unless their semantics explicitly specify one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{O}:X\to(\{\mathrm{ok}\}\times\mathbb{R})\cup(\mathcal{F}\times\{\bot\})\) preserves the distinction between numerical values and failures.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tagged response space separating values from typed failures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a set of failure codes disjoint from \(\{\mathrm{ok}\}\). A failure-aware oracle is represented as \[\mathcal{O}:X\to\bigl(\{\mathrm{ok}\}\times\mathbb{R}\bigr)\cup\bigl(\mathcal{F}\times\{\bot\}\bigr).\] A response \((\mathrm{ok},y)\) asserts that \(y=f(x)\), or satisfies the separately declared numerical-error model. A response \((q,\bot)\), with \(q\in\mathcal{F}\), asserts exactly the predicate assigned to code \(q\) and is never interpreted as a real-valued penalty. Censored numerical bounds require a distinct tagged response type.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Failure-aware semantics use tagged outcomes so successful values, typed failures, and censored bounds cannot be confused with numerical penalties.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure-Aware Oracle Semantics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tagged-union representation fits failure-aware semantics, but it is an application-dependent formalization with no source supporting the response space or interpretation rules.

assumptions_latex: The query set \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) has an open neighborhood \(U\).
There exists \(L\geq0\) such that the gradient is \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|_2\leq L\|x-y\|_2\) for all \(x,y\in U\), although oracle access reveals only function values.

notation.meaning: Open neighborhood of the query set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean smoothness with value-only oracle access.

source_refs.locator: 6 Ensuring well poisedness and suitable derivative-free models p. 89
10 Trust-region methods based on derivative-free models p. 173

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and let \(U\supseteq X\) be open. A smooth black-box objective on \(X\) is a function \(f:U	o\mathbb{R}\) that is continuously differentiable and has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient for some \(L\geq0\): \[\|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|_2\leq L\|x-y\|_2\qquad	ext{for all }x,y\in U.\] The regularity concerns the latent function; black-box access supplies values of \(f\), not evaluations of \(
abla f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth black-box objective has a Lipschitz-continuous gradient on a neighborhood of the query set, while the oracle exposes only function values.
knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Black-Box Objectives

source_witnesses.locator: 6 Ensuring well poisedness and suitable derivative-free models p. 89

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between latent gradient regularity and the separate convexity classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb R\), let \(f(x)=-x^2\). Then \(f'(x)=-2x\) is \(2\)-Lipschitz, so \(f\) is smooth under value-only access, but \(f\) is strictly concave and therefore not convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A value-only objective can have a Lipschitz gradient while being nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.title: Smoothness Does Not Imply Convexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fundamental value inequality induced by a Lipschitz latent gradient despite value-only access.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex, and let \(f\in C^1(U)\) have an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. For every \(x,y\in U\), \[\left|f(y)-f(x)-\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}(y-x)\right|\le \frac L2\|y-x\|_2^2.\] In particular, \(f(y)\le f(x)+\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}(y-x)+\frac L2\|y-x\|_2^2\). This is a property of the latent objective and does not imply derivative access.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Lipschitz latent gradient gives quadratic Taylor-error and descent-lemma bounds even though the oracle exposes only values.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Taylor-Remainder Bound
Nonsmooth Black-Box Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Locally Lipschitz objectives accessed only through function values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open. A function \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is a nonsmooth black-box objective on \(X\) if an optimization method may query values \(f(x)\) for \(x\in X\), but receives no derivatives or analytic representation, and \(f\) is locally Lipschitz yet not continuously differentiable on all of \(X\). Equivalently, there exists \(\bar x\in X\) at which \(f\) is nondifferentiable or its derivative fails to be continuous, while every \(x\in X\) has a neighborhood on which \(|f(y)-f(z)|\leq L_x\|y-z\|\) for some finite \(L_x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsmooth black-box objective is locally Lipschitz and value-query accessible, but lacks globally continuous differentiability and supplies no derivative or analytic representation.
assumptions_latex: Function evaluations are exact and finite on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) belongs to the locally Lipschitz, derivative-unavailable black-box regime.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 6. Positive Bases and Nonsmooth Optimization p. 95

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 6. Positive Bases and Nonsmooth Optimization p. 95

assumptions_latex: For the necessary condition, \(\bar x\) is a local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized first-order necessary condition for the locally Lipschitz regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\bar x\) is a local minimizer of a function locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\), then \(0\in\partial_C f(\bar x)\). Moreover, \[0\in\partial_C f(\bar x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f^\circ(\bar x;d)\geq0\ \text{for every }d\in\mathbb R^n.\] Thus \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial_C f(\bar x))\leq\varepsilon\) is an approximate Clarke-stationarity certificate, not a certificate of local or global minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every locally Lipschitz local minimizer is Clarke stationary; distance of the Clarke subdifferential from zero measures stationarity, not optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Clarke Stationarity at Local Minima

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of classical smooth first-order tests on nonsmooth black-box objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=|x|\), zero is the unique global minimizer, but \(f'(0)\) does not exist. Its Clarke subdifferential is \(\partial_Cf(0)=[-1,1]\), so \(0\in\partial_Cf(0)\). A stopping rule requiring a classical gradient at every candidate can therefore be undefined at a valid nonsmooth solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The absolute-value objective is minimized where its classical derivative is undefined, while Clarke stationarity remains valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Classical Gradient Tests Can Be Undefined
knowledge_statements.title: Classical Gradient Tests Can Be Undefined

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
Limiting gradients are taken through differentiability points at which the displayed gradient sequence converges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^\circ(\bar x;d)=\max_{v\in\partial_C f(\bar x)}v^Td\quad\text{for every }d\in\mathbb R^n.
review_flags: Uses the standard finite-dimensional Clarke convention.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical generalized first-order representation for locally Lipschitz objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a locally Lipschitz function, the Clarke subdifferential is \[\partial_C f(\bar x)=\operatorname{conv}\left\{\lim_{k\to\infty}\nabla f(x_k):x_k\to\bar x,\ f\text{ is differentiable at }x_k,\ \nabla f(x_k)\text{ converges}\right\}.\] It is nonempty, compact, and convex, and its support function gives the Clarke directional derivative: \[f^\circ(\bar x;d)=\max_{v\in\partial_C f(\bar x)}v^Td.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke subdifferential is the convex hull of limiting nearby gradients and supports the Clarke generalized directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.title: Clarke First-Order Representation

children.title: Convex Zeroth-Order Objectives
children.top_down_role: Derivative-free optimization in the general convex objective regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Zeroth-Order Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex objectives under a function-value oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex. A function \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is a convex zeroth-order objective if, for every \(x,y\in C\) and \(t\in[0,1]\), \[f(tx+(1-t)y)\leq t f(x)+(1-t)f(y),\] and the algorithm accesses \(f\) only through a value oracle \(O_f(x)=f(x)\). The classification concerns the mathematical objective and information model: differentiability may hold, but gradients, subgradients, and a symbolic formula are not supplied by the oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective satisfies the convexity inequality on a convex domain, while the optimization algorithm obtains only queried function values.
assumptions_latex: The oracle returns finite exact values \(O_f(x)=f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is convex under a zeroth-order information model.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity Supplies Neither Smoothness nor Strong Curvature
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating general convex zeroth-order objectives from smooth and strongly convex regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The value-oracle objective \(f(x)=|x|\) on \(\mathbb R\) is convex, but it is not differentiable at \(0\) and is not \(\mu\)-strongly convex for any \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The absolute-value objective is convex but neither smooth nor strongly convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex, nonsmooth, and not strongly convex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Supplies Neither Smoothness nor Strong Curvature

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global Minima and Convex Minimizer Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic optimization geometry of a convex value-oracle objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be convex on a convex set \(C\). Every local minimizer relative to \(C\) is global. If the minimum is attained, \(\operatorname{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\) is convex, but it need not be a singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex objectives have no nonglobal local minima, and their attained minimizer sets are convex but may contain multiple points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ local minimum}\Rightarrow x^*\text{ global minimum},\qquad \operatorname{argmin}_C f\text{ is convex when nonempty}.
knowledge_statements.title: Global Minima and Convex Minimizer Sets

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-mixture formulation equivalent to repeated binary convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be convex on a convex set \(C\). For \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\in C\) and \(\alpha_i\ge0\) with \(\sum_i\alpha_i=1\), \[f\!\left(\sum_i\alpha_i x_i\right)\le\sum_i\alpha_i f(x_i).\] Conversely, the case \(m=2\) is the defining chord inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity is equivalently expressed by Jensen's inequality for every finite convex combination.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Jensen Inequality

children.title: Strongly Convex Zeroth-Order Objectives
children.top_down_role: Derivative-free optimization under uniform objective curvature.

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Convex Zeroth-Order Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong convexity under a function-value oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(\mu>0\). A function \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is a \(\mu\)-strongly convex zeroth-order objective if, for all \(x,y\in C\) and \(t\in[0,1]\), \[f(tx+(1-t)y)\leq t f(x)+(1-t)f(y)-\frac{\mu}{2}t(1-t)\|x-y\|^2,\] while an algorithm accesses \(f\) only through value queries \(O_f(x)=f(x)\). Strong convexity implies convexity and, when a minimizer exists, makes it unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A value-oracle objective is strongly convex when its chord inequality contains a positive quadratic curvature term; any attained minimizer is then unique.
assumptions_latex: The oracle returns finite exact values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex and has at most one minimizer on \(C\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-error-to-distance implication intrinsic to an attained strongly convex minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be \(\mu\)-strongly convex on a convex set \(C\), with \(\mu>0\), and suppose \(x^*\in\operatorname{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\). Then for every \(x\in C\), \[f(x)-f(x^*)\ge\frac\mu2\|x-x^*\|_2^2.\] Consequently, \(f(x)-f(x^*)\le\varepsilon\) implies \(\|x-x^*\|_2\le\sqrt{2\varepsilon/\mu}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity converts objective suboptimality into a quantitative distance bound from the unique minimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic-Growth Error Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Convexity Does Not Guarantee Attainment on an Open Domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence boundary complementing uniqueness of any attained minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On the open convex domain \(C=(0,1)\), the function \(f(x)=x^2\) is \(2\)-strongly convex, but \(\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=0\) is not attained. Thus strong convexity guarantees at most one minimizer, not existence, without an additional attainment condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strongly convex objective can fail to attain its infimum on a nonclosed domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is strongly convex on }C\text{ but }\operatorname{argmin}_C f=\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Convexity Does Not Guarantee Attainment on an Open Domain

children.title: Curvature-Regime Transitions
children.top_down_role: Structural distinctions between general convexity plus stronger curvature regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature-Regime Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic regularization moves zeroth-order objectives between convexity regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex. For any \(\lambda>0\) and fixed \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(f_\lambda(x)=f(x)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\|x-x_0\|^2\). Then \(f_\lambda\) is \(\lambda\)-strongly convex on \(C\). Conversely, if \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex, then \(x\mapsto f(x)-\frac{\mu}{2}\|x-x_0\|^2\) is convex. These transitions preserve zeroth-order accessibility because each regularized value is computable from one query of \(f\) and known arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding known positive quadratic curvature turns a convex value-oracle objective into a strongly convex one; subtracting its strong-convexity curvature recovers convexity.
assumptions_latex: The quadratic term is exactly computable.
Function values of \(f\) are available through queries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_\lambda\) is \(\lambda\)-strongly convex, and removal of a valid quadratic modulus leaves a convex function.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp limit on removing a claimed quadratic curvature modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\frac\mu2x^2\) on \(\mathbb R\), with \(\mu>0\). For \(\lambda>\mu\), \[f(x)-\frac\lambda2x^2=-\frac{\lambda-\mu}{2}x^2\] is strictly concave. Thus subtracting a quadratic is guaranteed to preserve convexity only when its modulus does not exceed a valid strong-convexity modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Removing more quadratic curvature than is certified can turn a strongly convex objective into a concave one.
knowledge_statements.title: Over-Subtraction Destroys Convexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive and scaling rules for moving among convexity moduli while preserving value-oracle accessibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_j:C\to\mathbb R\) be \(\mu_j\)-strongly convex on a convex set \(C\), where \(\mu_j\ge0\), and let \(a_j\ge0\). Then \(F=\sum_j a_jf_j\) is \((\sum_j a_j\mu_j)\)-strongly convex. Thus an explicitly evaluable \(\lambda\)-strongly convex regularizer raises the certified modulus by \(\lambda\), while multiplication by \(a>0\) scales the modulus by \(a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative sums add certified curvature moduli, and positive scaling scales the modulus; known regularizers preserve value-only evaluation.

notation.meaning: certified curvature modulus of component j

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature Modulus Arithmetic
Nonconvex Zeroth-Order Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of convexity under a function-value information model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex. A function \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is a nonconvex zeroth-order objective if an algorithm accesses it only through value queries \(O_f(x)=f(x)\), and the convexity inequality fails: there exist \(x,y\in C\) and \(t\in(0,1)\) such that \[f(tx+(1-t)y)>t f(x)+(1-t)f(y).\] This classification does not require nonsmoothness; a smooth function may be nonconvex while remaining zeroth-order because the oracle reveals no derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zeroth-order objective is nonconvex when some chord violates the convexity inequality and the algorithm receives only function values.
assumptions_latex: The value oracle is defined throughout \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) lies outside the convex zeroth-order class.

assumptions_latex: Derivative notation is used to classify the example; the optimization oracle may still expose values only.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f'(0)=0,\qquad 0\notin\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R}f(x),\qquad 0\text{ is not a local minimizer}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of first-order stationarity as an optimality certificate in a smooth nonconvex value-oracle class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=(x^2-1)^2\) on \(\mathbb R\), \(f'(0)=0\), but \(f(0)=1\) whereas \(f(-1)=f(1)=0\). Thus zero is a stationary strict local maximum rather than a local or global minimizer. Consequently, even for a smooth nonconvex zeroth-order objective, \(\|\nabla f(x)\|=0\) does not certify optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth nonconvex value-oracle objective can have a stationary point that is not a minimizer, so stationarity alone does not certify optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Stationarity Does Not Certify Optimality

children.title: Discontinuous Objective Landscapes
children.top_down_role: Derivative-free search over objectives containing abrupt value changes.

assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\) is an accumulation point of \(X\).
All displayed objective values and side traces are finite.
For the jump definition, a continuous local separator \(\phi\) and both side traces exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is discontinuous at \(\bar x\); when \(\ell_+\neq\ell_-\), the interface has jump magnitude \(|\ell_+-\ell_-|\).

notation.meaning: point of discontinuity or interface point
persistent value separation in the discontinuity criterion

review_flags: The jump clause uses an explicit two-sided trace convention and does not label an arbitrary sequential discontinuity as a jump.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative-topology discontinuity and a precise two-sided interface-jump convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite-valued objective \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is discontinuous at an accumulation point \(\bar x\in X\) when there is \(\varepsilon>0\) such that, for every \(\delta>0\), some \(x\in X\) satisfies \(\|x-\bar x\|<\delta\) and \(|f(x)-f(\bar x)|\geq\varepsilon\). For a two-sided jump, additionally suppose a continuous function \(\phi\) locally separates the domain into \(X_+=\{x:\phi(x)>0\}\) and \(X_-=\{x:\phi(x)<0\}\), with \(\phi(\bar x)=0\), and that the relative side limits \[\ell_+=\lim_{x\to\bar x,\ x\in X_+}f(x),\qquad \ell_-=\lim_{x\to\bar x,\ x\in X_-}f(x)\] exist. The interface has a jump at \(\bar x\) precisely when \(\ell_+\neq\ell_-\), with jump magnitude \(|\ell_+-\ell_-|\); the assigned value \(f(\bar x)\) need not equal either trace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discontinuity means values remain separated from the value at an arbitrarily close limit point; a two-sided jump requires unequal traces across a specified local interface.
knowledge_statements.title: Discontinuities and Two-Sided Jumps
Discontinuous Objective Landscapes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Black-box landscapes having at least one finite jump or other discontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\). The objective landscape is discontinuous if there exist \(\bar x\in X\), a sequence \((x_k)\subset X\) with \(x_k\to\bar x\), and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(|f(x_k)-f(\bar x)|\geq\varepsilon\) for every \(k\). If, additionally, the limit \(\ell=\lim_{k\to\infty}f(x_k)\) exists and \(\ell\neq f(\bar x)\), the sequence exposes a jump of magnitude \(|\ell-f(\bar x)|\). A value oracle can reveal sampled values but does not identify unsampled discontinuity locations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A landscape is discontinuous when values along a convergent sequence remain separated from the value at its limit; a distinct limiting value constitutes a jump.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\) is an accumulation point of \(X\).
All displayed function values are finite.

children.title: Piecewise-Smooth Objective Regions
children.top_down_role: Locally regular objective regions separated by structural interfaces.

assumptions_latex: The partition contains finitely many pieces.
Each piece is contained in the closure of its relative interior.
Each regional branch is defined on an open neighborhood of its assigned piece.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ has a finite piecewise-}C^p\text{ regional representation on }X.

notation.meaning: assigned regional pieces forming a partition of the domain
relative interior of regional piece i
smooth branch assigned to region i

review_flags: This record states an explicit finite-partition convention; other uses of piecewise smoothness may allow locally finite partitions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite regional partition with smooth branch extensions and explicitly assigned interface values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(p\in\mathbb N_0\). A finite piecewise-\(C^p\) regional representation of \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) consists of pairwise disjoint sets \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\) with \(X=\bigcup_{i=1}^mA_i\), such that \(A_i\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{relint}_X A_i}\), together with open sets \(U_i\supseteq A_i\) and functions \(f_i\in C^p(U_i)\) satisfying \(f=f_i\) on \(A_i\). Each interface point is assigned to exactly one \(A_i\), so its objective value is defined, while branches incident through other regional closures need not have the same trace or derivatives there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite piecewise-smooth objective is defined by a finite partition whose assigned values agree with smooth branch extensions; incident branches may disagree at interfaces.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Piecewise-Smooth Regional Representation

assumptions_latex: Only finitely many regional pieces are incident at \(\bar x\).
Each incident branch has a finite continuous trace at \(\bar x\).
The incident regional closures cover a relative neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is continuous at }\bar x\iff \tau_i=f(\bar x)\text{ for every incident }i.

notation.meaning: trace of incident regional branch i at the interface

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value-trace condition for continuity and the boundary between continuous piecewise smoothness and global differentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At an interface point \(\bar x\), suppose the finitely many incident regional branches have continuous traces \(\tau_i=\lim_{x\to\bar x,\ x\in R_i}f_i(x)\), and their closures cover a relative neighborhood of \(\bar x\). Then \(f\) is continuous at \(\bar x\) if and only if every incident trace equals the assigned interface value \(f(\bar x)\). Equality of values does not imply differentiability: \(f(x)=|x|\) has branches \(-x\) and \(x\) whose traces agree at zero, but their derivative traces are \(-1\) and \(1\), so \(f\) is not differentiable there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuity at an interface requires every incident branch trace to equal the assigned value, but matching values alone need not make the objective differentiable.
knowledge_statements.title: Trace Compatibility Across Interfaces
Piecewise-Smooth Objective Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite smooth partition with potentially nonsmooth or discontinuous interfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). A function \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) has piecewise-\(C^p\) objective regions if there are finitely many pairwise disjoint open sets \(R_1,\ldots,R_m\) such that \(X\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^m\overline{R_i}\), and for each \(i\) there is an open neighborhood \(U_i\supseteq R_i\) and a function \(f_i\in C^p(U_i)\) satisfying \(f(x)=f_i(x)\) for every \(x\in R_i\). No agreement of the traces of \(f_i\) and \(f_j\) is required on interfaces \(\overline{R_i}\cap\overline{R_j}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A piecewise-smooth objective equals a smooth branch on each region of a finite partition, while adjacent branch values or derivatives may disagree at interfaces.
assumptions_latex: The number of regions \(m\) is finite.
Each branch is defined on a neighborhood of its region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is piecewise \(C^p\) on the regional partition.

children.title: Interface-Induced Search Behavior
children.top_down_role: Search behavior near boundaries between objective pieces.

assumptions_latex: The two finite side traces \(\ell_+\) and \(\ell_-\) exist at \(\bar x\).
The samples \(x_h^+\) and \(x_h^-\) approach \(\bar x\) from the positive and negative sides and have separation tending to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |d_h|\to\infty;\qquad J<0\Rightarrow f(x_h^+)\leq f(x_h^-)-\rho(h)\text{ eventually};\qquad J>0\Rightarrow f(x_h^+)>f(x_h^-)\text{ eventually}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General cross-interface value, apparent-slope, and acceptance asymptotics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_h^+\) and \(x_h^-\) approach an interface point \(\bar x\) from opposite sides, with finite side traces \(\ell_+\) and \(\ell_-\), and let \(J=\ell_+-\ell_-\neq0\). Then \[f(x_h^+)-f(x_h^-)=J+o(1).\] If \(\|x_h^+-x_h^-\|\to0\), the normalized apparent slope \[d_h=\frac{f(x_h^+)-f(x_h^-)}{\|x_h^+-x_h^-\|}\] satisfies \(|d_h|\to\infty\). Moreover, for every \(\rho(h)>0\) with \(\rho(h)\to0\), a move from \(x_h^-\) to \(x_h^+\) eventually satisfies \(f(x_h^+)\leq f(x_h^-)-\rho(h)\) when \(J<0\), and fails strict descent when \(J>0\). Thus both derivative surrogates and sufficiently local acceptance decisions are governed by the jump rather than either regional derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Samples approaching opposite sides of a jump retain a fixed value gap, so normalized apparent slopes diverge and local acceptance is determined by the jump's sign.
knowledge_statements.title: Jump-Dominated Cross-Interface Sampling
Interface-Induced Search Behavior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A stencil crossing a jump produces scale-dependent apparent slopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(f(x)=g_-(x)\) for \(x<0\) and \(f(x)=g_+(x)\) for \(x\geq0\), where \(g_-\) and \(g_+\) are continuously differentiable near zero and \(J=g_+(0)-g_-(0)\neq0\). For \(h>0\), the centered zeroth-order slope is \[d_h=\frac{f(h)-f(-h)}{2h}=\frac{J}{2h}+\frac{g_+'(0)+g_-'(0)}{2}+o(1).\] Hence \(|d_h|\to\infty\) as \(h\downarrow0\). A shrinking stencil that straddles the interface is therefore governed by the jump rather than either regional derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a shrinking value-difference stencil crosses a jump, its apparent slope grows like the jump divided by the stencil width and does not approximate either regional derivative.
assumptions_latex: \(g_-\) and \(g_+\) are continuously differentiable near zero.
The stencil uses exact values at \(-h\) and \(h\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|d_h|\to\infty\) as \(h\downarrow0\), so the stencil is interface-dominated.

children.title: Jump-Driven Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Reliability limits caused by objective jumps or unresolved discontinuity structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Jump-Driven Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Jumps invalidate vanishing local model-error assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=0\) for \(x<0\) and \(f(x)=1\) for \(x\geq0\). For every \(\Delta>0\), the interval \([-\Delta,\Delta]\) contains points whose objective values differ by one. Consequently, no affine function \(m_\Delta\) with slopes uniformly bounded as \(\Delta\downarrow0\) can satisfy \[\sup_{|x|\leq\Delta}|f(x)-m_\Delta(x)|\leq\kappa\Delta^2\] for a fixed finite \(\kappa\). Thus any derivative-free convergence result requiring uniformly vanishing smooth local-model error ceases to apply when trust regions repeatedly straddle a nonzero jump.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed jump cannot be approximated on shrinking two-sided neighborhoods with quadratic uniform error by affine models of bounded slope, breaking smooth model-based convergence assumptions.
assumptions_latex: Neighborhoods straddle the jump at zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No fixed \(\kappa<\infty\) yields uniform error \(O(\Delta^2)\) across the jump.

notation.meaning: affine local model at radius Delta

notation.meaning: closed ball containing the hidden lower objective region

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-query indistinguishability caused by an unsampled region behind a jump interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Run a deterministic finite value-query algorithm on the zero objective over a nonempty open set \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and let \(S\subset X\) be its finite query set. There are \(x_*\in X\) and \(r>0\) such that \(\overline B(x_*,r)\subset X\) and \(\overline B(x_*,r)\cap S=\varnothing\). The objectives \[f_0(x)=0,\qquad f_1(x)=\begin{cases}-1,&x\in B(x_*,r),\\0,&x\in X\setminus B(x_*,r),\end{cases}\] give the same value at every query and hence the same finite transcript, but \(\inf_Xf_0=0\) and \(\inf_Xf_1=-1\). Therefore finite value samples cannot certify global objective error below one over an unrestricted class permitting unsampled jump interfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hidden lower-valued region bounded by an unsampled jump can produce the same finite query transcript as a constant objective while changing the global optimum by one.
knowledge_statements.title: Unsampled Jump Indistinguishability
Moderate-Cost Local Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Budget-aware coordinate polling for moderately costly evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\in X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), initial step \(\Delta_0>0\), evaluation budget \(B\), contraction \(\theta\in(0,1)\), and expansion \(\gamma\geq1\), evaluate \(f(x_0)\). At iteration \(k\), query feasible points in \(P_k=\{x_k\pm\Delta_k e_i:i=1,\ldots,n\}\) until a point \(y\) with \(f(y)<f(x_k)\) is found or the poll is exhausted. On success set \(x_{k+1}=y\) and \(\Delta_{k+1}=\gamma\Delta_k\); otherwise set \(x_{k+1}=x_k\) and \(\Delta_{k+1}=\theta\Delta_k\). Stop when the budget is exhausted or \(\Delta_k\leq\Delta_{\min}\), and return the best evaluated feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coordinate polling accepts an improving trial, expands or retains the search scale after success, contracts it after failure, and returns the best point within budget.
assumptions_latex: Function values can be compared reliably.
Feasibility of each trial point is testable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is the feasible evaluated point with smallest observed objective value before stopping.

children.title: Expensive Simulation Optimization
children.top_down_role: Derivative-free optimization driven by computationally expensive simulator evaluations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable-cost resource interface for computationally expensive simulator calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An expensive-simulation policy selects simulator inputs sequentially. If call \(i\) has charged cost \(c(x_i,h_{i-1})>0\), a completed history is budget feasible when \(\sum_{i=1}^{K}c(x_i,h_{i-1})\leq B\), and another call is admitted only when its declared charge preserves this inequality. Equal call costs reduce this model to a fixed evaluation count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite charged-cost budget is allocated adaptively across simulator calls; equal costs recover a fixed call budget.

notation.meaning: charged cost of simulating x after history h

knowledge_statements.title: Charged-Cost Simulation Budget

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interpolation Is Not an Optimality Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifiability boundary for surrogate claims from finite simulator data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subsetneq X\) be finite and let a surrogate \(s\) interpolate the observations on \(D\). Without a function class or certified error envelope, objectives can agree with \(s\) on \(D\) while having arbitrarily different values and minimizers on \(X\setminus D\). Zero interpolation error on \(D\) therefore certifies neither global surrogate accuracy nor optimality of a surrogate minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact fit to finite simulator data gives no unsampled accuracy or global-optimality guarantee by itself.
assumptions_latex: No regularity class or certified error envelope is imposed away from \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Interpolation on \(D\) alone cannot certify global accuracy or optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Interpolation Is Not an Optimality Certificate
Expensive Simulation Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential surrogate search under a strict simulation budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a compact feasible set \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), simulation budget \(B\), and initial design \(D_0=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\), evaluate \(f\) on \(D_0\). For \(k=m,\ldots,B-1\), fit a surrogate \(s_k\) to all pairs \((x_i,f(x_i))\), choose an unevaluated point \[x_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X} A_k(x;s_k,D_k),\] evaluate the simulation once at \(x_{k+1}\), and set \(D_{k+1}=D_k\cup\{x_{k+1}\}\). The acquisition \(A_k\) must encode the chosen exploitation-exploration rule. After exactly \(B\) evaluations, return an evaluated point attaining the smallest observed value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expensive-simulation optimizer repeatedly fits a surrogate, selects one new point through an acquisition rule, evaluates it, and returns the best observation within budget.
assumptions_latex: Each simulation run consumes one budget unit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method returns \(x_j\in D_B\) satisfying \(f(x_j)=\min_{x_i\in D_B}f(x_i)\).

children.title: Physical Experiment Optimization
children.top_down_role: Derivative-free optimization driven by costly physical or laboratory trials.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic adaptive physical-trial interface with unambiguous run accounting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a run budget \(B\in\mathbb{N}\), a policy chooses \(x_{k+1}\in X_{\mathrm{safe}}\) from the completed history \(H_k=\{(x_i,Y_i):1\leq i\leq k\}\), where repeated designs are permitted and every execution consumes one run. After at most \(B\) runs it returns a recommendation computed from \(H_K\), \(K\leq B\), using the declared estimator of \(\rho(P_x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A physical-experiment optimizer adaptively allocates a finite run budget, may replicate designs, and returns a recommendation based only on completed trials.
assumptions_latex: Every physical execution consumes one run.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The completed run count satisfies \(K\leq B\), and the output depends only on \(H_K\).

notation.meaning: completed physical-trial history after k runs

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Run Physical Experiment Policy

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pre-execution safety requirement for irreversible physical trials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When inadmissible physical actions are forbidden, a design may be dispatched only after certifying \(x_k\in X_{\mathrm{safe}}\). Rejecting an unsafe response afterward is not a feasibility mechanism because the physical action has already occurred.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Safety-critical physical designs must be certified before execution.
assumptions_latex: Executing outside \(X_{\mathrm{safe}}\) is forbidden or may cause irreversible harm.
Membership in \(X_{\mathrm{safe}}\) is checkable before execution.
knowledge_statements.title: Pre-Run Physical Feasibility

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Statistical objective underlying costly physical trials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An admissible physical design \(x\in X_{\mathrm{safe}}\) induces a response distribution \(P_x\). The objective must declare a functional \(f(x):=\rho(P_x)\), such as a mean, quantile, failure probability, or mean-variance criterion. Individual observations estimate \(f(x)\); they are not themselves the objective unless \(P_x\) is degenerate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Physical optimization must declare which statistic or risk functional of the response distribution is optimized.
assumptions_latex: Each admissible design induces a response distribution \(P_x\).
The functional \(\rho\) is declared before designs are compared.
knowledge_statements.title: Physical-Response Optimization Objective

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifiability failure from uncontrolled temporal drift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(Y(x,t)=f(x)+d(t)+\varepsilon\). If each design is tested only at its own execution time and the schedule confounds design with time, distinct pairs \((f,d)\) can produce the same observations while inducing different rankings of \(f\). Randomization, blocking, calibration, replication across times, or a drift model is then required for identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When design and execution time are confounded, the same data can support different physical-design rankings.
assumptions_latex: Responses may depend on design and execution time.
The schedule does not separate design effects from time effects.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The design objective is not identifiable without additional design or modeling assumptions.
knowledge_statements.title: Drift-Confounding Boundary
Physical Experiment Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Replicated derivative-free search for costly noisy physical trials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a feasible experimental domain \(X\), total run budget \(B\), initial design \(D_0\), and replication rule \(r_k(x)\geq1\), perform the prescribed physical runs and record responses \(Y(x,j)\). At stage \(k\), compute \(\bar Y_k(x)=r_k(x)^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{r_k(x)}Y(x,j)\), use the accumulated data to select a feasible unevaluated or replicated design \(x_{k+1}\), and run the experiment there without exceeding \(B\). Selection may use a direct-search or surrogate criterion fixed in advance. Stop at budget exhaustion and return an evaluated design minimizing the reported sample mean, together with its replication count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A physical-experiment optimizer allocates a finite run budget across designs and replications, selects trials from accumulated responses, and reports the evaluated design with best sample mean.
assumptions_latex: Every proposed physical design is feasibility-checked before execution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(\hat x\) satisfies \(\bar Y(\hat x)=\min_{x\in D_B}\bar Y(x)\) over evaluated designs.
