knowledge_statements.statement_title: Marginal Accuracy Does Not Ensure Pathwise Reliability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence boundary separating marginal from conditional model-accuracy regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\alpha)\), where \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), and set \(E_k=\{Z=1\}\) for every \(k\). Then \(\mathbb P(E_k)=\alpha\) for every \(k\), but \(\mathbb P(E_k\text{ never occurs})=1-\alpha>0\). Thus uniform marginal bounds do not imply recurrent model accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform marginal accuracy probabilities are inadequate when accuracy events can be perfectly dependent across iterations.

notation.meaning: shared Bernoulli variable producing perfect temporal dependence

knowledge_statements.title: Marginal Accuracy Does Not Ensure Pathwise Reliability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Almost-sure recurrence supplied by a uniform conditional model-accuracy probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E_k\in\mathcal F_k\) and suppose \(\mathbb P(E_k\mid\mathcal F_{k-1})\geq\alpha>0\) almost surely for every \(k\). Then, for deterministic \(N\) and \(m\geq1\), \[\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcap_{k=N}^{N+m-1}E_k^c\mid\mathcal F_{N-1}\right)\leq(1-\alpha)^m\quad\text{a.s.}\] Consequently, \(\mathbb P(E_k\text{ infinitely often})=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform positive conditional accuracy probability ensures infinitely many accurate models without requiring independence.
knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Accuracy Recurrence
Probabilistic Model-Accuracy Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional probability conditions ensuring sufficiently frequent accurate stochastic trust-region models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E_k\) denote the event that the iteration-\(k\) random model satisfies the required deterministic accuracy bounds on its trust region, and let \(\mathcal F_{k-1}\) contain all information preceding model construction. A uniform probabilistic accuracy regime holds when there exists \(\alpha\in(0,1]\) such that
\[
\mathbb P(E_k\mid\mathcal F_{k-1})\geq\alpha\quad\text{almost surely for every }k.
\]
A vanishing-failure regime holds when numbers \(q_k\in[0,1]\) satisfy \(\mathbb P(E_k^c\mid\mathcal F_{k-1})\leq q_k\) almost surely and \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}q_k<\infty\). The selected convergence theorem determines which regime and threshold are sufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Model accuracy may be guaranteed uniformly with conditional probability α, or by summable conditional failure probabilities that force only finitely many failures.
assumptions_latex: Each \(E_k\) is measurable after constructing the iteration-\(k\) model.
Conditional probabilities are defined almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the vanishing-failure regime, \(\mathbb P(E_k^c\text{ infinitely often})=0\); the uniform regime supplies a per-iteration conditional accuracy lower bound.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the leaf, and the summable-failure conclusion is mathematically standard, but no source establishes these as the relevant stochastic-DFO model-accuracy regimes or identifies the theorem-specific uniform probability threshold.

children.title: Sampling-Growth Schedules
children.top_down_role: Ways evaluation effort scales as stochastic optimization progresses.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Replication bound for simultaneously accurate estimates at all points used in one iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose iteration \(k\) estimates \(f\) at \(q_k\) points, with each estimate averaging \(m_k\) conditionally independent, centered, \(\sigma\)-sub-Gaussian observations. If \[m_k\geq\frac{2\sigma^2}{t_k^2}\log\!\left(\frac{2q_k}{p_k}\right),\] then \[\mathbb P\!\left(\max_{1\leq j\leq q_k}|\widehat f_{k,j}-f_{k,j}|>t_k\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}\right)\leq p_k.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A logarithmic factor in the number of evaluated points makes all iteration estimates simultaneously accurate.
assumptions_latex: Each point estimate averages m_k conditionally independent observations.

notation.meaning: number of points estimated at iteration k

knowledge_statements.title: Simultaneous Sub-Gaussian Sampling Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Replication schedule based only on conditional unbiasedness and a variance bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If each point estimate averages \(m_k\) conditionally independent observations having conditional mean \(f_{k,j}\) and conditional variance at most \(v\), then \[m_k\geq\frac{q_kv}{p_kt_k^2}\] ensures \[\mathbb P\!\left(\max_{1\leq j\leq q_k}|\widehat f_{k,j}-f_{k,j}|>t_k\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}\right)\leq p_k.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With only finite variance, simultaneous accuracy requires polynomial rather than logarithmic dependence on the inverse failure budget.
assumptions_latex: Samples within each point estimate are conditionally independent.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Variance Sampling Schedule
Sampling-Growth Schedules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Schedules coupling replication counts to iteration-dependent accuracy targets in stochastic DFO.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y(x,\xi)\) be an unbiased observation of \(f(x)\), and let \(\widehat f_k(x)=m_k^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{m_k}Y(x,\xi_{k,i})\). Given tolerances \(t_k>0\) and failure budgets \(p_k\in(0,1)\), a sampling-growth schedule is a sequence of integers \(m_k\geq 1\) chosen so that \(\mathbb P(|\widehat f_k(x)-f(x)|>t_k\mid\mathcal F_{k-1})\leq p_k\) at every point compared during iteration \(k\). For conditionally \(\sigma\)-sub-Gaussian noise, it suffices to take \[m_k\geq \frac{2\sigma^2}{t_k^2}\log\!\left(\frac{2}{p_k}\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sampling-growth schedule increases replication counts enough to meet prescribed estimation tolerances and conditional failure probabilities at every DFO comparison.
assumptions_latex: The centered observation noise is conditionally \(\sigma\)-sub-Gaussian.
Samples used in each average are conditionally independent.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and sub-Gaussian sample-size bound are mathematically plausible and fit the leaf, but no cited source or inspectable locator supports them.

children.title: Convergence Regimes by Sampling Rate
children.top_down_role: Qualitative convergence behavior associated with different sampling-growth rates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer of a deterministic finite-horizon guarantee under controlled inaccurate-iteration probabilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a deterministic guarantee \(G_K\) holds whenever \(E_0,\ldots,E_K\) all occur. If \(\mathbb P(E_k^c\mid\mathcal F_{k-1})\leq r_k\) almost surely, then \[\mathbb P(G_K)\geq1-\sum_{k=0}^{K}r_k.\] Hence \(\sum_{k=0}^{K}r_k\leq\delta\) transfers \(G_K\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic finite-horizon guarantee transfers with high probability when the cumulative inaccurate-iteration budget is small.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Horizon Convergence Transfer
Convergence Regimes by Sampling Rate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Almost-sure reliability regimes induced by replication growth under sub-Gaussian observation noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose iteration \(k\) makes at most \(q_k\) sample-mean comparisons, each with tolerance \(t_k\), replication count \(m_k\), and conditionally \(\sigma\)-sub-Gaussian noise. Define \(r_k=2q_k\exp(-m_kt_k^2/(2\sigma^2))\). If \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}r_k<\infty\), then, with probability one, only finitely many iterations contain an estimation error exceeding \(t_k\). Thus a convergent deterministic DFO argument that tolerates finitely many inaccurate iterations transfers to the stochastic implementation. A sufficient logarithmic-growth regime is \(m_kt_k^2\geq 2\sigma^2(1+\varepsilon)\log k\) when \(q_k\) is uniformly bounded and \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Summable comparison-error probabilities imply that only finitely many inaccurate stochastic DFO iterations occur almost surely.
assumptions_latex: Each iteration uses at most \(q_k\) conditionally independent sample means.
The deterministic convergence argument is unchanged after finitely many inaccurate iterations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_k r_k<\infty\Longrightarrow \mathbb P(r_k\text{-controlled estimation failures occur infinitely often})=0\).

notation.meaning: number of comparisons at iteration k
union-bound probability of an inaccurate iteration

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The union-bound and Borel–Cantelli regime is plausible, but the stochastic-to-deterministic convergence transfer is method-dependent and requires an authoritative source with precise hypotheses.

children.title: Insufficient-Growth Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Regimes where sampling effort cannot support the intended accuracy.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Divergent Error Budgets Need Not Cause Recurrent Errors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence boundary for converse Borel–Cantelli reasoning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) satisfy \(\mathbb P(A)=p\in(0,1)\), and define \(E_k=A\) for every \(k\). Then \(\sum_k\mathbb P(E_k)=\infty\), but \(\mathbb P(E_k\text{ infinitely often})=p\), not one. Thus divergence of error probabilities alone does not establish almost-sure recurrence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A divergent sum of error probabilities does not force infinitely many errors when the events are dependent.

notation.meaning: single event shared by all iterations

knowledge_statements.title: Divergent Error Budgets Need Not Cause Recurrent Errors
Insufficient-Growth Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp summability obstruction for repeated noisy comparisons with shrinking objective gaps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider independent Gaussian comparison errors \(D_k\sim N(d_k,2\sigma^2/m_k)\), where the true difference satisfies \(d_k>0\), so choosing the second point when \(D_k<0\) is erroneous. The error probability is \(p_k=\Phi(-d_k\sqrt{m_k}/(\sqrt{2}\sigma))\). If \(d_k\sqrt{m_k}/\sigma\) is bounded, then \(p_k\) is bounded below by a positive constant; independence therefore implies that erroneous selections occur infinitely often almost surely. More generally, when \(\sum_k p_k=\infty\), independent selection errors occur infinitely often, so eventual comparison reliability cannot be certified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If sample growth does not dominate the shrinking comparison gap, selection errors retain positive probability and recur infinitely often.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Gaussian error probability and independent-event failure boundary are mathematically consistent and appropriately classified, but they have no inspectable citation.

children.title: False Improvement Events
children.top_down_role: Noisy comparisons that incorrectly indicate objective improvement.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of replication to remove false improvements when persistent bias strictly reverses a comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\widehat f_m(x)\to f(x)+\beta_x\) and \(\widehat f_m(y)\to f(y)+\beta_y\) almost surely. If \(f(y)-f(x)+a>0\) but \[f(y)+\beta_y<f(x)+\beta_x-a,\] then \(\mathbb P(\widehat f_m(y)\leq\widehat f_m(x)-a)\to1\). Thus replication cannot control false improvements caused by a strictly comparison-reversing differential bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replication removes variance but not a persistent bias that strictly reverses the incumbent–trial comparison.
knowledge_statements.title: Persistent Differential Bias Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tail bound for erroneous acceptance under independent sub-Gaussian estimation errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write \(\widehat f_k(x_k)=f(x_k)+\varepsilon_{x,k}\) and \(\widehat f_k(y_k)=f(y_k)+\varepsilon_{y,k}\). For a truly rejected trial let \(b_k=f(y_k)-f(x_k)+a_k>0\). If the errors are conditionally independent, centered, and sub-Gaussian with variance proxies \(\sigma^2/m_{x,k}\) and \(\sigma^2/m_{y,k}\), then \[F_k=\{\varepsilon_{y,k}-\varepsilon_{x,k}\leq-b_k\}\] and \[\mathbb P(F_k\mid\mathcal F_{k-1})\leq\exp\!\left[-\frac{b_k^2}{2\sigma^2(m_{x,k}^{-1}+m_{y,k}^{-1})}\right].\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: False acceptance becomes exponentially unlikely when replication makes the rejection gap large relative to comparison noise.
assumptions_latex: The two estimation errors are conditionally independent, centered, and sub-Gaussian with the stated proxies.

notation.meaning: amount by which the true trial fails the acceptance margin

knowledge_statements.title: Gap-Dependent False-Improvement Probability
False Improvement Events
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Erroneous acceptance of a trial point caused by noisy objective estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(k\), let \(x_k\) be the incumbent, \(y_k\) a trial point, and \(a_k\geq0\) the required improvement margin. With estimates \(\widehat f_k(x_k)\) and \(\widehat f_k(y_k)\), the false-improvement event is \[F_k=\{\widehat f_k(y_k)\leq \widehat f_k(x_k)-a_k\}\cap\{f(y_k)>f(x_k)-a_k\}.\] Thus the observed comparison passes the acceptance test although the corresponding exact-function comparison fails it. For \(a_k=0\), this specializes to accepting a point that appears no worse while its true objective value is strictly worse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A false improvement occurs when noisy estimates accept a trial point whose true objective decrease fails the required margin.
assumptions_latex: Both estimates use the same minimization convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_k\) is exactly the intersection of observed acceptance and true rejection.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The event correctly represents observed acceptance intersected with exact rejection and fits a definition container, but no source is cited.

children.title: Trial-Point Misselection
children.top_down_role: Selection of an inferior trial point because of evaluation uncertainty.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pairwise Gap Bound for Trial Misselection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-set misselection bound for independent sub-Gaussian sample means.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(j^*\) be the unique true minimizer and \(g_j=f(y_j)-f(y_{j^*})>0\) for \(j\ne j^*\). Suppose \(\widehat f_j\) has centered sub-Gaussian error with variance proxy \(\sigma^2/m_j\), conditionally independently across candidates. Selection by the smallest estimate satisfies \[\mathbb P(M\mid\mathcal F)\leq\sum_{j\ne j^*}\exp\!\left[-\frac{g_j^2}{2\sigma^2(m_j^{-1}+m_{j^*}^{-1})}\right].\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Misselection is bounded by the sum of pairwise probabilities that an inferior trial appears better than the true best trial.
assumptions_latex: j^*\text{ is the unique true minimizer}.
Candidate estimation errors are conditionally independent, centered, and sub-Gaussian with proxies \sigma^2/m_j.

notation.meaning: true gap of candidate j from the best candidate

knowledge_statements.title: Pairwise Gap Bound for Trial Misselection
Trial-Point Misselection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure to select a truly best candidate from a finite noisy trial set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_k=\{y_{k,1},\ldots,y_{k,q_k}\}\) be a finite trial set, and let \(\widehat j_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{1\leq j\leq q_k}\widehat f_k(y_{k,j})\) be the selected index under a fixed tie rule. Trial-point misselection is the event \[M_k=\left\{f(y_{k,\widehat j_k})>\min_{1\leq j\leq q_k}f(y_{k,j})\right\}.\] If \(j_k^*\) is the uniquely best true index and \(g_k=\min_{j\ne j_k^*}[f(y_{k,j})-f(y_{k,j_k^*})]>0\), then uniform estimation error below \(g_k/2\) excludes \(M_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Misselection occurs when minimizing noisy trial estimates chooses a point that is not truly best in the finite candidate set.
assumptions_latex: A deterministic rule resolves estimated-value ties.

notation.meaning: gap between the best and second-best true values

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-set misselection event and strict half-gap exclusion condition are coherent, but the record lacks an authoritative source and locator.

children.title: Selection-Error Control Regimes
children.top_down_role: Evaluation-management regimes organized by tolerated decision error.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Observable correctness certificate based on simultaneous confidence coverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite trial set, suppose intervals \([L_j,U_j]\) satisfy \[\mathbb P(\forall j,\ f(y_j)\in[L_j,U_j]\mid\mathcal F)\geq1-p.\] If the procedure certifies index \(\widehat j\) only when \(U_{\widehat j}<\min_{i\ne\widehat j}L_i\), then every certification made on the simultaneous coverage event is correct. Consequently, the conditional probability of issuing an incorrect certificate is at most \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separated simultaneous confidence intervals certify the true best trial, with incorrect certification probability at most the coverage failure probability.
assumptions_latex: The intervals have simultaneous conditional coverage at least 1-p.
Certification is issued only under strict interval separation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb P(\text{an incorrect selection certificate is issued}\mid\mathcal F)\leq p.

notation.meaning: confidence interval for the true value of trial j

knowledge_statements.title: Separated Confidence-Interval Selection Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: No Uniform Fixed-Sample Control Without a Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian boundary for fixed replication when the best-to-second-best gap may approach zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For two alternatives with independent Gaussian sample means based on \(m\) observations of variance \(\sigma^2\), let \(f_1=0\) and \(f_2=g>0\). Selecting the smaller sample mean has error probability \[\Phi\!\left(-\frac{g\sqrt m}{\sqrt2\sigma}\right).\] Therefore \[\sup_{g>0}\mathbb P(\text{misselection})=\frac12\] for every finite \(m\); no fixed finite replication count gives a uniform error bound below \(1/2\) over all positive gaps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed sampling cannot uniformly guarantee reliable selection when the true gap can be arbitrarily small.
assumptions_latex: The sample means are independent Gaussian means with variance \sigma^2/m.
Selection chooses the smaller sample mean.
knowledge_statements.title: No Uniform Fixed-Sample Control Without a Gap
Selection-Error Control Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-time, high-probability, and eventual almost-sure control of noisy selection errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For selection-error events \(E_k\), three standard control regimes are: per-iteration control, \(\mathbb P(E_k\mid\mathcal F_{k-1})\leq p_k\); finite-horizon control, \(\mathbb P(\bigcup_{k=0}^{K}E_k)\leq\sum_{k=0}^{K}p_k\); and eventual almost-sure control, \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}p_k<\infty\). The last condition implies \(\mathbb P(E_k\text{ infinitely often})=0\). For a finite trial set with true best-to-second-best gap \(g_k>0\), it suffices to control every estimation error below \(g_k/2\); union bounds may allocate \(p_k/q_k\) to each of \(q_k\) trial estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selection errors are controlled iterationwise, over a finite horizon, or eventually almost surely by increasingly strong probability budgets.
assumptions_latex: \(E_k\) is measurable after the iteration-k observations.
Conditional error bounds \(p_k\) hold almost surely.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The three probability-control regimes and summability conclusion are standard and fit a condition container, but no cited evidence supports the formulation or its DFO application.

children.title: Noise-Dominated Localization
children.top_down_role: Local search behavior when noise obscures meaningful spatial discrimination.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise confidence-based analogue of bounded-error comparison indistinguishability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let independent sample-mean errors at \(x\) and \(y\) be Gaussian with known standard errors \(s_x\) and \(s_y\). A two-sided \((1-\alpha)\) confidence interval for \(f(y)-f(x)\) has half-width \[q_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{s_x^2+s_y^2}.\] The pair is unresolved at confidence level \(1-\alpha\) whenever its observed difference has absolute value no greater than this half-width.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Gaussian pairwise comparison is unresolved when its confidence interval contains zero.
assumptions_latex: \text{sample-mean errors at }x\text{ and }y\text{ are independent Gaussian}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\widetilde f(y)-\widetilde f(x)|\leq q_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{s_x^2+s_y^2}\Longrightarrow0\text{ lies in the comparison confidence interval}.
knowledge_statements.title: Gaussian Pairwise Resolution Condition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation of value resolution into a localization radius near a strongly convex minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex with minimizer \(x^*\), then \[f(x)-f(x^*)\geq\frac\mu2\|x-x^*\|^2.\] Consequently, a value-resolution threshold \(u\geq0\) corresponds to \(r_u=\sqrt{2u/\mu}\): every point farther than \(r_u\) has objective gap exceeding \(u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong curvature converts a value-noise scale into a square-root spatial resolution scale.
knowledge_statements.title: Curvature-Induced Spatial Resolution
Noise-Dominated Localization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scale condition under which objective variation is indistinguishable from bounded evaluation noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let observations satisfy \(\widetilde f(x)=f(x)+e(x)\) with \(|e(x)|\leq\eta\). For two points \(x,y\), the observed difference obeys \[|[\widetilde f(y)-\widetilde f(x)]-[f(y)-f(x)]|\leq2\eta.\] A localization region \(B(x,ho)\) is noise dominated when \(\sup_{y\in B(x,\rho)}|f(y)-f(x)|\leq2\eta\); within it, the sign of an arbitrary true pairwise improvement cannot be inferred uniformly from one noisy evaluation per point. If \(f\) is locally \(L\)-Lipschitz, the sufficient scale condition is \(L\rho\leq2\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A region is noise dominated when its true objective variation is no larger than the worst possible error in a noisy comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{y\in B(x,\rho)}|f(y)-f(x)|\leq2\eta\) precludes uniform recovery of comparison signs.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The comparison-error bound and Lipschitz scale condition are coherent, but the localization definition and identifiability claim require a specific source.

children.title: Attainable Accuracy Floors
children.top_down_role: Practical resolution limits imposed by evaluation uncertainty.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Replication Required to Resolve a Stochastic Decrease
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Replication requirement for resolving a fixed true decrease under sub-Gaussian noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose independent observations at each of two points have centered \(\sigma^2\)-sub-Gaussian errors, and average \(m\) observations per point. For true decrease \(d>0\), \[\Pr(\widehat d_m\leq0)\leq\exp\!\left(-\frac{m d^2}{4\sigma^2}\right).\] Hence \(\Pr(\widehat d_m\leq0)\leq\alpha\) is ensured by \[m\geq\frac{4\sigma^2}{d^2}\log\frac1\alpha.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Resolving a true decrease under independent sub-Gaussian noise requires replication proportional to variance divided by squared signal.
assumptions_latex: \text{noise is independent across points and replications}
knowledge_statements.title: Replication Required to Resolve a Stochastic Decrease

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary distinguishing bounded adversarial error from independent stochastic noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A deterministic guarantee \(|e(x)|\leq\eta\) is not improved merely by repeating identical evaluations unless an additional stochastic model is imposed. By contrast, averaging \(m\) independent centered errors of variance \(\sigma^2\) yields standard deviation \(\sigma/\sqrt m\). Thus the bounded-error certification radius in the seed is irreducible under its stated assumptions, whereas a stochastic comparison floor can decrease with replication.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replication lowers independent centered noise but does not lower an adversarial bounded-error floor without stronger assumptions.
assumptions_latex: \text{the stochastic model assumes independent centered errors of variance }\sigma^2
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{sd}(\bar e_m)=\sigma/\sqrt m,\quad\text{while no analogous reduction follows from }|e|\leq\eta.
knowledge_statements.title: Irreducible Versus Replication-Reducible Floors
Attainable Accuracy Floors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case certification floor for quadratic decrease tests under uniformly bounded function-value noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a DFO step of radius \(\Delta_k\) passes an estimated sufficient-decrease test when \(\widetilde f(x_k)-\widetilde f(y_k)\geq c\Delta_k^2\), where \(c>0\), and suppose \(|\widetilde f(z)-f(z)|\leq\eta\) at each evaluated point \(z\). Then the estimated and true decreases differ by at most \(2\eta\), so acceptance certifies only \[f(x_k)-f(y_k)\geq c\Delta_k^2-2\eta.\] Consequently, when \(c\Delta_k^2\leq2\eta\), passing this test does not uniformly certify a positive true decrease. The associated certification radius is \[\Delta_{\mathrm{noise}}=\sqrt{\frac{2\eta}{c}}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded evaluation error creates a radius below which passing a quadratic sufficient-decrease test does not uniformly certify positive true decrease.
assumptions_latex: \(|\widetilde f(z)-f(z)|\leq\eta\) at the incumbent and trial point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta_k\leq\sqrt{2\eta/c}\Longrightarrow c\Delta_k^2-2\eta\leq0\), so acceptance does not uniformly certify positive true decrease.

children.title: Optimization-to-Noise Transition Regimes
children.top_down_role: Boundaries where optimization error ceases to dominate evaluation noise.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transition scale for a local DFO decrease law of general order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose useful trial decreases satisfy \(d(\Delta)\asymp c\Delta^p\), with \(c,p>0\), while absolute comparison uncertainty has scale \(u>0\). Then the transition radius has order \[\Delta_{\mathrm{tr}}\asymp(u/c)^{1/p}.\] If averaging gives \(u_m\asymp\sigma m^{-1/2}\), then \[\Delta_{\mathrm{tr}}\asymp\left(\frac{\sigma}{c\sqrt m}\right)^{1/p}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equating decrease and uncertainty scales gives the transition radius and shows how replication moves it.

notation.meaning: order of the local decrease law

knowledge_statements.title: Radius-Driven Transition Scale

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimensionless representation of the optimization-to-noise transition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\widehat d_k=d_k+\varepsilon_k\), where \(d_k>0\) and \(\varepsilon_k\sim N(0,s_k^2)\), define \(\mathrm{SNR}_k=d_k/s_k\). Then \[\Pr(\widehat d_k\leq0)=\Phi(-\mathrm{SNR}_k).\] Thus diverging SNR is optimization dominated, order-one SNR is transitional, and vanishing SNR is noise dominated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ratio of true decrease to comparison standard error quantitatively locates the optimization-to-noise transition.
knowledge_statements.title: Comparison Signal-to-Noise Ratio
Optimization-to-Noise Transition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regime split obtained by comparing the true incumbent-to-trial decrease with comparison-noise resolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_k\) be an incumbent and \(y_k\) a trial point, let \(d_k=f(x_k)-f(y_k)>0\) be their true decrease, and suppose the estimated decrease \(\widehat d_k\) satisfies \(|\widehat d_k-d_k|\leq u_k\). The comparison is sign-robust when \(d_k>u_k\), because then \(\widehat d_k>0\) for every admissible error. It is transitional when \(d_k\) and \(u_k\) are of comparable order, and noise dominated when \(0<d_k\leq u_k\), because an admissible error can make \(\widehat d_k\leq0\). For bounded per-point errors \(\eta_k\), one may take \(u_k=2\eta_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A comparison passes from optimization-dominated to noise-dominated behavior when its true objective decrease becomes comparable to the uncertainty in the estimated decrease.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_k>u_k\) guarantees \(\widehat d_k>0\), whereas \(0<d_k\leq u_k\) permits an admissible nonpositive estimate.

children.title: Global Surrogate-Bayesian DFO Family
children.top_down_role: Evaluation-efficient global black-box optimization using deterministic surrogate management or uncertainty-aware probabilistic models.

children.title: Gaussian-Process Surrogate Model Interface for DFO

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expressive limitation imposed by stationarity on the original input domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(k(x,x')=\kappa(x-x')\), then \(k(x,x)=\kappa(0)\) for every \(x\). Thus a stationary prior covariance cannot express location-dependent marginal variance, although posterior variance may vary because conditioning depends on observation locations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stationarity forces constant prior marginal variance, though posterior uncertainty can vary after conditioning.
knowledge_statements.title: Constant Prior Variance Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sample-path regularity controlled by the Matérn stationary-kernel parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(
u,\ell,\sigma^2>0\), the Matérn covariance \[k_

u}\|h\|}{\ell}ight)^

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Matérn smoothness parameter controls mean-square differentiability.

notation.meaning: modified Bessel function of the second kind

knowledge_statements.title: Matérn Smoothness Control

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bochner Representation of Continuous Stationary Kernels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral characterization of continuous stationary covariances on Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A continuous \(\kappa:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb C\) defines a stationary positive-semidefinite kernel \(k(x,x')=\kappa(x-x')\) if and only if a finite nonnegative Borel measure \(\mu\) exists such that \[\kappa(h)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{i\omega^{\mathsf T}h}\,d\mu(\omega).\] For a real covariance, \(\mu\) is symmetric and the exponential may be replaced by its cosine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bochner's theorem characterizes continuous stationary kernels as Fourier transforms of finite nonnegative measures.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \kappa\text{ is positive definite iff it is the Fourier transform of a finite nonnegative measure.}
knowledge_statements.title: Bochner Representation of Continuous Stationary Kernels

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical infinitely smooth stationary covariance with isotropic and anisotropic length scales.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \sigma^2>0 and M\succeq0, k(x,x')=\sigma^2\exp(-\tfrac12(x-x')^{\mathsf T}M(x-x')) is stationary and positive semidefinite. M=\ell^{-2}I gives the isotropic squared-exponential kernel, while diagonal M gives coordinatewise length scales. The associated process is mean-square differentiable to every finite order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The squared-exponential kernel is stationary and infinitely mean-square smooth, with anisotropy represented by a positive-semidefinite metric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k\text{ is stationary and positive semidefinite, with mean-square derivatives of every finite order}.
knowledge_statements.title: Squared-Exponential and Anisotropic Stationary Kernels

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationary covariance for exactly periodic structure on a scalar input.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \sigma^2,\ell,p>0, k(x,x')=\sigma^2\exp(-2\sin^2(\pi(x-x')/p)/\ell^2) is positive semidefinite, stationary on \mathbb R, and p-periodic in each argument. It is the squared-exponential kernel applied to the circular embedding x\mapsto(\cos(2\pi x/p),\sin(2\pi x/p)).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Applying a squared-exponential kernel to a circular embedding yields an exactly periodic stationary covariance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k\text{ is stationary, positive semidefinite, and }p\text{-periodic in each argument}.
knowledge_statements.title: Periodic Stationary Kernel

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationary covariance representing a continuous mixture of squared-exponential length scales.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \sigma^2,\alpha,\ell>0, k(h)=\sigma^2(1+\|h\|^2/(2\alpha\ell^2))^{-\alpha} is stationary and positive semidefinite. It is a scale mixture of squared-exponential covariances and converges pointwise to \sigma^2e^{-\|h\|^2/(2\ell^2)} as \alpha\to\infty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The rational-quadratic kernel mixes squared-exponential length scales and approaches the squared-exponential kernel as its shape parameter grows.
knowledge_statements.title: Rational-Quadratic Scale-Mixture Kernel

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinction between stationary prior covariance and data-dependent posterior covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For stationary prior kernel \(k(x,x')=\kappa(x-x')\) and observations at \(X_n\), \[k_n(x,x')=k(x,x')-k(x,X_n)(K+\tau^2I)^{-1}k(X_n,x').\] The second term depends on the locations of \(x,x'\) relative to \(X_n\), so \(k_n\) is not stationary in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditioning a stationary GP at fixed observation sites generally produces a nonstationary posterior covariance.
assumptions_latex: The fixed observation design is not translation invariant.
knowledge_statements.title: Conditioning Need Not Preserve Stationarity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic constructions preserving stationary Gaussian-process covariance structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(k_j(x,x')=\kappa_j(x-x')\) are stationary positive-semidefinite kernels and \(a_j\ge0\), then every finite sum \(\sum_j a_jk_j\) and finite product \(\prod_jk_j\) is stationary and positive semidefinite. If \(\kappa\) defines a stationary positive-semidefinite kernel on \(\mathbb R^d\) and \(A\in\mathbb R^{d\times r}\), then \(\widetilde k(u,u')=\kappa(A(u-u'))\) is stationary and positive semidefinite on \(\mathbb R^r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative sums, finite products, and linear pullbacks preserve stationary positive-semidefinite kernels.
assumptions_latex: Each \(k_j\) is stationary and positive semidefinite.
The sums and products are finite.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure of Stationary Kernels

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Isotropy as a Strict Stationary Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinction between translation-invariant and rotation-invariant stationary covariance kernels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A stationary kernel on \(\mathbb R^d\) is isotropic exactly when there is a function \(\psi:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\) such that \[k(x,x')=\psi(\|x-x'\|).\] Every isotropic kernel is stationary, but stationarity does not imply isotropy: for positive unequal length scales \(\ell_j\), \[k(x,x')=\exp\!\left(-\frac12\sum_{j=1}^d\frac{(x_j-x'_j)^2}{\ell_j^2}\right)\] is stationary and anisotropic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Isotropic kernels depend only on distance; stationary kernels need only depend on displacement and may have direction-dependent length scales.
assumptions_latex: For the anisotropic example, \(d\geq2\) and at least two length scales differ.
knowledge_statements.title: Isotropy as a Strict Stationary Specialization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Monte Carlo representation of a stationary kernel from its spectral measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a real stationary kernel have Bochner representation \(\kappa(h)=\int\cos(\omega^{\mathsf T}h)\,d\mu(\omega)\), set \(v=\mu(\mathbb R^d)=\kappa(0)>0\), and draw an independent sequence \((\omega_j,b_j)\) with \(\omega_j\sim\mu/v\) and \(b_j\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,2\pi]\). For feature dimension \(D\), define
\[z_{D,j}(x)=\sqrt{\frac{2v}{D}}\cos(\omega_j^{\mathsf T}x+b_j),\qquad j=1,\ldots,D.\]
Then \(\mathbb E[z_D(x)^{\mathsf T}z_D(x')]=\kappa(x-x')\), and for each fixed pair \((x,x')\), \(z_D(x)^{\mathsf T}z_D(x')\to\kappa(x-x')\) almost surely as \(D\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sampling frequencies from a stationary kernel's spectral measure produces unbiased random Fourier features with pointwise almost-sure kernel convergence.
assumptions_latex: \(\mu\) is a finite symmetric nonnegative spectral measure with positive total mass.
The frequency-phase pairs form an independent identically distributed sequence.
review_flags: Only fixed-pair pointwise convergence is asserted; no uniform approximation rate is claimed.
knowledge_statements.title: Random Fourier Feature Representation
Stationary-Kernel GP Surrogates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian-process surrogate whose prior covariance depends only on input displacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a domain \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), a stationary-kernel Gaussian-process surrogate is a random function \(F\sim\operatorname{GP}(m,k)\) whose covariance has the form \[k(x,x')=\kappa(x-x')\] for a positive-semidefinite function \(\kappa:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\). If observations satisfy \(y_i=F(x_i)+\varepsilon_i\) with independent \(\varepsilon_i\sim N(0,\tau^2)\), then the posterior at \(x\) is Gaussian with mean \(m(x)+k_x^{\mathsf T}(K+\tau^2I)^{-1}(y-m_X)\) and variance \(k(x,x)-k_x^{\mathsf T}(K+\tau^2I)^{-1}k_x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationary GP surrogate uses covariance determined only by displacement and yields Gaussian posterior predictions after noisy function observations.
assumptions_latex: Observation noise is independent Gaussian with variance \(\tau^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)\mid y\) has the displayed Gaussian posterior mean and variance.

notation.meaning: vector of prior means at observed inputs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stationary-kernel definition and Gaussian posterior formulas are standard and fit the topic, but no GP textbook section, theorem, or page is cited.

children.title: Nonstationary GP Kernels
children.top_down_role: Gaussian-process surrogates with location-dependent covariance behavior.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Naive Local-Parameter Substitution Need Not Preserve Positive Semidefiniteness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity boundary for inserting location-dependent parameters into stationary covariance formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replacing a parameter \(\theta\) in \(\kappa_\theta(x-x')\) by an arbitrary pairwise expression involving \(\theta(x)\) and \(\theta(x')\) need not preserve positive semidefiniteness. A proposed covariance is valid only if \([k(x_i,x_j)]_{i,j=1}^n\succeq0\) for every finite input set; symmetry and nonnegative diagonal entries are insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrarily making stationary-kernel parameters location dependent can produce an invalid covariance.
assumptions_latex: A stationary covariance family \(\{\kappa_\theta\}\) is given.
A pairwise kernel is formed from an input-dependent parameter field.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: [k(x_i,x_j)]_{i,j=1}^n\succeq0\text{ is required for every finite input set.}
knowledge_statements.title: Naive Local-Parameter Substitution Need Not Preserve Positive Semidefiniteness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Valid nonstationary covariance generated by location-dependent scale matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Sigma(x)\in\mathbb S_{++}^d\) and \(\sigma(x)\geq0\). Then \[k(x,x')=\sigma(x)\sigma(x')\frac{|\Sigma(x)|^{1/4}|\Sigma(x')|^{1/4}}{|(\Sigma(x)+\Sigma(x'))/2|^{1/2}}\exp\!\left[-\frac12(x-x')^{\mathsf T}\left(\frac{\Sigma(x)+\Sigma(x')}{2}\right)^{-1}(x-x')\right]\] is positive semidefinite. It is generally nonstationary when \(\sigma\) or \(\Sigma\) varies spatially.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Location-dependent Gaussian smoothing yields a valid covariance with spatially varying variance and anisotropy.
assumptions_latex: \(\Sigma(x)\) is symmetric positive definite for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k\text{ is a positive-semidefinite covariance with location-dependent geometry.}
knowledge_statements.title: Spatially Varying Gaussian-Kernel Construction
Nonstationary GP Kernels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-semidefinite GP covariance lacking translation invariance over the original input domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\). A nonstationary Gaussian-process kernel is a symmetric positive-semidefinite function \(k:X\times X\to\mathbb R\) for which no displacement-only function \(\kappa\) satisfies \(k(x,x')=\kappa(x-x')\) for all \(x,x'\in X\). Positive semidefiniteness means that, for every finite \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in X\) and \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), \[\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n a_i a_j k(x_i,x_j)\geq0.\] Such a kernel permits marginal variance, length scale, orientation, or smoothness to depend on location.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonstationary GP kernel remains positive semidefinite but cannot be expressed solely as a function of input displacement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(k\) is a valid nonstationary GP covariance precisely when it is positive semidefinite and not translation invariant on \(X\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positive-semidefinite, non-translation-invariant kernel definition is coherent and fits the leaf, but it lacks an inspectable authoritative citation.

children.title: Input-Warped GP Surrogates
children.top_down_role: Gaussian-process surrogates operating through transformed input coordinates.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Joint Marginal-Likelihood Learning of an Input Warp
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empirical-Bayes fitting of warp and latent-kernel parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(w_\phi\) be a parameterized warp, \((K_{\phi,\theta})_{ij}=k_\theta(w_\phi(x_i),w_\phi(x_j))\), \(C_{\phi,\theta}=K_{\phi,\theta}+S\), and \(r=y-m_X\). A learned input-warped GP may select \[(\widehat\phi,\widehat\theta)\in\arg\min_{\phi,\theta}\left\{\tfrac12r^{\mathsf T}C_{\phi,\theta}^{-1}r+\tfrac12\log\det C_{\phi,\theta}+\tfrac n2\log(2\pi)\right\}\] subject to declared warp constraints, then condition using the fitted pullback kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Warp and kernel parameters can be fitted jointly by GP marginal likelihood under explicit warp constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(C_{\phi,\theta}\) is positive definite for admissible parameters.
The warp family and its normalization constraints are declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\widehat\phi,\widehat\theta)\text{ minimizes the Gaussian negative log marginal likelihood over the admissible family.}
review_flags: The optimization may have local minima; the record defines the empirical-Bayes objective, not guaranteed global computation.
knowledge_statements.title: Joint Marginal-Likelihood Learning of an Input Warp

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identification boundary for jointly learned warps and latent kernels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Only the composed kernel \(k_{\phi,\theta}(x,x')=k_\theta(w_\phi(x),w_\phi(x'))\) is identified by the GP likelihood. If a latent-space bijection \(h\) and parameters \(\theta'\) satisfy \[k_{\theta'}(h(z),h(z'))=k_\theta(z,z')\] on the relevant latent set, then \((w_\phi,k_\theta)\) and \((h\circ w_\phi,k_{\theta'})\) induce the same GP covariance on \(X\). Thus a unique warp requires normalization or other constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Different warp–kernel parameter pairs can induce the same pullback kernel.
assumptions_latex: The compared pairs induce identical latent-space covariance.
Their composed mean functions are also identical or fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k_{\theta'}(h\circ w_\phi(x),h\circ w_\phi(x'))=k_\theta(w_\phi(x),w_\phi(x'))\Longrightarrow\text{ identical GP laws on }X.
knowledge_statements.title: Warp–Kernel Nonidentifiability
Input-Warped GP Surrogates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonstationary surrogate obtained by composing a stationary latent-space kernel with an input warp.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), let \(w:X\to Z\subseteq\mathbb R^p\) be a deterministic input warp, and let \(G\sim\operatorname{GP}(\mu,k_0)\) on \(Z\). The input-warped surrogate \(F(x)=G(w(x))\) is a Gaussian process on \(X\) with \[m_F(x)=\mu(w(x)),\qquad k_F(x,x')=k_0(w(x),w(x')).\] If \(k_0(z,z')=\kappa(z-z')\) is stationary, then \(k_F\) is positive semidefinite but is generally nonstationary in the original coordinates unless the warp preserves translations in the kernel geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An input-warped GP composes a latent GP with a deterministic map, inducing a generally nonstationary kernel on the original domain.

notation.meaning: kernel induced on the original input domain

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The composition representation and induced kernel are mathematically standard and representation is the correct content kind, but no authoritative source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Warp-Induced Geometry Effects
children.top_down_role: Search-space geometry created or distorted by learned input warps.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bi-Lipschitz Bounds on Warped Correlation Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global distance-distortion bounds induced by a quantitatively invertible warp.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(m\|x-x'\|\leq\|w(x)-w(x')\|\leq L\|x-x'\|\) for \(0<m\leq L\). If \(k_w(x,x')=\psi(\|w(x)-w(x')\|)\) with nonincreasing \(\psi\), then \[\psi(L\|x-x'\|)\leq k_w(x,x')\leq\psi(m\|x-x'\|).\] In particular, \(m>0\) prevents distinct inputs from collapsing to one warped location.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bi-Lipschitz warp bounds correlation-length distortion and prevents global input collapse.
assumptions_latex: \(w\) is bi-Lipschitz on \(\mathcal X\) with constants \(m,L\).
The base kernel has a nonincreasing radial profile \(\psi\).
knowledge_statements.title: Bi-Lipschitz Bounds on Warped Correlation Geometry

assumptions_latex: The input domain is \(\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), and \(w:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^p\) is differentiable.
The base kernel \(k_0\) is positive semidefinite and has a local metric matrix \(M_0(z)\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The warp induces the pullback metric \(G_w(x)=J_w(x)^{\mathsf T}M_0(w(x))J_w(x)\), so directions compressed or expanded by \(w\) acquire correspondingly longer or shorter effective correlation lengths.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: pullback geometry of a differentiable input-warped kernel
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local pullback geometry for differentiable input warps of Gaussian-process kernels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the warped kernel by \(k_w(x,x')=k_0(w(x),w(x'))\). If the base-kernel correlation near \(z=w(x)\) is governed to second order by the squared displacement \(\delta z^{\mathsf T}M_0(z)\delta z\), then a small input displacement \(h\) satisfies \(w(x+h)-w(x)=J_w(x)h+o(\lVert h\rVert)\). Consequently, the warped squared displacement is \(h^{\mathsf T}G_w(x)h+o(\lVert h\rVert^2)\), where \(G_w(x)=J_w(x)^{\mathsf T}M_0(w(x))J_w(x)\). Thus the warp creates position-dependent anisotropy and may collapse directions when \(J_w(x)\) is rank deficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An input warp pulls the base kernel metric back to the original domain, producing location-dependent length scales, anisotropy, and possible directional collapse.
knowledge_statements.title: Warp-Induced Geometry Effects

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property matches the warp-geometry leaf and is mathematically plausible, but no inspectable source is cited for the local-metric expansion or pullback interpretation.

children.title: Homoscedastic Observation-Noise GPs
children.top_down_role: Gaussian-process surrogates using a uniform observation-noise scale.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empirical-Bayes estimation of a common Gaussian observation variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For kernel parameters \(\theta\), common variance \(\sigma^2\ge0\), residual \(r=y-m_X\), and \(C_{\theta,\sigma}=K_\theta+\sigma^2I\), Gaussian empirical Bayes minimizes \[\mathcal L(\theta,\sigma^2)=\tfrac12r^{\mathsf T}C_{\theta,\sigma}^{-1}r+\tfrac12\log\det C_{\theta,\sigma}+\tfrac n2\log(2\pi)\] over admissible parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The common noise variance can be fitted jointly with kernel parameters by Gaussian marginal likelihood.
assumptions_latex: \(C_{\theta,\sigma}\) is positive definite at evaluated parameters.
The Gaussian homoscedastic likelihood is the declared model.
knowledge_statements.title: Constant-Noise Marginal-Likelihood Estimation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact reduction of repeated observations under constant independent Gaussian noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(y_j=f(x)+\varepsilon_j\), \(j=1,\ldots,r\), with independent \(\varepsilon_j\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)\), then \(\bar y=f(x)+\bar\varepsilon\), where \(\bar\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2/r)\). For known \(\sigma^2\), the likelihood for \(f(x)\) is proportional to that of this aggregated observation; within-site residuals carry information about \(\sigma^2\), not \(f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equal-variance Gaussian replicates reduce to their mean with variance divided by the replicate count.
assumptions_latex: Errors are independent Gaussian variables with common variance.
All replicates query the same latent input.
knowledge_statements.title: Aggregation of Equal-Variance Replicates

assumptions_latex: The errors are independent of \(f\) and obey \(\varepsilon_i\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)\) with one constant \(\sigma^2\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Conditioning uses the covariance matrix \(K+\sigma^2I_n\), yielding the stated posterior mean and covariance.

notation.meaning: covariance vector to a test point

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical GP regression model with constant Gaussian noise
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian-process regression with independent constant-variance observation errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A homoscedastic observation-noise GP places \(f\sim\mathcal{GP}(m,k)\) and observes \(y_i=f(x_i)+\varepsilon_i\), where \(\varepsilon_i\) are independent \(\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)\). For training mean vector \(m_X\), Gram matrix \(K\), and \(k_x=(k(x_1,x),\ldots,k(x_n,x))^{\mathsf T}\), the latent posterior mean is \(m_n(x)=m(x)+k_x^{\mathsf T}(K+\sigma^2I_n)^{-1}(y-m_X)\). Its covariance is \(k_n(x,x')=k(x,x')-k_x^{\mathsf T}(K+\sigma^2I_n)^{-1}k_{x'}\). Predictive observation variance at \(x\) is \(k_n(x,x)+\sigma^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A homoscedastic GP uses one Gaussian noise variance for every observation and conditions through the covariance matrix formed by adding that variance to the diagonal.
knowledge_statements.title: Homoscedastic Observation-Noise GPs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and posterior formulas match the homoscedastic observation-noise regime, but the record has no citation with an inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gaussian-process prediction with homoscedastic observation noise
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Posterior mean and marginal latent-function variance at finitely many prediction points using a scalar observation-noise variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a Gaussian process with mean function $m$, covariance kernel $k$, training inputs $X$, observations $y$, and scalar observation-noise variance $v$, let $X_*$ denote the prediction inputs and suppose $K(X,X)+vI$ is invertible. Define $T=K(X_*,X)\bigl(K(X,X)+vI\bigr)^{-1}$. Compute $\mu_*=m(X_*)+T\bigl(y-m(X)\bigr)$ and $S_*=K(X_*,X_*)-TK(X,X_*)$. Return $\mu_*$ and $v_*=\operatorname{diag}(S_*)+\varepsilon$, where $\varepsilon$ is a machine-scale numerical offset.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Form the cross-covariance times the inverse of the noise-adjusted training covariance. Use it to compute the posterior mean and covariance at the requested points, then return the covariance diagonal with a machine-scale offset as the marginal latent-function variances.
assumptions_latex: X_*\text{ is a finite list of prediction inputs}

source_evidence.locator: Probabilistic Surrogate Models / 15.5. Noisy Measurements / Algorithm 15.4

source_refs.locator: Probabilistic Surrogate Models / 15.5. Noisy Measurements / Algorithm 15.4

children.title: Heteroscedastic Observation-Noise GPs
children.top_down_role: Gaussian-process surrogates with input-dependent observation uncertainty.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient-statistic reduction for independent Gaussian replicates with known unequal variances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At one input, let \(y_j=f(x)+\varepsilon_j\) with independent \(\varepsilon_j\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_j^2)\). Define \(\lambda=\sum_j\sigma_j^{-2}\) and \(\bar y_w=\lambda^{-1}\sum_j\sigma_j^{-2}y_j\). For inference about \(f(x)\), the replicates are equivalent, up to a likelihood factor independent of \(f(x)\), to \(\bar y_w=f(x)+\bar\varepsilon\), where \(\bar\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,\lambda^{-1})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unequal-variance Gaussian replicates aggregate through a precision-weighted mean.
assumptions_latex: All variances are known and strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.title: Precision Aggregation of Heteroscedastic Replicates

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Learned input-dependent noise represented by a latent log-variance process.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A learned heteroscedastic model may specify \[f\sim\mathcal{GP}(m_f,k_f),\quad g\sim\mathcal{GP}(m_g,k_g),\quad y_i\mid f,g\sim\mathcal N(f(x_i),\exp(g(x_i))).\] Conditional on \(g_X\), inference for \(f\) uses \(K_f+\operatorname{diag}(\exp(g_X))\). Integrating the unknown \(g_X\) generally makes posterior inference non-Gaussian and requires approximation or sampling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A latent GP for log variance gives positive input-dependent noise but generally non-Gaussian marginal inference.
assumptions_latex: The joint prior of \(f\) and \(g\) is declared.
Errors are conditionally independent given the latent processes.
review_flags: Implementations must declare the approximation or sampling method used for latent-variance inference.
knowledge_statements.title: Latent Log-Variance Heteroscedastic GP

assumptions_latex: Conditional on the inputs, the errors are independent with \(\varepsilon_i\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_i^2)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Conditioning uses \(K+\Sigma\), where \(\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1^2,\ldots,\sigma_n^2)\), and predictive observation variance adds the test-point variance \(\sigma^2(x)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical GP regression model with input-dependent Gaussian noise
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian-process regression with known or separately estimated input-dependent noise variances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A heteroscedastic observation-noise GP places \(f\sim\mathcal{GP}(m,k)\) and observes \(y_i=f(x_i)+\varepsilon_i\), where \(\varepsilon_i\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2(x_i))\) independently. With \(\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma^2(x_1),\ldots,\sigma^2(x_n))\), its latent posterior mean is \(m_n(x)=m(x)+k_x^{\mathsf T}(K+\Sigma)^{-1}(y-m_X)\), and its latent posterior covariance is \(k_n(x,x')=k(x,x')-k_x^{\mathsf T}(K+\Sigma)^{-1}k_{x'}\). The predictive variance of a future noisy observation at \(x\) is \(k_n(x,x)+\sigma^2(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A heteroscedastic GP assigns observation variances by input, replacing the constant diagonal noise term with a nonuniform diagonal covariance matrix.
knowledge_statements.title: Heteroscedastic Observation-Noise GPs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly distinguishes input-dependent diagonal noise from the homoscedastic regime, but no inspectable source supports the stated conditioning and predictive-variance formulas.

children.title: Noise-Model Misspecification
children.top_down_role: Surrogate failures caused by an unsuitable observation-noise representation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Observational equivalence of distinct latent-signal and noise decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a fixed design, observations identify total covariance \(C=K+S\), not its decomposition without additional restrictions. If \(C=I_n\), then for every \(0<c<1\), both \((K,S)=(cI_n,(1-c)I_n)\) and \((K,S)=(0,I_n)\) give \(y\sim\mathcal N(m_X,I_n)\), while assigning different variability to signal and noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distinct latent-kernel and noise-covariance pairs can generate the same finite-design observation law.
assumptions_latex: Identification uses only the finite-design Gaussian observation distribution.
knowledge_statements.title: Signal–Nugget Nonidentifiability at Finite Designs

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of a centered observation model under systematic input-dependent error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(y=f_X+b_X+\eta\), with \(\mathbb E[\eta\mid X]=0\), while inference assumes centered noise and uses \(a_x=(K+S)^{-1}k_x\). Conditional on \(f_X\), the noise-induced prediction bias is \[\mathbb E[m_n(x)-m(x)-a_x^{\mathsf T}(f_X-m_X)\mid X]=a_x^{\mathsf T}b_X.\] Altering only the assumed covariance does not generally remove this bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A covariance-only noise model cannot generally correct systematic nonzero-mean evaluation error.
assumptions_latex: The fitted likelihood assumes zero-mean additive error.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonzero-Mean Noise Produces Posterior-Mean Bias

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reported covariance is calibrated to \(S\), not \(T\); under the true model the estimation-error covariance contains \((K+S)^{-1}T(K+S)^{-1}\), so credible intervals and acquisition uncertainty are generally miscalibrated.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: covariance mismatch in Gaussian-process conditioning
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Calibration failure caused by an incorrect Gaussian observation-noise covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose GP inference uses \(S\) and posterior weights \(a_x=(K+S)^{-1}k_x\), while the true observation-noise covariance is \(T\ne S\). The noise contribution to the true variance of the posterior-mean error at \(x\) is \(a_x^{\mathsf T}Ta_x=k_x^{\mathsf T}(K+S)^{-1}T(K+S)^{-1}k_x\), whereas the fitted model accounts for \(k_x^{\mathsf T}(K+S)^{-1}S(K+S)^{-1}k_x\). These expressions need not agree. In particular, fitting \(S=\sigma^2I_n\) when the \(\tau_i^2\) differ can overstate uncertainty in low-noise regions and understate it in high-noise regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the assumed and true noise covariances differ, GP uncertainty is generally miscalibrated, which can distort confidence bounds and acquisition decisions.
knowledge_statements.title: Noise-Model Misspecification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf, and the covariance-mismatch calculation is plausible, but the calibration claims and regional overstatement or understatement claim require an inspectable source.

assumptions_latex: Distinct sites \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^d\) and values \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\) are given.
The radial kernel \(\phi\) is conditionally positive definite of order compatible with the polynomial space \(\Pi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coefficients are determined by interpolation together with polynomial side constraints, producing a global radial-basis surrogate.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard conditionally positive-definite RBF interpolant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interpolatory radial-basis surrogate with a polynomial tail and side constraints.

source_refs.locator: 10 Trust-region methods based on derivative-free models p. 173

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p_1,\ldots,p_q\) be a basis of \(\Pi\). A radial-basis surrogate has the representation \(s(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i\phi(\lVert x-x_i\rVert)+\sum_{j=1}^q\beta_jp_j(x)\). Its coefficients satisfy \(s(x_i)=y_i\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\) and the side constraints \(\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_ip_j(x_i)=0\) for \(j=1,\ldots,q\). Equivalently, with \(\Phi_{ij}=\phi(\lVert x_i-x_j\rVert)\) and \(P_{ij}=p_j(x_i)\), they solve \(\begin{bmatrix}\Phi&P\\P^{\mathsf T}&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\lambda\\\beta\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}y\\0\end{bmatrix}\), whenever this system is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An RBF surrogate combines radial kernels centered at all sampled points with a polynomial tail, enforcing interpolation and polynomial orthogonality constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Radial-Basis Global Surrogates

source_witnesses.locator: 10 Trust-region methods based on derivative-free models p. 173

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Native-space error bound for the strictly positive-definite, no-tail RBF variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a strictly positive-definite kernel with Gram matrix \(\Phi\), let \(r(x)_i=\phi(\|x-x_i\|)\) and \[P_X(x)^2=\phi(0)-r(x)^{\mathsf T}\Phi^{-1}r(x).\] If \(f\in\mathcal H_\phi\) and \(s_X\) interpolates \(f\) on \(X\), then \[|f(x)-s_X(x)|\leq P_X(x)\|f\|_{\mathcal H_\phi},\qquad P_X(x_i)=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The RBF power function bounds pointwise native-space interpolation error and vanishes at sampled sites.
knowledge_statements.title: Power-Function Pointwise Error Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerical limitation of increasingly flat smooth RBF interpolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For common infinitely smooth families \(\phi_\varepsilon(r)=\phi(\varepsilon r)\) on fixed distinct sites, interpolation matrices can become severely ill-conditioned as \(\varepsilon\to0\), even when the limiting approximation is accurate. Consequently, an unprotected standard-basis solve may lose substantial accuracy, and a small algebraic residual alone does not certify an accurate surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Very flat smooth RBFs may be accurate in principle but numerically unstable in the standard basis.
assumptions_latex: A fixed finite site set and a shape-parameterized infinitely smooth RBF family are used.
knowledge_statements.title: Shape-Parameter Conditioning Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and uniqueness condition for augmented RBF interpolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi\) be strictly conditionally positive definite of order \(m\), and let distinct sites be \(\Pi_{m-1}\)-unisolvent. Then \[\begin{bmatrix}\Phi&P\\P^{\mathsf T}&0\end{bmatrix}\] is nonsingular, so every data vector has a unique RBF interpolant satisfying the polynomial side constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict conditional positive definiteness plus polynomial unisolvency makes the augmented RBF system uniquely solvable.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi\) is strictly conditionally positive definite of order \(m\).
knowledge_statements.title: Conditional-Positive-Definiteness Uniqueness Theorem

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Penalized no-tail RBF fitting for noisy observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a symmetric positive-definite Gram matrix \(\Phi\) and \(\rho>0\), minimize \(\|y-\Phi\lambda\|_2^2+\rho\lambda^{\mathsf T}\Phi\lambda\). The unique minimizer satisfies \((\Phi+\rho I)\widehat\lambda=y\), and \(s_\rho(x)=r(x)^{\mathsf T}\widehat\lambda\). As \(\rho\downarrow0\), exact interpolation is recovered; for \(\rho>0\), training residuals generally remain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive regularization trades exact RBF interpolation for smoothing and improved numerical stability.

notation.meaning: kernel vector between the sites and x

review_flags: The statement is restricted to the strictly positive-definite no-tail case; polynomial-tail smoothing uses an augmented block system.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularized RBF Smoothing Fit

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Canonical RBF Kernel and Tail Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Principal strictly positive-definite and conditionally positive-definite RBF variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Gaussian kernels \(e^{-(\varepsilon r)^2}\) and inverse multiquadrics \((1+(\varepsilon r)^2)^{-1/2}\), \(\varepsilon>0\), are strictly positive definite on every \(\mathbb R^d\) and may be used without a polynomial tail. Common conditionally positive-definite choices include the cubic kernel \(r^3\) and, in its classical planar form, the thin-plate spline \(r^2\log r\); they require polynomial augmentation and moment constraints of the kernel's conditional-positive-definiteness order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gaussian and inverse-multiquadric kernels need no polynomial tail, whereas cubic and thin-plate spline interpolation requires compatible polynomial augmentation.
assumptions_latex: For a conditionally positive-definite kernel, the sites are unisolvent for the required polynomial space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Kernel definiteness determines the required polynomial augmentation.}
review_flags: Dimension and order must be retained when extending the listed examples to general polyharmonic splines.
knowledge_statements.title: Canonical RBF Kernel and Tail Families

assumptions_latex: Sample sites \(x_i\in\mathbb R^d\), responses \(y_i\in\mathbb R\), and nonnegative weights \(w_i\) are given.
A finite-dimensional polynomial space \(\Pi_r\) of degree at most \(r\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A polynomial response surface is any minimizer of the weighted residual sum of squares over \(\Pi_r\), uniquely determined when the weighted design matrix has full column rank.

notation.meaning: polynomial space of degree at most \(r\)

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: weighted least-squares polynomial response surface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global weighted least-squares polynomial surrogate on a prescribed basis.

source_refs.locator: Part 4. Model-Based Methods p. 157

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a basis \(p_1,\ldots,p_q\) of \(\Pi_r\), write \(s_\beta(x)=\sum_{j=1}^q\beta_jp_j(x)\). A weighted polynomial response-surface surrogate satisfies \(\widehat\beta\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\beta\in\mathbb R^q}\sum_{i=1}^nw_i(y_i-s_\beta(x_i))^2\). With \(P_{ij}=p_j(x_i)\) and \(W=\operatorname{diag}(w_1,\ldots,w_n)\), every minimizer solves \(P^{\mathsf T}WP\widehat\beta=P^{\mathsf T}Wy\). If \(P^{\mathsf T}WP\) is nonsingular, then \(\widehat\beta=(P^{\mathsf T}WP)^{-1}P^{\mathsf T}Wy\) and the surrogate is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial response surface fits a fixed polynomial basis by weighted least squares and is unique when the weighted design matrix has full rank.
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Response-Surface Surrogates

source_witnesses.locator: Part 4. Model-Based Methods p. 157

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularized variant for rank-deficient or unstable polynomial coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\lambda>0\) and \(R\succeq0\), minimize \[\|W^{1/2}(y-P\beta)\|_2^2+\lambda\|R^{1/2}\beta\|_2^2.\] Every minimizer solves \((P^{\mathsf T}WP+\lambda R)\widehat\beta=P^{\mathsf T}Wy\), and it is unique exactly when \(\ker(W^{1/2}P)\cap\ker(R)=\{0\}\). Regularization generally sacrifices exact polynomial reproduction unless the penalty vanishes on the generating coefficient vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ridge regularization stabilizes polynomial fitting under a joint null-space condition, at the cost of bias.
knowledge_statements.title: Ridge-Regularized Polynomial Response Surface

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifiability and extrapolation limitations of global polynomial response surfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(P^{\mathsf T}WP\) is singular, the observations do not uniquely determine the coefficient vector without an additional selection rule. Even when it is nonsingular, least-squares optimality controls residuals only at weighted sample sites and gives no finite uniform extrapolation-error bound without further assumptions on the target, design, and domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank deficiency destroys uniqueness, and sampled least-squares fit alone does not certify safe extrapolation.
assumptions_latex: A fixed finite polynomial basis and weighted observations are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P^{\mathsf T}WP\text{ singular implies coefficient nonuniqueness; sampled residual control alone does not bound extrapolation error.}
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Extrapolation and Rank Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact recovery of responses contained in the fitted polynomial space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(P\) has full column rank and \(W\succ0\), then \[H_W=P(P^{\mathsf T}WP)^{-1}P^{\mathsf T}W\] is the \(W\)-orthogonal projector onto \(\operatorname{col}(P)\). Hence \(H_W^2=H_W\), and data \(y=P\beta_\star\) are reproduced exactly with recovery of \(\beta_\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted polynomial regression is a weighted projection and exactly reproduces data generated by its basis.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection and Exact-Reproduction Property

children.title: Tree-Based Surrogates
children.top_down_role: Global surrogate representations built from recursive partitions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical recursive-partition fitting step for a real-valued response surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For node indices \(I\), an axis-aligned split \((j,t)\) gives \(I_L=\{i\in I:x_{ij}\leq t\}\) and \(I_R=I\setminus I_L\). With \(\bar y_A=|A|^{-1}\sum_{i\in A}y_i\), the greedy split minimizes \[\sum_{i\in I_L}(y_i-\bar y_{I_L})^2+\sum_{i\in I_R}(y_i-\bar y_{I_R})^2,\] equivalently maximizing reduction in parent-node squared error. Recursion stops under declared depth, leaf-size, or improvement rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regression tree recursively chooses the axis-aligned split giving the greatest reduction in within-leaf squared error.
assumptions_latex: Both children of a permissible split are nonempty.
Squared-error loss and constant leaf predictions are used.

notation.meaning: left and right child index sets

knowledge_statements.title: Greedy Squared-Error Regression-Tree Split

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation and search limitation of a piecewise-constant regression tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If distinct \(x,x'\) lie in the same terminal leaf, then \(s_T(x)=s_T(x')\), irrespective of their objective values. The fitted tree cannot rank such points without subdivision or an auxiliary rule. Its classical gradient is zero in leaf interiors and undefined on split boundaries, so it supplies no meaningful within-leaf descent direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant-leaf tree cannot rank points within one leaf, and its derivatives provide no useful local descent direction.
assumptions_latex: \(s_T\) is constant on every terminal leaf.
knowledge_statements.title: Within-Leaf Resolution Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality of constant leaf predictions under squared loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed partition with nonempty leaf index sets \(I_m\), \[c_m=\operatorname*{argmin}_{c\in\mathbb R}\sum_{i\in I_m}(y_i-c)^2=\frac1{|I_m|}\sum_{i\in I_m}y_i.\] Empirical-risk minimization over functions constant on the fixed leaves therefore separates into independent leafwise means.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed partition, each leaf mean is the unique squared-error-optimal constant prediction.
assumptions_latex: Every terminal leaf contains at least one observation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c_m=|I_m|^{-1}\sum_{i\in I_m}y_i\text{ uniquely minimizes leafwise squared error}.
knowledge_statements.title: Leafwise Empirical-Risk Optimality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical regularization of a greedily grown regression tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite grown tree \(T_0\), training loss \(R(T)\), and terminal-leaf count \(|T|\), cost-complexity pruning selects \(T_\alpha\in\arg\min_{T\preceq T_0}\{R(T)+\alpha|T|\}\), \(\alpha\ge0\). A validation rule may select among the resulting candidate subtrees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cost-complexity pruning trades training fit against leaf count, with validation selecting a regularized subtree.

notation.meaning: T is a pruned subtree of T0

knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Complexity Subtree Pruning

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Principal single-tree extensions beyond axis-aligned constant leaves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A model tree assigns each terminal leaf \(L_m\) a local predictor \(g_m\), so \(s(x)=\sum_mg_m(x)\mathbf1\{x\in L_m\}\); affine leaves use \(g_m(x)=a_m+b_m^{\mathsf T}x\). An oblique tree permits splits \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le t\), whereas an axis-aligned tree restricts \(a\) to a coordinate direction. Constant-leaf axis-aligned regression trees are recovered by constant \(g_m\) and coordinate splits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Model trees place local regressions in leaves, while oblique trees split along general hyperplanes.
assumptions_latex: Terminal leaves form a disjoint partition of the modeled domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Model-Tree and Oblique-Split Variants

assumptions_latex: The domain \(\mathcal X\) is recursively partitioned into terminal leaves \(L_1,\ldots,L_M\).
Each leaf contains at least one training response.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The surrogate is constant on each terminal leaf and predicts using that leaf's fitted response statistic.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single regression-tree surrogate with terminal-leaf predictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tree-based surrogate is determined by a recursive partition \(\mathcal X=\bigsqcup_{m=1}^ML_m\) and leaf values \(c_1,\ldots,c_M\). Its prediction is \(s_T(x)=\sum_{m=1}^Mc_m\mathbf 1\{x\in L_m\}\). Under squared-error fitting, a leaf value is \(c_m=|I_m|^{-1}\sum_{i\in I_m}y_i\), where \(I_m=\{i:x_i\in L_m\}\). A derivative-free optimizer may minimize \(s_T\) or use empirical dispersion within the selected leaf, but the fitted mean itself is discontinuous only across partition boundaries and constant inside each leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regression-tree surrogate partitions the domain recursively and assigns each terminal region a fitted response, typically the mean of observations in that region.
knowledge_statements.title: Tree-Based Surrogates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The piecewise-constant regression-tree representation fits the exact leaf, but no inspectable source is supplied for the representation or its stated DFO use.

children.title: Density-Based Surrogates
children.top_down_role: Global-search surrogates based on modeled densities over promising regions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational candidate selection for a thresholded density surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given fitted densities \(\ell\) and \(g\), draw \(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(M)}\sim\ell\) and return \[x^+\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{1\leq r\leq M}\frac{\ell(x^{(r)})}{g(x^{(r)})}.\] Where both densities are positive, this is equivalent to minimizing \(g/\ell\), the ordering in the seed's expected-improvement representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample from the promising-region density and select the candidate with the largest good-to-bad density ratio.
knowledge_statements.title: Density-Ratio Candidate Selection

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Well-definedness and exploration limitations of density-ratio ranking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The ratio \(g(x)/\ell(x)\) is finite and defined only where \(\ell(x)>0\). Exclusive sampling from \(\ell\) never proposes a region \(A\) with \(\int_A\ell(x)\,dx=0\). Conversely, points with \(\ell(x)>0\) and estimated \(g(x)=0\) receive an unbounded good-to-bad score, requiring smoothing, support floors, or explicit exploration when such zeros are unreliable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Density-ratio search cannot explore outside the good density's support and can become singular at estimated zero bad density.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \int_A\ell(x)\,dx=0\Rightarrow P(x^+\in A)=0\text{ under exclusive sampling from }\ell.
knowledge_statements.title: Density-Support and Zero-Denominator Boundary

assumptions_latex: A threshold \(y^\star\) splits observations into \(G=\{y<y^\star\}\) and \(B=\{y\ge y^\star\}\).
Conditional densities \(\ell(x)=p(x\mid G)\) and \(g(x)=p(x\mid B)\) are estimable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(\gamma=P(G)\), expected-improvement ordering is equivalent to maximizing \(\bigl(\gamma+(1-\gamma)g(x)/\ell(x)\bigr)^{-1}\).

notation.meaning: density of inputs in the good-response group
density of inputs in the bad-response group

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: thresholded conditional-density surrogate underlying density-ratio optimization
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Thresholded conditional-density surrogate and its density-ratio acquisition ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(y^\star\) so that \(\gamma=P(y<y^\star)\), and model \(p(x\mid y)=\ell(x)\) when \(y<y^\star\) and \(p(x\mid y)=g(x)\) otherwise. Bayes' rule gives \(p(y\mid x)=p(x\mid y)p(y)/p(x)\) with \(p(x)=\gamma\ell(x)+(1-\gamma)g(x)\).
