Then \[\mathbb E\left[(f(X)-g(W_r^{\mathsf T}X))^2\right]\le C_P\,\mathbb E\left[\|W_\perp^{\mathsf T}\nabla f(X)\|_2^2\right]=C_P\sum_{i=r+1}^d\lambda_i.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a uniform conditional Poincaré inequality, the inactive eigenvalue tail bounds the mean-square error of the conditional-mean ridge approximation.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) has a square-integrable weak gradient under the reference distribution.
\([W_r,W_\perp]\) is orthogonal, and \(W_r\) spans the leading rank-\(r\) eigenspace of the gradient second-moment matrix.
Conditional distributions on inactive fibers satisfy the stated uniform Poincaré inequality.

notation.meaning: Conditional-mean ridge approximation at active coordinate y.
Uniform conditional Poincaré constant on inactive fibers.

knowledge_statements.title: Inactive-Eigenvalue Ridge Approximation Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global optimization equivalence for an exact ridge objective over its attainable projected domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=g(W_r^{\mathsf T}x)\) on nonempty \(\mathcal X\), and set \(\mathcal Y=W_r^{\mathsf T}\mathcal X\). Then \[\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathcal Y}g(y).\] If \(y^*\) minimizes \(g\) on \(\mathcal Y\), every \(x^*\in\mathcal X\) satisfying \(W_r^{\mathsf T}x^*=y^*\) globally minimizes \(f\) on \(\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an exact ridge objective, optimization in attainable active coordinates is equivalent to ambient optimization, and every feasible lift of a reduced minimizer is optimal.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Reduced Optimization Equivalence
Active-Subspace Bayesian Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bayesian optimization through a learned low-dimensional linear embedding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(W\in\mathbb R^{d\times r}\) have orthonormal columns with \(r<d\). An active-subspace surrogate represents
\[f(x)=g(W^\top x)+\varepsilon(x),\]
where \(g:\mathbb R^r\to\mathbb R\) is modeled probabilistically and \(\varepsilon\) is the residual outside the selected subspace. Acquisition optimization is performed over the attainable reduced domain \(W^\top\mathcal X\); a selected reduced point \(y\) must be lifted to some \(x\in\mathcal X\) satisfying \(W^\top x=y\). Exact dimension reduction corresponds to \(\varepsilon\equiv0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective is modeled through a low-dimensional linear projection, with acquisition in the attainable reduced domain and an explicit lift back to a feasible design.
assumptions_latex: The reduced acquisition is restricted to \(W^\top\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=g(W^\top x)\) exactly when \(\varepsilon(x)=0\) for all \(x\in\mathcal X\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is coherent, but “active subspace” can denote a gradient-informed construction rather than an arbitrary learned linear embedding. A source is needed to fix the intended terminology and validate the lifting formulation.

children.title: Structure-Misspecification Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Failure regimes caused by inaccurate additive or subspace assumptions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Irreducible uniform error when a reduced representation identifies points having different objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Z\) and \(\mathcal H_P=\{g\circ P:g:\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R\}\). Then
\[\inf_{h\in\mathcal H_P}\|f-h\|_\infty\geq\frac12\sup_{\substack{x,x'\in\mathcal X\\P(x)=P(x')}}|f(x)-f(x')|.\]
Consequently, positive variation on a fiber of \(P\) prevents arbitrarily accurate uniform approximation by functions factoring through \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variation between points identified by a reduced representation produces at least half that variation as unavoidable uniform approximation error.
assumptions_latex: The surrogate class consists only of functions factoring through \(P\).
The uniform norm and supremum are interpreted in the extended-real sense when necessary.

notation.meaning: fiber of inputs sharing representation z

knowledge_statements.title: Fiber-Oscillation Boundary for Reduced Structure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rectangular Mixed-Difference Boundary for Additive Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General uniform-error lower bound for approximating a two-coordinate interaction by singleton-additive functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For four points \((a,c),(a,d),(b,c),(b,d)\) in a product domain, define \(\Delta f=f(a,c)-f(a,d)-f(b,c)+f(b,d)\). Every singleton-additive function \(h(x_1,x_2)=g_1(x_1)+g_2(x_2)\) satisfies \(\Delta h=0\). Consequently, \[\|f-h\|_\infty\ge\frac{|\Delta f|}{4}.\] Thus any nonzero rectangular mixed difference certifies irreducible singleton-additive approximation error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero four-corner interaction contrast gives a sharp uniform-error lower bound against every sum of two univariate functions.
assumptions_latex: The domain contains the four displayed corner points.
The uniform norm is taken over a set containing those corners.

notation.meaning: rectangular four-corner mixed difference of f

knowledge_statements.title: Rectangular Mixed-Difference Boundary for Additive Structure
Structure-Misspecification Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Irreducible error caused by imposing an incorrect additive structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(\mathcal X=[-1,1]^2\), let \(f(x_1,x_2)=x_1x_2\). For every singleton-additive model \(h(x_1,x_2)=g_1(x_1)+g_2(x_2)\),
\[\sup_{(x_1,x_2)\in\mathcal X}|f(x_1,x_2)-h(x_1,x_2)|\geq1.\]
Thus a surrogate restricted to singleton additive components cannot uniformly approximate this interaction below error one, regardless of data quantity or component flexibility. The boundary disappears if the structural family includes the joint group \(\{1,2\}\) or an equivalent interaction component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interaction function x1x2 has uniform error at least one under every sum of two univariate functions, demonstrating irreducible additive-structure misspecification.
assumptions_latex: The approximation class contains only functions \(g_1(x_1)+g_2(x_2)\).
Error is measured in the uniform norm on \([-1,1]^2\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf and the explicit uniform-error claim is mathematically precise, but no source or marked standard-field rationale supports the nontrivial sharp bound.

children.title: Surrogate Misspecification
children.top_down_role: Mismatch between surrogate structure and black-box behavior.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact example of positive best-approximation error for a global affine surrogate class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X=[-1,1]\), \(f_0(x)=x^2\), and \(\mathcal M=\{x\mapsto a+bx:a,b\in\mathbb R\}\). Under the uniform norm, \[\inf_{m\in\mathcal M}\|f_0-m\|_\infty=\frac12,\] attained by \(m^*(x)=1/2\). Thus the affine class remains misspecified even with noiseless unlimited data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The best affine uniform approximation to the quadratic response on minus one to one is the constant one half, with irreducible error one half.
assumptions_latex: The surrogate class contains all affine functions.

notation.meaning: Uniform norm on the search interval.

knowledge_statements.title: Irreducible Affine-Surrogate Misspecification
Surrogate Misspecification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mismatch between the true response law and the surrogate model class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal M\) be the set of response functions or conditional data distributions admitted by a surrogate. The surrogate is misspecified for a true response \(f_0\) when \(f_0\notin\mathcal M\); for a probabilistic observation model \(P_0\), misspecification means \(P_0\notin\mathcal P\), where \(\mathcal P\) is the modeled distribution family. Relative to a discrepancy \(d\), misspecification is irreducible when
\[\inf_{m\in\mathcal M}d(f_0,m)>0.\]
This condition concerns representational adequacy and is distinct from finite-data parameter-estimation error within a correctly specified class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A surrogate is misspecified when its model class excludes the true response or data law; positive best-approximation error makes the mismatch irreducible.
assumptions_latex: A surrogate model class \(\mathcal M\) or distribution family \(\mathcal P\) is fixed.
The discrepancy \(d\) is defined on the relevant response space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_0\notin\mathcal M\), with irreducibility certified by \(\inf_{m\in\mathcal M}d(f_0,m)>0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly distinguishes model-class exclusion, positive best-approximation error, and finite-data estimation error, but it has no authoritative citation with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Posterior Overconfidence
children.top_down_role: Uncertainty estimates that are too narrow for reliable search decisions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient condition under which persistent predictive bias and collapsing reported uncertainty force asymptotic undercoverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(x\in\mathcal X\), \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), and \(z=z_{1-\alpha/2}\). If some \(\delta>0\) satisfies \[P_0\!\left(\left|\mu_t(x;D_t)-f_0(x)\right|\geq\delta,\ z\sigma_t(x;D_t)<\delta\right)\to1,\] then \[P_0\!\left(f_0(x)\in[\mu_t(x;D_t)-z\sigma_t(x;D_t),\mu_t(x;D_t)+z\sigma_t(x;D_t)]\right)\to0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the predictive center remains separated from the truth while the reported credible radius becomes smaller than that separation, interval coverage tends to zero.
assumptions_latex: \(D_t\) is random under the data-generating law \(P_0\).
The displayed persistent-error condition holds for some \(\delta>0\).

notation.meaning: Reported half-width of the nominal credible interval.
Persistent separation between predictive center and truth.

knowledge_statements.title: Variance-Collapse Overconfidence Criterion
Posterior Overconfidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Frequentist undercoverage criterion for a probabilistic surrogate used in Bayesian derivative-free optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_t\) be random under the data-generating law \(P_0\), let \(f_0:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) be the true objective, and let \(\nu\) be a reference measure on \((\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\). For \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), define \(I_{t,\alpha}(x;D_t)=[\mu_t(x;D_t)-z_{1-\alpha/2}\sigma_t(x;D_t),\mu_t(x;D_t)+z_{1-\alpha/2}\sigma_t(x;D_t)]\). The surrogate is posterior-overconfident at level \(1-\alpha\) on \(A\in\mathcal A\) if \(\nu(A)>0\) and \[P_0\!\left(f_0(x)\in I_{t,\alpha}(x;D_t)\right)<1-\alpha\qquad\text{for every }x\in A.\] Uniform overconfidence by a margin \(\varepsilon>0\) means that these coverage probabilities are at most \(1-\alpha-\varepsilon\) throughout \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Posterior overconfidence occurs when nominal surrogate credible intervals, viewed over repeated datasets, cover the true objective less often than their stated confidence level on a search region of positive reference measure.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal X,\mathcal A,\nu)\) is a measured search space.
\(D_t\) is random under \(P_0\), and \(f_0:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) is the true objective.
The surrogate fitted to \(D_t\) reports \(\mu_t(x;D_t)\) and \(\sigma_t(x;D_t)>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_0(f_0(x)\in I_{t,\alpha}(x;D_t))<1-\alpha\) on a set of positive \(\nu\)-measure.

notation.meaning: Nominal posterior credible interval computed from the random dataset.
Reference measure on the search space.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Posterior overconfidence is expressed through undercoverage of nominal credible intervals over repeated datasets.
Exact Bayesian-optimization calibration source not supplied.

children.title: Miscalibration-Induced Search Failure
children.top_down_role: Global-search failures arising from inaccurate predictive calibration.

knowledge_statements.title: Miscalibration-Induced Search Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient exclusion mechanism for lower-confidence-bound Bayesian search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) have minimum value \(f^*\), define \(B_\varepsilon=\{x\in\mathcal X:f(x)\le f^*+\varepsilon\}\), and let \(x_t\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal X}a_t(x)\), where \(a_t(x)=\mu_t(x)-\sqrt{\beta_t}\sigma_t(x)\). If there are \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(T\) such that \[\inf_{x\in\mathcal X\setminus B_\varepsilon}a_t(x)<\inf_{x\in B_\varepsilon}a_t(x)\qquad\text{for every }t\ge T,\] then \(x_t\notin B_\varepsilon\) and \(f(x_t)-f^*>\varepsilon\) for every \(t\ge T\). Persistent surrogate miscalibration that enforces this ordering therefore excludes the \(\varepsilon\)-optimal region from subsequent queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Search fails at the query level when surrogate miscalibration persistently makes some suboptimal point more attractive than every epsilon-optimal point, excluding all subsequent queries from the epsilon-optimal region.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) attains its minimum value \(f^*\), and \(B_\varepsilon\) is nonempty.
At iteration \(t\), the policy selects an attained minimizer of \(a_t(x)=\mu_t(x)-\sqrt{\beta_t}\sigma_t(x)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Persistent acquisition misranking can exclude an optimal region and cause nonvanishing per-query regret.
Exact source for this sufficient failure condition is not supplied.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary collapse of a noiseless Gaussian-process amplitude estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y=0\in\mathbb R^n\) and let a noiseless zero-mean Gaussian-process model have covariance \(K(\sigma,\ell)=\sigma^2R_\ell\), where \(\sigma>0\) and \(R_\ell\succ0\). Its log marginal likelihood is \[L(\sigma,\ell)=-n\log\sigma-\frac12\log\det R_\ell-\frac n2\log(2\pi).\] Hence \(L(\sigma,\ell)\to+\infty\) as \(\sigma\downarrow0\), so no maximum over \(\sigma>0\) exists unless a constraint or regularization prevents boundary collapse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For zero residuals in a noiseless Gaussian process, marginal likelihood is unbounded as signal amplitude approaches zero, so fitting can collapse to the boundary.
assumptions_latex: The mean and observation-noise variance are fixed at zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{\sigma>0}L(\sigma,\ell)=+\infty\text{, and no positive-amplitude maximum-likelihood estimate exists}.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Residual Marginal-Likelihood Degeneracy

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local diagnostic for weakly identified interior likelihood optima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\hat\theta\) be an interior stationary point of a twice continuously differentiable log likelihood \(L_D\), and define \(I_D(\hat\theta)=-\nabla^2L_D(\hat\theta)\). If \(I_D(\hat\theta)\succ0\), then \(\hat\theta\) is a strict local maximizer. Within the positive-definite regime, a small \(\lambda_{\min}(I_D)\) or large spectral condition number diagnoses weak local curvature. Singularity prevents this positive-definite local certificate, but neither positive definiteness nor good conditioning certifies global uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The negative likelihood Hessian certifies a strict local fit when positive definite and diagnoses weak local curvature when ill-conditioned.
assumptions_latex: \(L_D\) is twice continuously differentiable near an interior stationary point \(\hat\theta\).
knowledge_statements.title: Observed-Curvature Identification Diagnostic

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit Gaussian-process likelihood flatness in the length scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider one noiseless observation \(y_1\) from a zero-mean Gaussian process with covariance \(k_{\sigma,\ell}(x,x')=\sigma^2r_\ell(x,x')\), where \(r_\ell(x,x)=1\). The covariance matrix is \([\sigma^2]\), and the log marginal likelihood \[-\frac{y_1^2}{2\sigma^2}-\frac12\log\sigma^2-\frac12\log(2\pi)\] is independent of \(\ell\). Hence every admissible length scale is likelihood-equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With one stationary-kernel observation, marginal likelihood contains no information about the correlation length scale.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Observation Length-Scale Nonidentifiability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hyperparameter instability caused by observationally equivalent maximizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L_D:\Theta\to\mathbb R\) be a surrogate log likelihood. If a set \(M\subset\Theta\) containing at least two distinct points satisfies \(L_D(\theta)=\sup_{\vartheta\in\Theta}L_D(\vartheta)\) for every \(\theta\in M\), then maximum-likelihood hyperparameters are not identifiable from \(D\). A single-valued fitting rule must select among equivalent maximizers, and perturbations or different optimizer initialization can select separated members of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A ridge or separated collection of likelihood maximizers makes fitted hyperparameters nonidentifiable and selection-dependent.
assumptions_latex: Hyperparameters are fitted by maximum likelihood.
The global maximizer set contains at least two distinct points.
knowledge_statements.title: Likelihood-Ridge Nonidentifiability
Hyperparameter Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discontinuity criterion for fitted surrogate hyperparameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathfrak D,d_{\mathfrak D})\) be a metric space of datasets and let \(H:\mathfrak D\to\Theta\) map each dataset to fitted surrogate hyperparameters in the metric space \((\Theta,d_\Theta)\). The fitting procedure is hyperparameter-unstable at \(D\in\mathfrak D\) if \(H\) is discontinuous at \(D\); equivalently, there are \(\varepsilon_0>0\) and datasets \((D_n)_{n\ge1}\) such that \[d_{\mathfrak D}(D_n,D)\longrightarrow0\quad\text{and}\quad d_\Theta(H(D_n),H(D))\ge\varepsilon_0\qquad\text{for every }n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hyperparameter instability at a dataset means that arbitrarily small dataset perturbations can cause a fixed, nonvanishing change in the fitted surrogate hyperparameters.
assumptions_latex: Datasets lie in a metric space \((\mathfrak D,d_{\mathfrak D})\).
Hyperparameters are selected by \(H:\mathfrak D\to\Theta\), where \((\Theta,d_\Theta)\) is a metric space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Arbitrarily small data perturbations can produce a fixed positive change in fitted hyperparameters.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Instability of a fitted parameter map can be formalized as discontinuity with respect to dataset perturbations.
A source specializing this condition to surrogate hyperparameters is needed.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient probabilistic condition for eventual abandonment of an optimal neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an adapted query sequence and a measurable neighborhood \(U\supseteq X^*\), if \[\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\mathbb P(x_t\in U\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})<\infty\quad\text{almost surely},\] then \(x_t\in U\) occurs only finitely often almost surely. Thus the summability condition is sufficient for exploration starvation, but it is not equivalent to failure of simple-regret, recommendation-regret, or query-regret consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Summable conditional probabilities of visiting an optimal neighborhood imply that the neighborhood is visited only finitely often.
knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Visitation Starvation Test

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit failure caused by permanently excluding the global minimizer's region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X=[0,1]\), \(f(x)=x\), and let a deterministic minimization policy start at \(x_1=1\). Suppose its fitted surrogate assigns every unsampled point a predicted value at least \(1\), and ties are always resolved at \(x=1\). Then \(x_t=1\) and \(r_t^{\min}=1\) for every \(t\). In particular, the optimal neighborhood \(U=[0,1/2)\) is never visited.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A purely greedy, overconfident surrogate can repeatedly sample a suboptimal point and permanently ignore the minimizer's region.
assumptions_latex: The acquisition rule supplies no exploration incentive to unsampled points.
knowledge_statements.title: Greedy Exploitation Trap

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exploration-heavy sequence separating simple regret from query and average regret.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathcal X=[0,1]\) with \(f(x)=x\), let \(x_{2j-1}=0\) and \(x_{2j}=1\). Then \(r_t^{\min}=0\) for every \(t\), but \(q_{2j}=1\), so \(q_t\not\to0\), and \(R_T/T\to1/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternating between the minimizer and a bad exploratory point gives zero simple regret but neither query convergence nor average no-regret.
knowledge_statements.title: Persistent Exploration Without Query Convergence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinct visitation and performance criteria for sequential surrogate-based minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\), \(f^*=\min_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\), queries \(x_t\), and recommendations \(\hat x_t\). Exploration starvation occurs if some neighborhood \(U\supseteq X^*\) is visited only finitely often with positive probability. Define \(q_t=f(x_t)-f^*\), \(r_t^{\min}=\min_{s\le t}f(x_s)-f^*\), \(r_t^{\mathrm{rec}}=f(\hat x_t)-f^*\), and \(R_T=\sum_{t=1}^Tq_t\). Query, best-observed, recommendation, and no-regret consistency respectively require \(q_t\to0\), \(r_t^{\min}\to0\), \(r_t^{\mathrm{rec}}\to0\), and \(R_T/T\to0\). Query consistency implies best-observed consistency and, by Cesàro averaging, no-regret; the converse implications and recommendation consistency require additional assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exploration starvation, query convergence, best-observed convergence, recommendation convergence, and average no-regret are distinct requirements.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) attains a finite minimum on \(\mathcal X\).
The displayed regrets are finite and nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q_t\to0\Longrightarrow r_t^{\min}\to0\text{ and }R_T/T\to0;\text{ the remaining implications do not hold in general}.
knowledge_statements.title: Exploration and Regret Failure Notions

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) has a nonempty set \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\).
A randomized sequential policy selects \(x_t\) using the history filtration \((\mathcal F_t)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The policy fails the exploration requirement or fails asymptotic optimization consistency.

notation.meaning: Information available before the next query.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Exploration failure is captured by summable visitation probabilities, while exploitation failure is captured by nonvanishing simple regret.
A source for this unified taxonomy criterion is needed.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency-based boundary covering insufficient exploration and ineffective exploitation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An exploration failure occurs if some open neighborhood \(U\supseteq X^*\) satisfies \[\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\mathbb P(x_t\in U\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})<\infty\quad\text{almost surely},\] because the policy then need not revisit an optimal neighborhood indefinitely. An exploitation failure occurs if the best-observed simple regret \(r_t=\min_{1\le s\le t}f(x_s)-\min_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\) does not converge to \(0\) in probability. A surrogate policy exhibits exploration-exploitation failure when at least one of these two consistency requirements fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The balance fails if the policy can abandon an optimal neighborhood or if its best observed objective value does not converge to the global optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Exploration–Exploitation Failure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The criteria are mathematically coherent as a proposed failure taxonomy, but no inspectable source supports this particular unification of conditional visitation and simple-regret consistency.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric sample-size obstruction to locally informative surrogates on a high-dimensional cube.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\subset[0,1]^d\), let \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}([0,1]^d)\), and let \(v_d=\pi^{d/2}/\Gamma(d/2+1)\). For every \(r>0\), \[\mathbb P\!\left(\min_{1\le i\le n}\|X-x_i\|_2\le r\right)\le n v_d r^d.\] Consequently, coverage probability at least \(1-\delta\) requires \[n\ge \frac{1-\delta}{v_d r^d}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-radius neighborhoods around n sites cover at most n ball-volumes of the cube, so high-probability local coverage requires a rapidly growing number of sites as dimension increases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb P(\operatorname{dist}(X,S)\le r)\le n v_d r^d,\qquad n\ge(1-\delta)/(v_d r^d).

notation.meaning: Volume of the Euclidean unit ball in dimension d.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse-Coverage Boundary in High Dimension
High-Dimensional Surrogate Collapse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete distance-concentration mechanism for fixed-length-scale squared-exponential Gaussian-process surrogates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n,X\) be independent \(N(0,I_d)\) vectors, with fixed \(n\), and let \[k_d(x,y)=\tau^2\exp\!\left(-\frac{\lVert x-y\rVert^2}{2\ell^2}\right)\] for fixed \(\tau,\ell>0\). For distinct \(i,j\), \[k_d(X_i,X_j)\longrightarrow0,\qquad k_d(X,X_i)\longrightarrow0\quad\text{in probability as }d\to\infty,\] and the Gram matrix \(K_d=(k_d(X_i,X_j))_{i,j=1}^n\) converges entrywise in probability to \(\tau^2I_n\). For Gaussian-process regression with fixed positive observation-noise variance and tight training residuals, the posterior mean and variance at the independent test point converge in probability to their prior values. This is a high-dimensional surrogate-collapse mechanism when the length scale does not grow with dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With fixed length scale, independent Gaussian points separate as dimension grows, squared-exponential correlations vanish, and a standard Gaussian-process posterior reverts to its prior at an independent test point under controlled observations.
assumptions_latex: The covariance kernel is squared exponential with fixed \(\tau,\ell>0\).
For the posterior-reversion conclusion, Gaussian-process regression has fixed positive observation-noise variance and tight training residuals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Off-diagonal and test-training covariances converge to zero in probability, and the specified posterior reverts to its prior at the independent test point.

notation.meaning: Squared-exponential covariance kernel in dimension d.
Kernel Gram matrix of the training inputs.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Gaussian distance concentration yields degeneration of a fixed-length-scale squared-exponential kernel.
A source for the Gaussian-process and Bayesian-optimization interpretation remains required.

children.title: Randomized Zeroth-Order Methods
children.top_down_role: Randomized feedback, estimator, smoothing, and descent families for deterministic and stochastic zeroth-order optimization.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information limitation imposed by one scalar response per round.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under one-point feedback, suppose \(\mathcal F_t=\sigma(\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t,Y_t)\), where \(Y_t\) is the sole new oracle response. Then the round supplies no second contemporaneous response at another newly queried point. In particular, a same-round finite difference using two new oracle values is unavailable from one-point feedback alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One-point feedback cannot provide a same-round comparison between two newly queried points; that requires another response or stored information.
assumptions_latex: Y_t\text{ is the sole oracle response returned in round }t
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{A two-response contemporaneous contrast is unavailable from round-}t\text{ one-point feedback alone.}
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Round Comparison Boundary
One-Point Feedback
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-query stochastic zeroth-order feedback model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal F_t)\) be the algorithm's history filtration. At round \(t\), the algorithm chooses an \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\)-measurable point \(x_t\in\mathcal X\) and receives exactly one scalar observation \[Y_t=F(x_t,\xi_t),\qquad \mathbb E[Y_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]=f(x_t),\] where \(\xi_t\) is sampled after \(x_t\) is chosen with the prescribed conditional oracle law. No second function value or derivative information is revealed in that round.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One-point feedback provides exactly one conditionally unbiased noisy function value at the adaptively selected query in each round, with no simultaneous comparison value or derivative information.
assumptions_latex: The stochastic oracle is \(F:\mathcal X\times\Xi\to\mathbb R\).
The query \(x_t\) is measurable with respect to \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\).
Oracle randomness is sampled after query selection and satisfies \(\mathbb E[F(x_t,\xi_t)\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]=f(x_t)\).
Only one oracle call is permitted in each round.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The one-point model reveals one scalar zeroth-order observation per round.
Exact zeroth-order oracle-model source not supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conditional Mean of the Observable Paired Difference
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mean identity intrinsic to conditionally unbiased two-point feedback.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For conditionally unbiased responses at \(x_t^\pm=x_t\pm\delta_tu_t\), \[\mathbb E\!\left[\frac{Y_t^+-Y_t^-}{2\delta_t}\middle|\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t,u_t,\delta_t\right]=\frac{f(x_t+\delta_tu_t)-f(x_t-\delta_tu_t)}{2\delta_t}.\] The identity depends only on the two conditional marginal means and therefore holds for independent or coupled response noises.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conditional mean of the observed paired difference is the symmetric finite difference of the objective, regardless of noise coupling.
knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Mean of the Observable Paired Difference
Two-Point Feedback
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric paired-query stochastic feedback allowing an explicitly specified noise coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal F_t)\) be the history filtration. At round \(t\), the algorithm chooses \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\)-measurable \(x_t\), \(u_t\), and \(\delta_t>0\), with \(x_t\pm\delta_tu_t\in\mathcal X\), and observes \[Y_t^+=F(x_t+\delta_tu_t,\xi_t^+),\qquad Y_t^-=F(x_t-\delta_tu_t,\xi_t^-).\] The feedback law satisfies \[\mathbb E[Y_t^\pm\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t,u_t,\delta_t]=f(x_t\pm\delta_tu_t).\] Its specification includes the conditional joint law of \((\xi_t^+,\xi_t^-)\), whose components may be independent or coupled. The scaled difference \((Y_t^+-Y_t^-)/(2\delta_t)\) is an observable directional finite difference.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two-point feedback returns conditionally unbiased noisy values at two symmetric perturbations of an adaptively chosen center, with the dependence between their noises included in the feedback model.
assumptions_latex: The center, direction, and positive radius are selected from the past history.
Both perturbed points belong to \(\mathcal X\).
Each response is conditionally unbiased given the history and complete selected query pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The round reveals the paired vector \((Y_t^+,Y_t^-)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Two-point feedback is a paired-query zeroth-order oracle model.
Exact zeroth-order oracle-model source not supplied.

children.title: Multi-Point Feedback
children.top_down_role: Zeroth-order feedback obtained from several coordinated query points.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact scalar-query accounting for batched multi-point feedback.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If feedback round \(t\) returns \(q_t\) scalar responses, then after \(T\) completed rounds the scalar evaluation count is \[N_T=\sum_{t=1}^{T}q_t.\] Hence a round bound is not an oracle-call bound without control of the batch sizes; if \(q_t\le q_{\max}\), then \(N_T\le q_{\max}T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The scalar evaluation count is the sum of the batch sizes, so feedback-round and oracle-call complexities are distinct.
assumptions_latex: q_t\ge2\text{ is the batch size in round }t
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_T=\sum_{t=1}^{T}q_t,\qquad q_t\le q_{\max}\ \forall t\implies N_T\le q_{\max}T.

notation.meaning: Total scalar function evaluations through round T.
Number of scalar responses in round t.

knowledge_statements.title: Round Complexity versus Query Complexity
Multi-Point Feedback
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General batched zeroth-order feedback with an explicit joint noise law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal F_t)\) be the history filtration. A multi-point feedback round selects an \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\)-measurable finite batch \((x_{t,1},\ldots,x_{t,q_t})\in\mathcal X^{q_t}\), where \(q_t\ge2\), and returns \[Y_t=\bigl(F(x_{t,1},\xi_{t,1}),\ldots,F(x_{t,q_t},\xi_{t,q_t})\bigr).\] For every \(j\), \[\mathbb E[F(x_{t,j},\xi_{t,j})\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_{t,1},\ldots,x_{t,q_t}]=f(x_{t,j}).\] The conditional joint distribution of \((\xi_{t,1},\ldots,\xi_{t,q_t})\) is part of the feedback regime and may couple the responses. The algorithm updates only after receiving the entire vector \(Y_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multi-point feedback returns a conditionally unbiased batch of two or more function observations before the algorithm updates, with the joint dependence among observation noises included in the model.
assumptions_latex: At round \(t\), the algorithm selects \(q_t\ge2\) queries from the past history before updating.
Each oracle response is conditionally unbiased given the history and the full selected batch.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feedback is the jointly distributed vector \(Y_t=(F(x_{t,j},\xi_{t,j}))_{j=1}^{q_t}\).

notation.meaning: Number of queries in round t.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Multi-point feedback consists of a batch of jointly distributed zeroth-order observations obtained before an update.
Exact multi-query oracle-model source not supplied.

children.title: Common-Random-Number Feedback
children.top_down_role: Feedback using shared random inputs across comparative evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Common-Random-Number Feedback
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shared-randomness coupling for batched stochastic function evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal F_t)\) be the history filtration, and let \((x_{t,1},\ldots,x_{t,q_t})\) be a batch selected from \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\). Common-random-number feedback samples one random input \(\xi_t\) after the batch is selected and reuses it at every query point: \[Y_{t,j}=F(x_{t,j},\xi_t),\qquad j=1,ldots,q_t.\] The conditional law of \(\xi_t\) is such that \[\mathbb E[Y_{t,j}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_{t,1},\ldots,x_{t,q_t}]=f(x_{t,j})\] for each \(j\). The response vector is generally dependent; for two queries, shared variation may cancel in \(F(x^+,\xi_t)-F(x^-,\xi_t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Common-random-number feedback samples one shared random input after selecting a batch and uses it at every query, deliberately coupling otherwise conditionally unbiased responses.
assumptions_latex: Several query points are selected within the same feedback round.
The shared input is sampled after batch selection with conditional marginals that make each response unbiased.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All responses use the same draw \(\xi_t\), inducing cross-query dependence.

notation.meaning: Shared random input in round t.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Common random numbers reuse one exogenous draw across compared simulation inputs.

children.title: Variance Coupling Across Queries
children.top_down_role: Dependence patterns created by coordinated points or shared randomness.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Covariance-Matrix Representation of Coupled Estimator Variance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variance representation for linear contrasts of coupled query responses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_q)^{\mathsf T}\) be square-integrable with covariance matrix \(\Sigma\), and let \(a\in\mathbb R^q\) be deterministic. Then \[\operatorname{Var}(a^{\mathsf T}Y)=a^{\mathsf T}\Sigma a=\sum_{i=1}^q a_i^2\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)+2\sum_{i<j}a_i a_j\operatorname{Cov}(Y_i,Y_j).\] Thus fixed marginal variances do not determine the variance of a coupled contrast.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The variance of a linear contrast is the covariance quadratic form, so marginal noise levels alone are insufficient.

notation.meaning: Covariance matrix of the response vector.

knowledge_statements.title: Covariance-Matrix Representation of Coupled Estimator Variance

assumptions_latex: \(Y_1\) and \(Y_2\) are square-integrable oracle responses from two queries.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: This is the elementary variance identity for a difference and exactly characterizes the effect of cross-query covariance.
Application-specific source for coupled zeroth-order feedback is not supplied.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact variance identity governing coupled two-query differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any square-integrable paired responses \((Y_1,Y_2)\), \[\operatorname{Var}(Y_1-Y_2)=\operatorname{Var}(Y_1)+\operatorname{Var}(Y_2)-2\operatorname{Cov}(Y_1,Y_2).\] Relative to independent responses with the same marginals, a coupling with \(\operatorname{Cov}(Y_1,Y_2)>0\) reduces the variance of the difference by \(2\operatorname{Cov}(Y_1,Y_2)\); negative covariance increases it by the corresponding amount. For the scaled difference \((Y_1-Y_2)/(2\delta)\), the entire identity is divided by \(4\delta^2\). Hence variance reduction from common random numbers is conditional on producing positive cross-query covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The variance of a paired difference decreases exactly with twice the cross-query covariance; common random numbers help only when they induce positive covariance.
knowledge_statements.title: Variance Coupling Across Queries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The variance identity and its covariance interpretation are correct and the property kind fits the leaf, but the record has no inspectable citation for its coupled-feedback application.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Truncation-versus-evaluation-error boundary for coordinate differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\widetilde f(y)=f(y)+\eta_y\) with \(|\eta_y|\le\varepsilon_f\), evaluation error contributes at most \(\varepsilon_f/h\) to a central coordinate quotient and \(2\varepsilon_f/h\) to a forward quotient. Under the central truncation bound \(M_i h^2/6\), \(|\widetilde c_i-\partial_i f(x)|\le M_i h^2/6+\varepsilon_f/h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluation errors are divided by the sampling radius, preventing indefinite improvement as the radius shrinks.
assumptions_latex: The exact central quotient has truncation error at most \(M_i h^2/6\).
knowledge_statements.title: Evaluation-Error Amplification

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Central coordinate truncation error under third-derivative control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(|\partial_{iii}f(x+te_i)|\le M_i\) for \(|t|\le h\), then \(c_i=(f(x+he_i)-f(x-he_i))/(2h)\) satisfies \(|c_i-\partial_i f(x)|\le M_i h^2/6\). Hence \(\|c-\nabla f(x)\|_2\le (h^2/6)(\sum_iM_i^2)^{1/2}\). The quotient is exact when each coordinate-line restriction is quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Central coordinate differences are second-order accurate under bounded third derivatives and exact on quadratic coordinate restrictions.
assumptions_latex: Each coordinate-line restriction is three times differentiable on the queried interval.
knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Central-Difference Accuracy

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward and backward coordinate estimators with baseline reuse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \([g_h^+(x)]_i=(f(x+he_i)-f(x))/h\) and \([g_h^-(x)]_i=(f(x)-f(x-he_i))/h\). If \(\nabla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on the queried segments, then \(|[g_h^\pm(x)]_i-\partial_i f(x)|\le Lh/2\), so \(\|g_h^\pm(x)-\nabla f(x)\|_2\le \sqrt dLh/2\). With reuse of \(f(x)\), either full estimator costs \(d+1\) evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward and backward coordinate differences cost d plus one evaluations with baseline reuse and have first-order error under Lipschitz-gradient smoothness.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient on every queried segment.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Coordinate Differences

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable and has \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.
The points \(x\pm he_i\) are feasible for every coordinate, with \(h>0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The displayed estimator and Lipschitz-gradient error bound follow from standard coordinatewise central finite differences.
Supplied coordinate-search locators do not specifically certify this estimator formula.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic central coordinate estimator and its basic smoothness error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The central coordinate finite-difference estimator is \[g_h^{\mathrm{cd}}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^d\frac{f(x+he_i)-f(x-he_i)}{2h}e_i.\] It requires \(2d\) function evaluations when no queried values are reused. If \(\nabla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, then each component satisfies \[\left|\frac{f(x+he_i)-f(x-he_i)}{2h}-\partial_i f(x)\right|\le\frac{Lh}{2}.\] Consequently, \(\lVert g_h^{\mathrm{cd}}(x)-\nabla f(x)\rVert_2\le\sqrt d\,Lh/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Central coordinate differences use two evaluations per coordinate and approximate the gradient with Euclidean error at most one half times the smoothness constant, step size, and square root of dimension.
knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate Finite-Difference Estimators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The central coordinate estimator, its 2d evaluation count without reuse, and the Lipschitz-gradient error bound are correct. The supplied inventory locators concern coordinate search rather than this estimator and bound.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension dependence of one symmetric spherical sample.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is \(K\)-Lipschitz on \(x+\delta B_d\), the seed's symmetric estimator satisfies \(\|g_\delta(x;u)\|_2\le dK\) almost surely and \(\mathbb E\|g_\delta(x;u)\|_2^2\le d^2K^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded sphere directions produce bounded samples, with a worst-case norm growing linearly in dimension.
knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz Sample-Magnitude Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient bias induced by uniform-ball smoothing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(
abla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(x+\delta B_d\), then \(
abla f_\delta(x)=\mathbb E[
abla f(x+\delta v)]\) and \(\|
abla f_\delta(x)-
abla f(x)\|_2\le L\delta\mathbb E\|v\|_2=L\delta d/(d+1)\le L\delta\), where \(v\) is uniform on \(B_d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform-ball smoothing perturbs an L-smooth gradient by at most L delta times d over d plus one.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform-Ball Smoothing Bias

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reusable-baseline estimator for uniform-ball smoothing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u\sim\operatorname{Unif}(S^{d-1})\). If the ball-smoothing identity is valid, \(G_\delta^+(x;u)=\frac d\delta(f(x+\delta u)-f(x))u\) satisfies \(\mathbb E[G_\delta^+(x;u)]=\nabla f_\delta(x)\). It uses one displaced value and a baseline reusable across directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dimension-scaled one-sided sphere difference is unbiased for the uniform-ball-smoothed gradient.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is continuous on a neighborhood of \(x+\delta B_d\), and all queries are admissible.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Spherical Estimator
Spherical-Direction Estimators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric uniform-sphere estimator for the gradient of uniform-ball smoothing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u\sim\operatorname{Unif}(S^{d-1})\), let \(\delta>0\), and suppose \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is continuous on a neighborhood of \(x+\delta B_d\). Define \[f_\delta(x)=\mathbb E_{v\sim\operatorname{Unif}(B_d)}[f(x+\delta v)]\] and \[g_\delta(x;u)=\frac{d}{2\delta}\bigl(f(x+\delta u)-f(x-\delta u)\bigr)u.\] Then \[\mathbb E_u[g_\delta(x;u)]=\nabla f_\delta(x).\] Thus the estimator is unbiased for the gradient of the ball-smoothed objective, not generally for \(\nabla f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an objective continuous near the smoothing ball, a symmetric difference along a uniformly random sphere direction, scaled by dimension, is unbiased for the gradient of the uniformly ball-smoothed objective.
assumptions_latex: \(u\) is uniform on the unit sphere \(S^{d-1}\).
\(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is continuous on a neighborhood of \(x+\delta B_d\).

notation.meaning: Unit sphere and unit ball in d dimensions.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The spherical smoothing identity is standard for uniform-sphere zeroth-order estimators.
Exact randomized zeroth-order reference and locator are not supplied.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain boundary caused by Gaussian perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every finite \(R\) and \(\mu>0\), \(\mathbb P(\|\mu u\|_2>R)>0\). Thus availability of \(f\) only on \(B(x,R)\) does not define the unmodified Gaussian estimator. A global extension, a failed-query rule, or truncation or rejection that changes the sampling law is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gaussian perturbations leave every bounded neighborhood with positive probability.
assumptions_latex: The oracle is available only on a bounded neighborhood of \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unmodified Gaussian estimator has positive probability of an inadmissible query.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Support Query Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient bias induced by Gaussian convolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f\) is differentiable, \(
abla f\) is globally \(L\)-Lipschitz, and the Gaussian expectations are finite, then \(
abla f_\mu(x)=\mathbb E[
abla f(x+\mu u)]\) and \(\|
abla f_\mu(x)-
abla f(x)\|_2\le L\mu\mathbb E\|u\|_2\le L\mu\sqrt d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a globally L-smooth objective, Gaussian smoothing changes the gradient by at most L times the radius times square root of dimension.
assumptions_latex: The Gaussian expectations and differentiation interchange are valid.
knowledge_statements.title: Gaussian Smoothing Bias Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided Gaussian finite differences targeting the Gaussian-smoothed gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)\), define \(G_\mu^{\mathrm{anti}}(x;u)=[f(x+\mu u)-f(x-\mu u)]u/(2\mu)\). Whenever Gaussian convolution is differentiable and the required expectations are finite, symmetry gives \(\mathbb E[G_\mu^{\mathrm{anti}}(x;u)]=\nabla f_\mu(x)\). It uses two displaced evaluations and cancels even Taylor terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An antithetic Gaussian pair is unbiased for the Gaussian-smoothed gradient under valid convolution-differentiation hypotheses.
assumptions_latex: The required expectations are finite and differentiation of the Gaussian convolution is justified.
review_flags: The conclusion requires stronger hypotheses than mere local integrability.
knowledge_statements.title: Antithetic Gaussian Estimator

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) is locally integrable and the displayed expectations are finite.
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports the Gaussian smoothing identity; a precise zeroth-order source is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided estimator for isotropic Gaussian smoothing in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(f_\mu(x)=\mathbb{E}[f(x+\mu u)]\) and
\[
G_\mu(x;u)=\frac{f(x+\mu u)-f(x)}{\mu}u.
\]
Whenever differentiation may be interchanged with Gaussian integration, Stein's identity gives
\[
\nabla f_\mu(x)=\frac{1}{\mu}\mathbb{E}[f(x+\mu u)u]=\mathbb{E}[G_\mu(x;u)],
\]
because \(\mathbb{E}[u]=0\). Thus a single Gaussian direction and two function values produce an unbiased estimator of the gradient of the Gaussian-smoothed objective, not generally of \(\nabla f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Gaussian finite-difference direction is unbiased for the gradient of the Gaussian-smoothed objective, although generally biased for the original gradient.
knowledge_statements.title: Gaussian-Direction Estimators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits Gaussian-direction estimators and the content kind is appropriate, but no citation is supplied. The stated local-integrability and finiteness assumptions do not by themselves precisely justify differentiation of the Gaussian convolution or Stein integration by parts, so an authoritative locator is needed to establish sufficient hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Averaging independent importance-weighted coordinate samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For conditionally independent identically distributed draws \(I_1,\ldots,I_b\), let \(\overline G_b=b^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^bG_\mu(x;I_r)\). Then \(\mathbb E[\overline G_b\mid x]=D_\mu f(x)\) and \(\mathbb E[\|\overline G_b-D_\mu f(x)\|_2^2\mid x]=b^{-1}\mathbb E[\|G_\mu-D_\mu f(x)\|_2^2\mid x]\). Without reuse it costs \(2b\) evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent coordinate samples preserve the target and reduce sampling variance by the batch size.
assumptions_latex: The coordinate draws are conditionally independent and identically distributed.
The conditional second moment is finite.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent Mini-Batch Coordinate Estimation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessity of positive sampling coverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(p_j=0\), adding an affine term \(cx_j\) does not change any sampled coordinate difference, although it changes the full difference vector in coordinate \(j\). Consequently no estimator using only those observations can be unbiased for the full vector over all affine objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinate that is never sampled is unidentifiable.
assumptions_latex: Coordinate \(j\) is sampled with probability zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_j=0\) precludes universal unbiased estimation of the full coordinate-difference vector.
knowledge_statements.title: Missing-Coordinate Identifiability Failure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact variance and variance-minimizing sampling probabilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z=D_\mu f(x)\) and \(G=z_Ie_I/p_I\), with \(\mathbb P(I=i)=p_i>0\). Then \(\mathbb E\|G-z\|_2^2=\sum_i z_i^2/p_i-\|z\|_2^2\). On the nonzero support of \(z\), this is minimized by \(p_i=|z_i|/\|z\|_1\), with minimum second moment \(\|z\|_1^2\). Uniform sampling gives \((d-1)\|z\|_2^2\) variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact variance is controlled by the coordinate probabilities, and magnitude-proportional sampling is optimal when the difference magnitudes are known.
assumptions_latex: Every coordinate with \(z_i\ne0\) has positive sampling probability.
review_flags: The optimal distribution depends on generally unknown current coordinate-difference magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate-Sampling Second Moment

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\), \(\mu>0\), and all queried points belong to the oracle domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[G_\mu(x;I)]=D_\mu f(x)\), the vector of coordinatewise central differences.
review_flags: The supplied coordinate-method locator does not specifically establish this zeroth-order estimator identity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Importance-weighted central differences with one randomly sampled coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(i\in\{1,\ldots,d\}\), define
\[
[D_\mu f(x)]_i=\frac{f(x+\mu e_i)-f(x-\mu e_i)}{2\mu}.
\]
The coordinate-randomized estimator is
\[
G_\mu(x;I)=\frac{f(x+\mu e_I)-f(x-\mu e_I)}{2\mu p_I}e_I.
\]
Conditioning on \(I\) and summing over its distribution yields
\[
\mathbb{E}[G_\mu(x;I)]=\sum_{i=1}^d [D_\mu f(x)]_i e_i=D_\mu f(x).
\]
If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\), then \(D_\mu f(x)\to\nabla f(x)\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Importance weighting makes a randomly selected coordinate difference unbiased for the full vector of coordinatewise central differences.
knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate-Randomized Estimators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The estimator identity is algebraically precise, matches the coordinate-randomized leaf, and is appropriately classified as a representation. No source reference or inspectable locator supports this zeroth-order construction or its limiting statement.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional requirement for general simultaneous perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because the component quotient contains \(1/\Delta_i\), a well-defined finite-variance estimator requires \(\mathbb P(\Delta_i=0)=0\) and suitable inverse moments, typically \(\mathbb E[\Delta_i^{-2}]<\infty\). Rademacher perturbations satisfy this with \(\Delta_i^{-1}=\Delta_i\); mass at zero makes the estimator undefined, and excessive mass near zero can yield infinite variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simultaneous perturbations must avoid zero and control inverse moments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite-variance simultaneous perturbation requires nonzero components almost surely and controlled inverse second moments.
knowledge_statements.title: Inverse-Moment Requirement

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variance blow-up from noisy simultaneous evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the two evaluations contain independent zero-mean noises \(\xi_+,\xi_-\), each with variance \(\sigma^2\) and independent of a Rademacher perturbation, the noise contribution has expected squared norm \(d\sigma^2/(2\mu^2)\). Thus fixed observation noise makes the estimator variance diverge as \(\mu\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Observation noise is amplified as dimension divided by the squared perturbation radius.
assumptions_latex: \(\xi_+,\xi_-\) are independent, mean zero, and have variance \(\sigma^2\).
The noises are independent of the perturbation.
knowledge_statements.title: Observation-Noise Amplification

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Rademacher SPSA variance on affine objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=a^\top x+b\) and independent Rademacher components, the two-sided estimator is \(G=\Delta\Delta^\top a\). Hence \(\mathbb E[G]=a\), \(\mathbb E\|G\|_2^2=d\|a\|_2^2\), and \(\mathbb E\|G-a\|_2^2=(d-1)\|a\|_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two evaluations recover an unbiased affine gradient estimate, but a single perturbation retains dimension-dependent variance.
assumptions_latex: The perturbation components are independent Rademacher variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine SPSA Variance

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) is three times continuously differentiable near \(x\), with locally bounded third derivatives.
review_flags: No supplied source locator specifically covers simultaneous perturbation or its second-order bias.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided Rademacher simultaneous perturbation with two function evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
With \(\Delta=(\Delta_1,\ldots,\Delta_d)\), define each component by
\[
[G_\mu(x;\Delta)]_i=\frac{f(x+\mu\Delta)-f(x-\mu\Delta)}{2\mu\Delta_i},\qquad i=1,\ldots,d.
\]
The same two function evaluations determine all \(d\) components. A third-order Taylor expansion and the identities \(\Delta_i^{-1}=\Delta_i\), \(\mathbb{E}[\Delta_i\Delta_j]=0\) for \(i\ne j\), give
\[
\mathbb{E}[G_\mu(x;\Delta)]=\nabla f(x)+O(\mu^2)
\]
as \(\mu\downarrow0\), where the implicit constant may depend on \(d\) and the local third-derivative bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two symmetric evaluations along one Rademacher perturbation estimate every gradient component, with second-order bias under bounded third derivatives.
knowledge_statements.title: Simultaneous-Perturbation Estimators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The simultaneous-perturbation formula and second-order bias claim fit the terminal container, but the dimension-dependent Taylor remainder and required neighborhood assumptions need support from a specific SPSA or zeroth-order source. No citation is supplied.

children.title: Structured Direction Estimators
children.top_down_role: Zeroth-order estimators using problem-informed direction structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessity of full-span second moment for universal affine-gradient recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(M=\mathbb E[vv^\top]\) is singular, choose \(0\ne a\in\ker M\). Then \(\mathbb E[(a^\top v)^2]=a^\top Ma=0\), so \(a^\top v=0\) almost surely. The affine objectives \(0\) and \(a^\top x\) yield identical sampled directional differences although their gradients differ. Thus full-span covariance is necessary for universal affine-gradient identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular direction covariance leaves a nonzero gradient direction invisible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Universal affine-gradient identification is impossible for singular \(M\).

notation.meaning: Null space of the direction covariance.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular-Covariance Identifiability Failure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal covariance geometry under a fixed direction-energy budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(M\succ0\) and \(\operatorname{tr}M=\tau\), then \(\operatorname{tr}(M^{-1})\ge d^2/\tau\), with equality exactly when \(M=(\tau/d)I_d\). Thus isotropic covariance minimizes aggregate inverse-covariance amplification among full-span direction laws with fixed \(\mathbb E\|v\|_2^2=\tau\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With fixed average direction energy, isotropic covariance is best conditioned under the trace-inverse criterion.
knowledge_statements.title: Isotropic Covariance Minimizes Correction Amplification

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Central-difference bias for a full-span structured direction law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the seed estimator, if \(M=\mathbb E[vv^\top]\succ0\), \(\nabla^2f\) is \(\rho\)-Lipschitz on every queried segment, and the moment is finite, then \(\|\mathbb E[G_\mu(x;v)]-\nabla f(x)\|_2\le(\rho\mu^2/6)\mathbb E[\|M^{-1}v\|_2\|v\|_2^3]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full-span structured central estimator has second-order bias governed by direction norms and inverse covariance.
knowledge_statements.title: General Structured-Direction Bias Bound

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\), \(\mu>0\), and \(v\) is drawn from a prescribed structured set \(\mathcal{V}\subset\mathbb{R}^d\).
\(M=\mathbb{E}[vv^\top]\) is positive definite and the required function values are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_\mu(x;v)\) is covariance-corrected and reproduces every linear objective's gradient in expectation.
review_flags: The node admits several structure models; this record selects covariance-corrected directions from a prescribed structured set.
No supplied locator directly supports this general definition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General covariance-corrected definition covering structured direction families with full span.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A structured direction estimator associated with \(\mathcal{V}\) is
\[
G_\mu(x;v)=M^{-1}v\,\frac{f(x+\mu v)-f(x-\mu v)}{2\mu},\qquad v\in\mathcal{V},
\]
where the structure of \(\mathcal{V}\) may encode blocks, transforms, graphs, or other prescribed geometry. The requirement \(M\succ0\) ensures that all directions in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) are identifiable after covariance correction. In particular, for every affine function \(f(x)=a^\top x+b\),
\[
\mathbb{E}[G_\mu(x;v)]=M^{-1}\mathbb{E}[vv^\top]a=a.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A structured estimator samples from a prescribed direction family and corrects its covariance, exactly recovering gradients of affine objectives when the family spans the space.
knowledge_statements.title: Structured Direction Estimators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The covariance-corrected construction is a plausible definition for this broad structured-direction leaf, and its affine-exactness property is consistent with that definition. Because this record selects one particular meaning among several possible structure models, a specific source locator is required.

children.title: Sparse Direction Estimators
children.top_down_role: Zeroth-order estimators supported on restricted coordinate subsets.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of identifiability when a coordinate never appears.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(q_j=0\), then \(M\) is singular and \(v_j=0\) almost surely. The objectives \(f_0(x)=0\) and \(f_1(x)=cx_j\) therefore yield identical allowed differences although their gradients differ by \(ce_j\). No covariance correction can recover that coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinate omitted from every support is unidentifiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Full affine-gradient estimation is impossible when \(q_j=0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Inclusion Coordinate Failure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covariance conditioning imposed by sparse signed perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(v_i=\varepsilon_i\mathbf1_{\{i\in S\}}\), with signs mutually independent and independent of \(S\), \(M=\operatorname{diag}(q_i)\) and \(\operatorname{tr}M=\sum_iq_i=\mathbb E|S|=:s\). Hence \(\lambda_{\min}(M)\le s/d\) and \(\|M^{-1}\|_2\ge d/s\). Equality requires balanced probabilities \(q_i=s/d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An average support budget s forces inverse-covariance amplification of at least d over s.
assumptions_latex: The Rademacher signs are mutually independent and independent of the support.
knowledge_statements.title: Support-Budget Conditioning Tradeoff

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bias controlled by smoothness, support size, and covariance correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(M\succ0\), \(\nabla^2f\) is \(\rho\)-Lipschitz on every queried segment, and the moment is finite, then \(\|\mathbb E[G_\mu(x;v)]-\nabla f(x)\|_2\le(\rho\mu^2/6)\mathbb E[\|M^{-1}v\|_2\|v\|_2^3]\). For signed-support directions, \(\|v\|_2=\sqrt{|S|}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sparse central differences have second-order bias amplified by support size and inverse covariance.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Central-Difference Bias Bound

assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}\) is a random nonempty support and \(\varepsilon_i\) are independent Rademacher signs.
\(q_i=\mathbb{P}(i\in S)>0\), \(\mu>0\), and the queried function values are finite.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sparse signed perturbations with coordinate inclusion probabilities and covariance correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Set \(v_i=\varepsilon_i\mathbf{1}_{\{i\in S\}}\). Then \(v\) is sparse and
\[
\mathbb{E}[vv^\top]=M=\operatorname{diag}(q_1,\ldots,q_d).
\]
The corresponding sparse direction estimator is
\[
G_\mu(x;v)=M^{-1}v\,\frac{f(x+\mu v)-f(x-\mu v)}{2\mu}.
\]
For an affine objective \(f(x)=a^\top x+b\), its directional difference equals \(a^\top v\), and hence
\[
\mathbb{E}[G_\mu(x;v)]=M^{-1}\mathbb{E}[vv^\top]a=a.
\]
The oracle perturbation changes only the coordinates in \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sparse signed perturbations modify only sampled coordinates; inverse inclusion-probability correction preserves exactness for affine objectives.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Direction Estimators

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Batch central differences along a rotationally balanced orthonormal frame.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The orthogonal-direction batch estimator is
\[
G_{\mu,m}(x)=\frac{d}{m}\sum_{j=1}^m q_j\frac{f(x+\mu q_j)-f(x-\mu q_j)}{2\mu}.
\]
Orthogonality prevents repeated sampling of the same direction within a batch, while the marginal isotropy condition supplies the normalization. For every affine objective \(f(x)=a^\top x+b\),
\[
\mathbb{E}[G_{\mu,m}(x)]=\frac{d}{m}\sum_{j=1}^m\mathbb{E}[q_jq_j^\top]a=a.
\]
For nonlinear objectives, this estimator averages central directional differences over the random orthonormal frame.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Central differences along a random orthonormal frame form a rotationally balanced batch estimator that is exact in expectation for affine objectives.
knowledge_statements.title: Orthogonal Direction Estimators

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform-ball smoothing and its boundary-sphere gradient formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the spherical, or uniform-ball, smoothing by
\[
f_\mu^{\mathrm{ball}}(x)=\mathbb{E}[f(x+\mu z)].
\]
The divergence theorem gives the boundary representation
\[
\nabla f_\mu^{\mathrm{ball}}(x)=\frac{d}{\mu}\mathbb{E}[f(x+\mu u)u].
\]
Since \(\mathbb{E}[u]=0\), the same gradient equals
\[
\frac{d}{\mu}\mathbb{E}[(f(x+\mu u)-f(x))u].
\]
Thus uniform-ball smoothing is naturally paired with function evaluations in uniformly random sphere directions; the factor \(d\) is the ball surface-to-volume normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform-ball average has a gradient represented by function values on the boundary sphere, yielding the standard spherical zeroth-order estimator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gaussian Convolution and Stein Gradient Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Isotropic Gaussian smoothing and its one-point and baseline-subtracted function-value gradient estimators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be globally Lipschitz, \(\mu>0\), and \(u\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)\). Define \(f_\mu(x)=\mathbb E[f(x+\mu u)]\). Then \(f_\mu\) is continuously differentiable and \[\nabla f_\mu(x)=\frac1\mu\mathbb E[f(x+\mu u)u]=\frac1\mu\mathbb E[(f(x+\mu u)-f(x))u].\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gaussian convolution smooths a Lipschitz objective, and Stein's identity expresses its gradient using perturbed function values.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Isotropic Gaussian convolution and its Stein gradient representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Gaussian smoothing at scale \(\mu\) is the convolution
\[
f_\mu(x)=\mathbb{E}[f(x+\mu u)].
\]
Under conditions permitting differentiation or Gaussian integration by parts, the smoothed function satisfies
\[
\nabla f_\mu(x)=\frac{1}{\mu}\mathbb{E}[f(x+\mu u)u]
=\frac{1}{\mu}\mathbb{E}[(f(x+\mu u)-f(x))u].
\]
The second equality follows from \(\mathbb{E}[u]=0\). The convolution can therefore be differentiable even when \(f\) is not, and its gradient is accessible using only function values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gaussian smoothing convolves the objective with isotropic Gaussian noise; Stein's identity expresses its gradient using only perturbed function values.
knowledge_statements.title: Gaussian Smoothing

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regularity and approximation properties of Gaussian smoothing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preservation of Lipschitz continuity, induced smoothness, and pointwise approximation error under Gaussian smoothing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(F:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is \(B\)-Lipschitz and \(F_\delta(\theta)=\mathbb E_{z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)}[F(\theta+\delta z)]\) for \(\delta>0\). Then \(F_\delta\) is \(B\)-Lipschitz and \((B\sqrt d/\delta)\)-smooth, and for every \(\theta\in\mathbb R^d\), \[|F_\delta(\theta)-F(\theta)|\le B\delta\sqrt d.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gaussian smoothing preserves the Lipschitz constant, yields smoothness constant B square-root-d divided by delta, and approximates the original function pointwise within B delta square-root-d.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_\delta\text{ is }B\text{-Lipschitz and }\frac{B\sqrt d}{\delta}\text{-smooth, and }\forall\theta\in\mathbb R^d,\ |F_\delta(\theta)-F(\theta)|\le B\delta\sqrt d

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regularity and approximation bounds for Gaussian smoothing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension-dependent regularity, bias, and estimator-moment bounds under an $L$-Lipschitz gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ have an $L$-Lipschitz gradient, let $\mu>0$, and let $u\sim\mathcal N(0,I_n)$. For $f_\mu(x)=\mathbb E[f(x+\mu u)]$,
\[
\nabla f_\mu(x)=\mathbb E\left[\frac{f(x+\mu u)-f(x)}{\mu}u\right]
\]
has Lipschitz constant $L_\mu\le L$. Moreover, for every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
\[
|f_\mu(x)-f(x)|\le\frac{\mu^2Ln}{2},\qquad
\|\nabla f_\mu(x)-\nabla f(x)\|\le\frac{\mu L}{2}(n+3)^{3/2},
\]
and
\[
\frac{1}{\mu^2}\mathbb E\left[(f(x+\mu u)-f(x))^2\|u\|^2\right]
\le\frac{\mu^2L^2}{2}(n+6)^3+2(n+4)\|\nabla f(x)\|^2.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gaussian smoothing preserves gradient Lipschitz continuity up to constant L and satisfies explicit objective-bias, gradient-bias, and finite-difference second-moment bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_\mu\le L\text{ and the displayed bounds hold for every }x\in\mathbb R^n

If \(f\) is differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, then \(\|\nabla f_{\mu,A}(x)-\nabla f(x)\|\leq L\mu\mathbb E\|Az\|\leq L\mu\|A\|_F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Anisotropic smoothing bias is controlled by the expected shaped perturbation length and therefore by the Frobenius norm of the geometry matrix.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and function-value gradient representation for full-dimensional matrix-shaped Gaussian smoothing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be globally Lipschitz, \(A\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\) invertible, \(\mu>0\), and \(z\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)\). Define \(f_{\mu,A}(x)=\mathbb E[f(x+\mu Az)]\). This is convolution with \(\mathcal N(0,\mu^2AA^\top)\), and \[\nabla f_{\mu,A}(x)=\frac1\mu A^{-\top}\mathbb E[f(x+\mu Az)z]=\frac1\mu A^{-\top}\mathbb E[(f(x+\mu Az)-f(x))z].\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invertible matrix shapes the Gaussian covariance, and inverse-transpose correction converts function values into an unbiased gradient estimator for the smoothed objective.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) is measurable and all displayed expectations and derivatives exist.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-rank anisotropic Gaussian smoothing determined by a fixed geometry matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
f_{\mu,A}(x)=\mathbb{E}[f(x+\mu Az)].
\]
This is convolution with a centered Gaussian having covariance \(\mu^2AA^\top\). Gaussian integration by parts yields
\[
\nabla f_{\mu,A}(x)=\frac{1}{\mu}A^{-\top}\mathbb{E}[f(x+\mu Az)z].
\]
Because \(\mathbb{E}[z]=0\), \(f(x)\) may be subtracted inside the expectation. Consequently,
\[
\frac{1}{\mu}A^{-\top}(f(x+\mu Az)-f(x))z
\]
is an unbiased function-value estimator of \(\nabla f_{\mu,A}(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invertible matrix shapes Gaussian smoothing, and inverse-transpose covariance correction gives an unbiased gradient estimator for the anisotropically smoothed objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Anisotropic Smoothing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inverse-transpose formula is consistent with full-rank anisotropic Gaussian smoothing and the representation content kind. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subspace Gaussian Smoothing and Projected Gradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Function-value representation of the smoothed directional gradient in a known subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be globally Lipschitz, let \(U\in\mathbb R^{d\times r}\) satisfy \(U^\top U=I_r\), and let \(z\sim\mathcal N(0,I_r)\). Define \(f_{\mu,U}(x)=\mathbb E[f(x+\mu Uz)]\). Its derivative along \(\operatorname{range}(U)\) is \[U\nabla_y\mathbb E[f(x+U(y+\mu z))]\big|_{y=0}=\frac1\mu U\mathbb E[(f(x+\mu Uz)-f(x))z].\] If the full gradient of \(f_{\mu,U}\) exists, the left side equals \(UU^\top\nabla f_{\mu,U}(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subspace smoothing yields a function-value estimator of the smoothed gradient component represented by the chosen subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The subspace directional gradient equals \(\mu^{-1}U\mathbb E[(f(x+\mu Uz)-f(x))z]\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\in\mathbb R^{d\times r}\) have orthonormal columns and suppose \(f(x)=g(U^\top x)\). For \(z\sim\mathcal N(0,I_r)\), \[\mathbb E[f(x+\mu Uz)]=g_\mu(U^\top x),\qquad g_\mu(y)=\mathbb E[g(y+\mu z)].\] Wherever differentiable, \(\nabla_x g_\mu(U^\top x)=U\nabla g_\mu(U^\top x)\), so no gradient component is omitted and sampling occurs in intrinsic dimension \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the objective truly depends only on a known subspace, subspace smoothing is exactly Gaussian smoothing of the reduced objective.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian smoothing restricted to a known active or modeled subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the structure-aware subspace smoothing
\[
f_{\mu,U}(x)=\mathbb{E}[f(x+\mu Uz)].
\]
It averages only along \(\operatorname{range}(U)\), leaving the orthogonal coordinates unsmoothed. Gaussian integration by parts in \(\mathbb{R}^r\) gives the projected-gradient identity
\[
UU^\top\nabla f_{\mu,U}(x)=\frac{1}{\mu}U\mathbb{E}[f(x+\mu Uz)z].
\]
Equivalently, subtracting \(f(x)\) inside the expectation does not change the right-hand side. The construction estimates only the component of the smoothed gradient represented by the chosen structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smoothing within a known subspace yields a function-value representation of the gradient projected onto that subspace, while ignoring orthogonal variation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine counterexample for smoothing and estimation confined to an incorrect proper subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\in\mathbb R^{d\times r}\) have orthonormal columns with \(r<d\), and choose nonzero \(a\in\operatorname{range}(U)^\perp\). For \(f_a(x)=a^\top x\), \(f_a(x+\mu Uz)-f_a(x)=0\) for every \(z\in\mathbb R^r\) and \(\mu>0\), although \(\nabla f_a(x)=a\neq0\). Thus observations restricted to \(\operatorname{range}(U)\) cannot identify the full gradient without an assumption excluding orthogonal variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A missed direction can contain a nonzero gradient even though every permitted subspace difference is zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Full-gradient identification fails on the affine family \(f_a(x)=a^\top x\) for nonzero \(a\perp\operatorname{range}(U)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Noise amplification in inverse-transpose-corrected anisotropic Gaussian estimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be invertible, \(z\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)\), and let independent oracle errors \(\xi_+,\xi_0\), also independent of \(z\), be centered with variances at most \(\sigma^2\). The estimator noise \(N=(\xi_+-\xi_0)A^{-\top}z/\mu\) satisfies \[\mathbb E\|N\|^2\leq\frac{2\sigma^2}{\mu^2}\|A^{-1}\|_F^2.\] This upper bound diverges as \(\sigma_{\min}(A)\downarrow0\).

assumptions_latex: The two errors are centered, mutually independent, independent of \(z\), and each has variance at most \(\sigma^2\).
