children.title: Latency Regimes
children.top_down_role: Evaluation management under heterogeneous or time-varying completion delays.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive heavy-tail definition for evaluation latency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A latency variable \(T\) has a regularly varying tail of index \(\alpha>0\) when \(\mathbb P(T>t)=t^{-\alpha}L(t)\), where \(L(ct)/L(t)\to1\) for every \(c>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regular variation defines a polynomial heavy-tail latency regime.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularly Varying Heavy-Tail Regime

knowledge_statements.scope_note: History-dependent duration model without a probabilistic delay guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Latency is adversarial relative to a scheduler when request durations may depend on submitted points and scheduler history and the model imposes no finite uniform almost-sure, moment, or tail bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adversarial latency allows history-dependent delays without a finite probabilistic completion guarantee.
assumptions_latex: The admissible duration rule is stated independently of any claimed scheduler guarantee.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{No bounded-delay or finite-moment conclusion follows from the regime alone}.
knowledge_statements.title: Adversarial Latency Regime

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform almost-sure completion-time bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A latency sequence \((T_i)\) is uniformly bounded when some \(\tau<\infty\) satisfies \(T_i\leq\tau\) almost surely for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every evaluation completes within one common finite bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Latency Regime

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Light-tail condition for a sequence of evaluation durations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence \((T_i)\) is uniformly exponentially integrable when some \(\lambda>0\) satisfies \(C=\sup_i\mathbb E[e^{\lambda T_i}]<\infty\). Then \(\sup_i\mathbb P(T_i>t)\leq Ce^{-\lambda t}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common positive exponential moment yields a uniform exponential delay bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Exponential-Tail Regime

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moment boundary for heavy-tailed evaluation durations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\mathbb P(T>t)=t^{-\alpha}L(t)\), then \(\mathbb E[T^p]<\infty\) for \(p<\alpha\) and \(\mathbb E[T^p]=\infty\) for \(p>\alpha\); the boundary \(p=\alpha\) depends on \(L\). In particular, \(\alpha<1\) implies \(\mathbb E[T]=\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sufficiently heavy latency tail invalidates analyses requiring finite mean evaluation time.
assumptions_latex: T\text{ has a regularly varying tail of index }\alpha.
knowledge_statements.title: Mean-Latency Failure Under Regular Variation

assumptions_latex: Evaluation durations are nonnegative random variables \(T_1,T_2,\ldots\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bounded, light-tail, heavy-tail, and adversarial regimes impose successively weaker control on completion delays and therefore support different scheduling guarantees.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational latency classes for concurrent black-box evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A latency sequence is bounded if \(T_i\leq\tau<\infty\) almost surely for every \(i\). It is light-tailed if there exists \(\lambda>0\) such that \(\sup_i\mathbb E[\exp(\lambda T_i)]<\infty\). It is heavy-tailed when \(\mathbb E[T_i]<\infty\) may hold but no uniform positive exponential moment is assumed. It is adversarial when durations may depend on submitted points or scheduler history and no finite probabilistic delay bound is imposed. Any runtime or utilization claim must state which regime, dependence assumptions, and cancellation policy it uses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Latency regimes distinguish uniformly bounded, light-tailed, heavy-tailed, and adversarial evaluation times; runtime guarantees must identify the applicable regime.
knowledge_statements.title: Latency Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits, but no source is supplied. The proposed heavy-tail clause is an absence-of-assumption statement that can include light-tailed sequences, so the classes are not a well-defined successive hierarchy and the conclusion is unsupported.

children.title: Straggler Effects
children.top_down_role: Progress loss and synchronization pressure caused by unusually slow evaluations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of independent speculative replicas on one straggling evaluation's completion time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let one logical evaluation be launched on \(r\ge1\) independent replicas with identically distributed nonnegative completion times \(T_1,\ldots,T_r\), and accept the first valid response. Its completion time is \(T_{(1)}=\min_jT_j\), and for every \(t\ge0\), \[\Pr(T_{(1)}>t)=\Pr(T_1>t)^r.\] Replication reduces the survival probability but consumes up to \(r\) physical attempts; the power law need not hold without independence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent speculative replicas reduce a job's tail probability to the r-th power of the original survival probability, at the cost of extra attempts.
assumptions_latex: Replica completion times are independent and identically distributed.
The first valid response is sufficient.
Launching or cancelling replicas is permitted.

Straggler Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case makespan degradation from one unusually slow black-box evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider one concurrent batch containing \(p\ge 2\) evaluations assigned to \(p\) identical workers at time zero. If \(p-1\) evaluations have duration \(1\) and one has duration \(L\ge 1\), the batch makespan is \(T_p=L\), whereas its average-work lower bound is \(T_{\mathrm{avg}}=(L+p-1)/p\). Thus the parallel efficiency relative to that bound is \[E_p=\frac{T_{\mathrm{avg}}}{T_p}=\frac{L+p-1}{pL},\] which converges to \(1/p\) as \(L\to\infty\). Hence a single unbounded straggler can eliminate nearly all batch-level parallel benefit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a synchronized batch, one arbitrarily slow evaluation can determine the makespan and reduce parallel efficiency toward one over the worker count.
assumptions_latex: All \(p\) evaluations start simultaneously and the batch waits for every result.

parallel efficiency relative to the average-work lower bound

children.title: Resource-Failure Handling
children.top_down_role: Containment and recovery for worker, device, queue, or service failures.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness boundary for redispatch after an uncertain worker failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an evaluation of \(x\) may commit a side effect or consume a charged evaluation before its acknowledgement is lost. If the coordinator redispatches \(x\) after the loss, then without an idempotency key or atomic commit record the execution may contain two committed evaluations of \(x\). Thus bounded retry limits attempts but does not imply exactly-once execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Retrying an evaluation whose completion is uncertain can duplicate work or side effects unless requests are idempotent or atomically recorded.
assumptions_latex: A lost response does not reveal whether the original evaluation committed.
Redispatch is permitted after a lost response.
No idempotency key or atomic commit record identifies repeated requests.
knowledge_statements.title: Retry Duplication Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-request recovery with explicit dispatch, deadline, accounting, and abandonment semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite request set \(I\), give request \(i\) at most \(r_i+1\) dispatched attempts and each attempt an enforceable finite deadline \(\tau_i\). Every nonterminal request is dispatched within finite time or explicitly abandoned. A valid response marks success; a failed or timed-out attempt increments \(a_i\) and either enables another attempt or marks terminal failure when the limit is reached. Charge every dispatched attempt by the declared accounting rule and stop when every request is successful, terminally failed, or abandoned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded retry terminates only when every request is eventually dispatched or abandoned and every dispatched attempt has an enforceable finite deadline.
assumptions_latex: Every nonterminal request is dispatched within finite time or explicitly abandoned.
Every dispatched attempt is classified by its deadline as valid, failed, or timed out.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{i\in I}a_i\leq\sum_{i\in I}(r_i+1),\qquad \text{and every request reaches a terminal state in finite time}.

notation.meaning: number of dispatched attempts for request i
retry limit after the initial attempt

knowledge_statements.title: Termination-Sound Bounded-Retry Recovery

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Successful-completion boundary when all suitable capacity can disappear permanently.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every worker capable of evaluating a nonterminal request may remain unavailable forever, no retry policy can guarantee a valid response. Bounded retry can guarantee only finite terminal classification unless eventual usable capacity and a successful attempt are additionally assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Retries cannot guarantee successful evaluation after permanent loss of all suitable resources; they can guarantee only failure or abandonment.
assumptions_latex: A pending request requires at least one suitable worker.
The failure model permits every suitable worker to remain unavailable indefinitely.

Resource-Failure Handling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded retry protocol for failed or timed-out derivative-free evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given trial points \(X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_N\}\), timeout \(\tau>0\), and retry limit \(r\in\mathbb N_0\), initialize attempt counters \(a_i=0\). Dispatch each unfinished \(x_i\) to an available worker. Accept and store any finite, valid response \(y_i\). On worker failure, invalid response, or elapsed time exceeding \(\tau\), increment \(a_i\); redispatch \(x_i\) while \(a_i\le r\), and otherwise place \(i\) in the terminal failure set \(F\). Stop when every index has either an accepted response or belongs to \(F\), and output \(\{(x_i,y_i):i\notin F\}\) together with \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Retry each failed or timed-out evaluation only up to a fixed limit, then return successful values together with an explicit terminal-failure set.
assumptions_latex: Each evaluation attempt is observable as valid, invalid, failed, or timed out.
The timeout \(\tau\) and retry limit \(r\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every point is returned with either one accepted response or membership in \(F\), after at most \(r+1\) attempts.

children.title: Robust Scheduling Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Operating limits where scheduling policies cease to preserve useful throughput.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite deterministic operating bound for independent evaluations with finite service times on identical workers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\) independent nonpreemptive evaluations have durations \(t_1,\ldots,t_n<\infty\) and be dispatched by a work-conserving list schedule to \(p\ge1\) identical workers. With \(W=\sum_{i=1}^n t_i\) and \(t_{\max}=\max_i t_i\), the makespan satisfies \[\max\{W/p,t_{\max}\}\le T\le W/p+(1-1/p)t_{\max}\le W/p+t_{\max}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finite independent jobs on identical workers, work-conserving list scheduling finishes within average work plus one largest-job term.
assumptions_latex: All evaluations are independent and ready for dispatch.
Workers are identical and evaluations are nonpreemptive.
Every \(t_i\) is finite and the scheduler is work-conserving.
knowledge_statements.title: Work-Conserving List-Scheduling Bound
Robust Scheduling Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions separating finite completion guarantees from adversarial nontermination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite evaluation set, a scheduler has a finite worst-case completion bound only if every evaluation reaches a terminal state in uniformly bounded time, either through a valid response or enforced abandonment. In particular, suppose one dispatched evaluation may run forever, cannot be preempted or timed out, and is required before the scheduling round terminates. An adversary may assign that evaluation infinite duration, making the round makespan \(T=\infty\), regardless of the number of other workers. Consequently, no finite bound depending only on job count and worker count exists without a finite timeout, abandonment rule, or uniform service-time bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite robust makespan guarantees require bounded service or enforceable abandonment; one required, nonpreemptible hanging evaluation destroys every finite worst-case bound.
assumptions_latex: The scheduling round requires a terminal state for every required evaluation.
At least one required evaluation has no service-time bound.
That evaluation cannot be preempted, timed out, or abandoned.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup T=\infty\), so no finite worst-case makespan bound follows from job and worker counts alone.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\), where \(\varnothing\ne D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and choose \(c\in\mathbb R^n\) and scales \(s_i>0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\). With \(S=\operatorname{diag}(s_1,\ldots,s_n)\), define \(x=c+Sz\), \(D_z=S^{-1}(D-c)\), and \(g:D_z\to\mathbb R\) by \(g(z)=f(c+Sz)\). Then \[\inf_{x\in D}f(x)=\inf_{z\in D_z}g(z).\] Moreover, the argmin sets, whether empty or nonempty, correspond bijectively under \(x=c+Sz\); in particular, every minimizer satisfies \(x^\star=c+Sz^\star\). Thus scaling changes coordinates and numerical geometry but not the represented optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive diagonal variable scaling gives an equivalent optimization problem: infimum values agree, and any minimizers correspond bijectively through the affine coordinate transformation.

children.title: Objective Scaling
children.top_down_role: Normalization of objective magnitudes, offsets, or multiple response scales.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary for minimization-order preservation under affine objective transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\ne\varnothing\) and \(g=\alpha f+\beta\) on \(D\). If \(\alpha<0\), then \(g(x)\le g(y)\) if and only if \(f(x)\ge f(y)\), and the minimizers of \(g\) are exactly the maximizers of \(f\), with either set possibly empty. If \(\alpha=0\), then \(g\) is constant and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_Dg=D\). Thus positive multiplication is necessary for an affine transformation to preserve the ordering of every nonconstant objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative scaling reverses minimization order, while zero scaling erases it; only a positive affine multiplier universally preserves order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Universal order preservation fails for nonconstant objectives whenever \(\alpha\le0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Nonpositive Objective-Scale Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduction-Ratio Invariance under Positive Affine Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of consistent objective and model scaling on actual-to-predicted reduction ratios.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g=\alpha f+\beta\) and \(m_g=\alpha m_f+\beta\), where \(\alpha>0\). For an incumbent \(x\) and trial \(y\) with \(m_f(x)-m_f(y)\ne0\), \[\frac{g(x)-g(y)}{m_g(x)-m_g(y)}=\frac{f(x)-f(y)}{m_f(x)-m_f(y)}.\] Hence a decision based only on this ratio is invariant when the objective and model are scaled consistently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Consistently scaling an objective and its model leaves the actual-to-predicted reduction ratio unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scaled and unscaled actual-to-predicted reduction ratios are equal.
knowledge_statements.title: Reduction-Ratio Invariance under Positive Affine Scaling
Objective Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive affine rescaling of black-box objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\), choose \(\alpha>0\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\), and define \(g(x)=\alpha f(x)+\beta\). For all \(x,y\in D\), \(g(x)\le g(y)\) if and only if \(f(x)\le f(y)\). Consequently, \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}g(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}f(x).\] Objective differences satisfy \(g(x)-g(y)=\alpha(f(x)-f(y))\); therefore, any absolute acceptance tolerance or model-error threshold expressed in objective units must also be multiplied by \(\alpha\) to preserve the same decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive affine objective scaling preserves ordering and minimizers, but absolute objective tolerances must be scaled by the same positive multiplier.

children.title: Domain Scaling
children.top_down_role: Transformation of bounds, trust regions, polling radii, or feasible-domain geometry.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transformation of local distance regions under normalization of a finite box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\operatorname{diag}(u_1-\ell_1,\ldots,u_n-\ell_n)\) with \(u_i>\ell_i\), and write \(x=\ell+Sz\). For corresponding centers \(x_k=\ell+Sz_k\), the physical Euclidean region \(\|x-x_k\|_2\le\Delta\) is exactly \[\|S(z-z_k)\|_2\le\Delta.\] Conversely, \(\|z-z_k\|_2\le\delta\) maps to \(\|S^{-1}(x-x_k)\|_2\le\delta\). Both corresponding regions are Euclidean balls only when \(S\) is a scalar multiple of the identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Box normalization maps Euclidean balls to weighted balls or ellipsoids unless all box widths are equal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Physical and normalized local regions correspond through the weighted norms induced by \(S\) and \(S^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Trust-Region Geometry under Box Normalization

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\) is bijective to \([0,1]^n\), the two infimum values agree, and existing minimizers satisfy \(x^\star=\ell+(u-\ell)\odot z^\star\).

notation.meaning: vectors of lower and upper box bounds

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: affine normalization of a nondegenerate box
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalization of a finite box domain to a dimensionless reference box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i,u_i]\) with \(\ell_i<u_i\) for every \(i\), and let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\). Define \(z_i=(x_i-\ell_i)/(u_i-\ell_i)\), so \(z\in[0,1]^n\), and define \(g:[0,1]^n\to\mathbb R\) by \(g(z)=f(\ell+(u-\ell)\odot z)\). This coordinate map is bijective, with inverse \(x=\ell+(u-\ell)\odot z\), and \[\inf_{x\in D}f(x)=\inf_{z\in[0,1]^n}g(z).\] The argmin sets correspond bijectively, whether or not they are empty. Hence box normalization preserves feasible points and any minimizers while making coordinate widths dimensionless and equal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine coordinate map sends any nondegenerate finite box to the unit box, preserves corresponding objective values and infima, and maps any minimizers bijectively.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain Scaling

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\), and consider \(x=c+Sz\) and \(g(z)=\alpha f(c+Sz)+\beta\), where \(S\) is diagonal with strictly positive entries and \(\alpha>0\). children.title: Model Conditioning Diagnostics
children.top_down_role: Numerical stability indicators for fitted local or global surrogate models.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The diagnostic passes exactly when \(A\) has full column rank and \(\kappa_2(A)\le\kappa_{\max}\).

notation.meaning: spectral condition number of the design matrix

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Singular-value diagnostic for a normalized derivative-free interpolation or regression system.

source_refs.locator: 6 Ensuring well poisedness and suitable derivative-free models p. 89

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m,q\in\mathbb N_0\) satisfy \(m+1\ge q+1\), let \(Y=\{y^0,\ldots,y^m\}\subset\mathbb R^n\), and choose \(x_c\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\Delta>0\). For a fixed basis \(\phi_0,\ldots,\phi_q\), form \(A\in\mathbb R^{(m+1)\times(q+1)}\) with \(A_{ij}=\phi_j((y^i-x_c)/\Delta)\) for \(i=0,\ldots,m\) and \(j=0,\ldots,q\). Given \(\kappa_{\max}\ge1\), the model system passes the conditioning diagnostic exactly when \(A\) has full column rank and \[\kappa_2(A)=\frac{\sigma_{\max}(A)}{\sigma_{\min}(A)}\le\kappa_{\max}.\] If \(A\) lacks full column rank, the diagnostic reports singularity; otherwise a larger condition number indicates greater worst-case amplification of data perturbations in the least-squares coefficient solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalize the sample coordinates, form the model design matrix, and pass the diagnostic exactly when the matrix has full column rank and its spectral condition number does not exceed the chosen threshold.
knowledge_statements.title: Model Conditioning Diagnostics

source_witnesses.locator: 6 Ensuring well poisedness and suitable derivative-free models p. 89

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerical consequence of solving a full-column-rank normalized model fit through normal equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}\) have full column rank. Then \(A^{\mathsf T}A\) is positive definite and \[\kappa_2(A^{\mathsf T}A)=\frac{\lambda_{\max}(A^{\mathsf T}A)}{\lambda_{\min}(A^{\mathsf T}A)}=\left(\frac{\sigma_{\max}(A)}{\sigma_{\min}(A)}\right)^2=\kappa_2(A)^2.\] Thus normal equations square the spectral condition number diagnosed on \(A\); if \(A\) is rank deficient, \(A^{\mathsf T}A\) is singular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normal equations square the spectral condition number of a full-column-rank normalized model matrix; rank deficiency makes the normal-equation matrix singular.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}\) has full column rank.
Conditioning is measured in the spectral norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa_2(A^{\mathsf T}A)=\kappa_2(A)^2\); rank deficiency of \(A\) implies singularity of \(A^{\mathsf T}A\).

notation.meaning: Normalized interpolation or regression design matrix.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\in\mathbb N_0\), and let \(Y=\{y^0,\ldots,y^m\}\subset\mathbb R^n\) be poised for interpolation in an \((m+1)\)-dimensional model space. children.title: Finite-Precision Effects
children.top_down_role: Loss of reliable numerical behavior caused by machine precision and scale.

assumptions_latex: \(U\subseteq\mathbb R\) is open, \(x\in U\), and \(h\ne0\) is such that \(x+h\in U\).
\(f\) is twice continuously differentiable on an interval containing \(x\) and \(x+h\) for the truncation comparison.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R\) be open, let \(f:U\to\mathbb R\), and choose \(x\in U\) and \(h\ne0\) with \(x+h\in U\). Suppose \(\widehat f(t)=f(t)(1+\delta_t)\) with \(|\delta_t|\le u\) for \(t\in\{x,x+h\}\), and define \(\widehat d_h=(\widehat f(x+h)-\widehat f(x))/h\). Then its roundoff contribution satisfies \[\left|\widehat d_h-\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}\right|\le\frac{u\bigl(|f(x+h)|+|f(x)|\bigr)}{|h|}.\] If \(f\) is twice continuously differentiable on an interval containing \(x\) and \(x+h\), the forward-difference truncation error is \(O(|h|)\), whereas this roundoff bound grows like \(1/|h|\). Thus reducing the sampling displacement indefinitely does not guarantee a more accurate derivative-free slope estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a scalar forward difference, decreasing the sampling displacement reduces smooth truncation error but amplifies relative evaluation errors, so finite precision prevents indefinite accuracy improvement.

Under correctly rounded round-to-nearest arithmetic, if \(0<h<(x^+-x)/2\), then \(\operatorname{fl}(x+h)=x\). Thus an oracle addressed by the rounded argument receives the same encoded point for the nominal queries \(x\) and \(x+h\).

\(x\) and its next larger representable number \(x^+\) are finite.

notation.meaning: Next representable floating-point number above x.

knowledge_statements.title: Sampling-Point Collapse under Rounding

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scale selection for a difference estimate with first-order truncation and inverse-scale roundoff terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A,B,u>0\), let \(E(h)=Ah+Bu/h\) for \(h>0\). Then \[E(h)\ge 2\sqrt{ABu},\] with equality exactly at \(h_\star=\sqrt{Bu/A}\). Hence this error model predicts a best displacement of order \(\sqrt u\), not an arbitrarily small displacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Balancing first-order truncation against amplified roundoff gives a displacement proportional to the square root of the roundoff scale.
assumptions_latex: The applicable error upper bound has the form \(Ah+Bu/h\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bound is minimized at \(h_\star=\sqrt{Bu/A}\), where its value is \(2\sqrt{ABu}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Roundoff–Truncation Balance

children.title: Cancellation Detection
children.top_down_role: Recognition of unreliable differences caused by subtractive cancellation.

knowledge_statements.title: Cancellation Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A posteriori subtraction-conditioning test for differences of nearby objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For two nonzero finite computed objective values \(a\) and \(b\), define the cancellation ratio \[\rho(a,b)=\frac{|a-b|}{|a|+|b|}.\] Under independent relative input perturbations bounded by \(u\), the relative perturbation of the exact difference is bounded by \(u/\rho(a,b)\) whenever \(a\ne b\). Given an admissible amplification \(\eta>0\), the subtraction is flagged as cancellation-prone when \(\rho(a,b)\le u/\eta\), equivalently when the perturbation bound is at least \(\eta\). If \(a=b\), set \(\rho=0\) and flag complete cancellation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compare the objective difference with the magnitudes being subtracted; a tiny ratio signals strong amplification of relative evaluation errors.
assumptions_latex: \(a,b\in\mathbb R\) are finite computed objective values.
Each input has relative perturbation magnitude at most \(u\).
\(\eta>0\) is the permitted relative-error amplification threshold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cancellation is flagged when \(\rho(a,b)\le u/\eta\), with \(\rho(a,a)=0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard condition number of scalar subtraction
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cancellation ratio and perturbation calculation are coherent and condition is appropriate for this diagnostic leaf. However, no inspectable source is supplied for the adopted relative-error model, threshold convention, or scalar-subtraction condition estimate.

children.title: Noise Detection
children.top_down_role: Empirical identification of stochastic or deterministic evaluation variability.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Gaussian Variance Test for Evaluation Noise
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Calibrated repeated-evaluation test under an explicit Gaussian oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_m\) be independent \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) evaluations at one fixed encoded point, with \(m\ge2\), and let \(s_m^2=(m-1)^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^m(Y_j-\bar Y_m)^2\). For \(\sigma_0>0\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), reject \(H_0:\sigma\le\sigma_0\) when \[(m-1)s_m^2/\sigma_0^2>\chi^2_{m-1,1-\alpha}.\] The rejection probability equals \(\alpha\) at \(\sigma=\sigma_0\) and is at most \(\alpha\) throughout the null hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under independent Gaussian replication, a chi-square statistic gives an exactly calibrated test for variance above a declared baseline.
assumptions_latex: The \(Y_j\) are independent and identically distributed \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated rule has size \(\alpha\) for testing \(H_0:\sigma\le\sigma_0\).

notation.meaning: Upper one-minus-alpha quantile of a chi-square distribution with nu degrees of freedom.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Gaussian Variance Test for Evaluation Noise

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Protocol-level detection of observable variability at one fixed encoded query.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For repeated recorded evaluations \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_m\) at the same encoded point and nominal settings, with \(m\ge2\), define \(R_m=\max_jY_j-\min_jY_j\). Given a prespecified tolerance \(\tau\ge0\), declare detectable nonrepeatability when \(R_m>\tau\). This certifies only that the recorded responses differ by more than the protocol tolerance; it does not identify a distribution or distinguish stochastic noise, changing simulator state, and numerical effects.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated responses whose range exceeds a declared tolerance provide an observable repeatability failure, but not a diagnosis of its source.
assumptions_latex: \(m\ge2\) evaluations use the same encoded point and nominal settings.
\(\tau\ge0\) is fixed before applying the diagnostic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_m>\tau\) is a protocol-level certificate of detectable nonrepeatability among the recorded evaluations.

notation.meaning: Range of the repeated recorded responses.

knowledge_statements.title: Replication-Based Repeatability Diagnostic

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic detection of pointwise stochastic variability from repeated evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_1,Y_2,\ldots\) be iid evaluations at one fixed encoded point with \(\mathbb E[Y_1^2]<\infty\) and variance \(\sigma^2\). Then \(s_m^2\to\sigma^2\) almost surely. Consequently, for a fixed \(t\ge0\), the rule \(s_m>t\) eventually declares variability almost surely when \(t<\sigma\), and eventually does not declare variability almost surely when \(t>\sigma\). No such separated conclusion follows from this statement when \(t=\sigma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With iid finite-variance replication, sample variance is strongly consistent, so fixed thresholds separated from the true standard deviation are eventually classified correctly.
assumptions_latex: Evaluations are iid at the same encoded point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_m^2\to\sigma^2\) almost surely, yielding eventual correctness for separated fixed thresholds.
knowledge_statements.title: Consistency of Replication-Based Variance Detection
Noise Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational repeated-evaluation detector for additive numerical noise in a black-box objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the observed value at a fixed point \(x\) be \(Y_j(x)=f(x)+\varepsilon_j(x)\) for \(j=1,\ldots,m\), with \(m\ge 2\). Define \(\bar Y_m(x)=m^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^mY_j(x)\) and \(s_m^2(x)=(m-1)^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^m(Y_j(x)-\bar Y_m(x))^2\). For prescribed absolute and relative tolerances \(\tau_a,\tau_r\ge0\), the evaluation is declared detectably noisy at \(x\) when \[s_m(x)>\tau_a+\tau_r\lvert\bar Y_m(x)\rvert.\] This condition detects repeatability failure at the tested point; it does not by itself identify the noise distribution or distinguish stochastic noise from changing numerical state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated evaluations detect noise when their sample standard deviation exceeds a chosen absolute-plus-relative tolerance; this does not identify the noise source.
assumptions_latex: \(m\ge 2\) evaluations are made at the same encoded point and nominal settings.
\(\tau_a,\tau_r\ge0\) are fixed before applying the detector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_m(x)>\tau_a+\tau_r\lvert\bar Y_m(x)\rvert\) certifies detectable nonrepeatability under the stated protocol.

notation.meaning: The j-th observed objective value at x.
Sample standard deviation of repeated observations.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Introduction: Tools and Challenges in Derivative-Free and Blackbox Optimization p. 3

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 1. Introduction: Tools and Challenges in Derivative-Free and Blackbox Optimization p. 3

Because the detector and its calibration are protocol-specific, an inspectable source supporting the rule is required.

children.title: Numerical-Noise Confounding
children.top_down_role: Regimes where rounding, cancellation, and oracle noise cannot be reliably distinguished.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical-Noise Confounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifiability boundary between the latent objective and unrestricted additive evaluation error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an oracle returns \(y(x)=f(x)+\varepsilon(x)\) on a queried set \(Q\). If no structural restriction is imposed on \(\varepsilon\), then the decomposition is unidentifiable: for every function \(\delta:Q\to\mathbb R\), define \(\tilde f(x)=f(x)+\delta(x)\) and \(\tilde\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon(x)-\delta(x)\). Then \[y(x)=\tilde f(x)+\tilde\varepsilon(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in Q.\] Consequently, evaluation data alone cannot determine whether an observed variation is objective structure or numerical noise; replication, bounds, distributional assumptions, or regularity assumptions are required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without restrictions on evaluation error, the same observations admit infinitely many objective-noise decompositions, so signal and noise cannot be separated.
assumptions_latex: The available information consists only of oracle values \(y(x)\) on \(Q\).
The additive error function is otherwise unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((f,\varepsilon)\) is not identifiable from \(y\) on \(Q\).

notation.meaning: Arbitrary transfer between signal and error.

source_refs.locator: 1.3 Limitations of derivative-free optimization p. 5

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3 Limitations of derivative-free optimization p. 5

children.title: Budget-Based Stopping
children.top_down_role: Termination based on evaluation, time, memory, or monetary limits.

assumptions_latex: A finite budget \(B>0\) and nonnegative request costs \(c_i\) are specified.
Before a request is issued, its charge or a valid reserved upper bound is known, so the hard budget cannot be exceeded.
The protocol fixes how failures and batched evaluations are charged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No charged request is issued once its charge would make cumulative cost exceed \(B\), and the incumbent at termination is returned without a stationarity claim.

notation.meaning: Charged cost of oracle request i.
Cumulative charged evaluation cost after k requests.
Number of requests admitted by the hard budget.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stopping rule based on a hard budget of charged black-box evaluations.

source_refs.locator: 1.4 How derivative-free algorithms should work p. 7

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c_i\ge 0\) be the charged cost of the \(i\)-th oracle request and let \(C_k=\sum_{i=1}^k c_i\), with \(C_0=0\). Given a hard budget \(B>0\), define \[K_B=\max\{k\in\mathbb N_0:C_k\le B\}.\] Provided each prospective charge is known or safely reserved before its request is issued, budget-based stopping permits requests only through \(K_B\); no request whose charge would make the cumulative cost exceed \(B\) is issued. The algorithm returns the incumbent \(x_{K_B}^{\mathrm{best}}\), selected using the declared feasibility and objective ordering. This resource-exhaustion condition makes no stationarity claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Admit charged evaluations only while their cumulative cost remains within the preset hard budget, then return the incumbent without claiming stationarity.
knowledge_statements.title: Budget-Based Stopping

source_witnesses.locator: 1.4 How derivative-free algorithms should work p. 7

knowledge_statements.statement_title: No Solution-Quality Certificate from Budget Exhaustion Alone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information limitation of termination solely because a finite evaluation budget is exhausted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an algorithm make finitely many value queries \(Q=\{x_1,\ldots,x_k\}\) in a domain \(D\) containing some \(z\notin Q\), and let its output depend only on the observations. For every response vector on \(Q\), there exist objectives \(f_0,f_1:D\to\mathbb R\) agreeing at every queried point such that \(f_1(z)<\min_{x\in Q}f_1(x)\), while \(f_0\) need not take a smaller value outside \(Q\). The algorithm has identical observations and output on both objectives, although its sampled incumbent is suboptimal for \(f_1\). Therefore budget exhaustion alone certifies resource compliance, not optimality, stationarity, or a nontrivial objective-gap bound over an unrestricted objective class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After finitely many unrestricted black-box queries, an unsampled point can hide a better value, so budget exhaustion provides no solution-quality certificate.
assumptions_latex: Only finitely many value queries are made.
The domain contains an unsampled point.
No regularity or structural restriction is imposed on the objective outside queried points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Budget exhaustion alone cannot certify optimality, stationarity, or a nontrivial global objective-error bound.
knowledge_statements.title: No Solution-Quality Certificate from Budget Exhaustion Alone

children.title: Stationarity-Based Stopping
children.top_down_role: Termination based on derivative-free evidence of local stationarity.

assumptions_latex: The problem is unconstrained and the local model \(m_k\) is differentiable.
The algorithm has verified its required model-accuracy condition near \(x_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conditions \(\chi_k\le\epsilon_g\) and \(\Delta_k\le\epsilon_\Delta\) constitute the declared model-based approximate-stationarity stopping signal.

notation.meaning: Local derivative-free model at iteration k.
Norm of the model gradient at the current point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-based stopping condition for unconstrained smooth derivative-free trust-region methods.

source_refs.locator: 10 Trust-region methods based on derivative-free models p. 173

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(k\), let \(x_k\) be the current point, let \(m_k\) be a differentiable local model on a trust region of radius \(\Delta_k>0\), and define \(\chi_k=\lVert\nabla m_k(x_k)\rVert\). For prescribed tolerances \(\epsilon_g>0\) and \(\epsilon_\Delta>0\), stationarity-based stopping is permitted when \[\chi_k\le\epsilon_g\qquad\text{and}\qquad\Delta_k\le\epsilon_\Delta,\] provided the model satisfies the algorithm's stated accuracy requirement on that trust region. Without that model-accuracy condition, this test is only heuristic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth unconstrained model-based method may stop when its model gradient and trust-region radius are both small and the model satisfies the method's stated accuracy condition.
knowledge_statements.title: Stationarity-Based Stopping

source_witnesses.locator: 10 Trust-region methods based on derivative-free models p. 173

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Small Model Gradient Without Model Accuracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of interpreting model criticality alone as true stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=x\) on \(\mathbb R\) and let \(m_k(x)\equiv0\) at \(x_k=0\) for any radius \(\Delta_k>0\). Then \(\|\nabla m_k(x_k)\|=0\) although \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|=1\). Thus small model gradient and radius do not certify true first-order stationarity without a valid model-gradient error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inaccurate constant model has zero model gradient where the true objective has nonzero gradient, so model criticality alone is not a stationarity certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Small Model Gradient Without Model Accuracy

children.title: Conflicting Stopping Signals
children.top_down_role: Priority and interpretation when resource limits and stationarity indicators disagree.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of collapsing certified and forced termination into one unqualified stop flag.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider two terminal states with the same aggregate flag \(T_k=B_k\vee(S_k\wedge R_k)\). In one state \(B_k\) is true and \(S_k\wedge R_k\) is false; in the other \(B_k\) is false and \(S_k\wedge R_k\) is true. Both have \(T_k=\mathrm{true}\), but only the second supports a stationarity claim. Therefore the aggregate Boolean flag cannot determine the correct returned status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Combining forced and certified termination into one Boolean stop flag loses the information needed to report success correctly.
assumptions_latex: Resource exhaustion and certified stationarity are distinct terminal causes.
The returned interface exposes only the aggregate flag \(T_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_k\text{ alone does not certify stationarity}.
knowledge_statements.title: Boolean Stop-Signal Information Loss

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Returned-status semantics when hard resource, stationarity, and reliability predicates coexist.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B_k\) denote exhaustion of a hard resource limit, \(S_k\) a stationarity signal whose stated preconditions hold, and \(R_k\) validity of the numerical information needed to interpret that signal. A stopping policy may terminate when \(B_k\) holds, but it returns certified stationarity only when \(S_k\wedge R_k\) holds. If \(B_k\wedge\neg(S_k\wedge R_k)\), it returns a resource-limit status without a stationarity claim; if \(S_k\wedge\neg R_k\), it returns a numerically-unreliable or indeterminate status rather than success.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hard limit may force termination, but certified success requires both the stationarity predicate and its reliability preconditions; other stops retain qualified statuses.
assumptions_latex: B_k\text{ denotes a hard resource limit that forbids further required work}.
R_k\text{ states that the information used by }S_k\text{ satisfies those preconditions}.

notation.meaning: validity predicate for the stationarity evidence

knowledge_statements.title: Status-Preserving Stopping Precedence
Conflicting Stopping Signals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary when resource, stationarity, and numerical-reliability criteria disagree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_k\) denote a valid stationarity signal, \(R_k\) a valid numerical-reliability signal, and \(C_k\ge B\) budget exhaustion. A conflict occurs whenever at least two applicable predicates prescribe incompatible actions; in particular, \[(C_k\ge B)\wedge\neg S_k\] requires termination without a stationarity claim, while \[S_k\wedge\neg R_k\] forbids interpreting the stationarity signal as reliable. A complete stopping policy must specify precedence and the returned status. Conjunction of the raw signals is not a valid certificate when one signal's preconditions fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Budget exhaustion can force an uncertified stop, while apparent stationarity under unreliable evaluations must not be reported as a valid certificate.
assumptions_latex: Each stopping predicate has an explicitly stated validity domain.
The evaluation budget is a hard constraint when exhausted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Conflicting signals require a precedence rule and a qualified termination status rather than an unconditional success declaration.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: stopping predicates certify only conclusions supported by their satisfied preconditions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf and the policy principle is plausible, but no source supports the meanings and precedence implications assigned to the abstract predicates. An authoritative stopping-policy or solver-status reference is needed before this formulation can be reviewed reliably.

children.title: Black-Box Benchmark Families
children.top_down_role: Collections of executable simulators, applications, or opaque evaluation services.

assumptions_latex: All solver-visible instance information is contained in the declared oracle response and query history.
The protocol specifies admissible queries, response spaces, charging, status semantics, and whether oracle randomness is controlled.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The family is black-box relative to the information restriction imposed by the declared oracles \(O_\omega\).

notation.meaning: Observed output, charged cost, and evaluation status.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Benchmark families whose instances are accessible solely through declared oracle interfaces.

source_refs.locator: 1.1. What Are Derivative-Free and Blackbox Optimization? p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A black-box benchmark family is a test-problem family \(\mathcal P=\{P_\omega\}_{\omega\in\Omega}\) equipped with declared oracle interfaces \(O_\omega\). For an admissible query \(x\in X_\omega\) and, when applicable, random state \(\eta\in H_\omega\), the oracle returns \[O_\omega(x,\eta)=(y,c,\ell)\in Y_\omega\times[0,+\infty)\times L_\omega,\] where \(y\) is the observed output, \(c\) is the charged cost, and \(\ell\) is status information. Solvers may use the query history but may not access hidden formulas, derivatives, solutions, or undisclosed instance parameters. Deterministic and stochastic instances are distinguished by the oracle specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A black-box benchmark family exposes each problem only through a declared oracle returning observations, costs, and statuses while withholding hidden formulas, derivatives, solutions, and undisclosed parameters.
knowledge_statements.title: Black-Box Benchmark Families

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1. What Are Derivative-Free and Blackbox Optimization? p. 3

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural property distinguishing hidden implementation from solver-visible information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let two implementations have identical declared oracle maps on every admissible query history, including identical laws for outputs, charged costs, statuses, and randomness. No solver restricted to that interface can distinguish the implementations from its transcript. Conversely, exposing an additional formula, derivative, solution, or hidden parameter refines the interface and may destroy black-box equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Implementations producing the same declared oracle transcripts are indistinguishable to interface-restricted solvers; black-box status changes when extra information is exposed.
assumptions_latex: Solvers receive information only through the declared oracle and their query histories.
The implementations induce identical transcript distributions for every admissible solver policy.
knowledge_statements.title: Black-Box Status Is Interface-Relative

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Experimental condition for comparing solver runs under a common black-box protocol.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two solver runs on instance \(P_\omega\) are protocol-comparable only if they use the same admissible query set, response and status semantics, charging rule, stopping rule, and distribution or coupling of oracle randomness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fair black-box comparison requires common query, response, charging, stopping, and randomness protocols.
assumptions_latex: Both runs target the same benchmark instance.
The declared protocol records all solver-visible information and charged costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \pi_A=\pi_B\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{the runs share one declared oracle contract}.

notation.meaning: protocols used for solvers A and B

children.title: Benchmark Representativeness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on transferring observed benchmark behavior to broader problem populations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete boundary showing dependence of solver rankings on benchmark population weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider two benchmark instances \(P_1,P_2\) with lower-is-better losses \(M(A,P_1)=0\), \(M(A,P_2)=2\), \(M(B,P_1)=1\), and \(M(B,P_2)=0\). Under weights \((w,1-w)\), \(L_A=2(1-w)\) and \(L_B=w\). Thus \(A\) ranks above \(B\) when \(w>2/3\), whereas \(B\) ranks above \(A\) when \(w<2/3\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same per-instance results can rank two solvers oppositely when benchmark instance weights change.
assumptions_latex: Aggregate performance is the weighted arithmetic mean of lower-is-better losses.

notation.meaning: weight assigned to the first instance

knowledge_statements.title: Weighting-Induced Ranking Reversal

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on interpreting results obtained under different targets, budgets, or charging rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let solver performance be a functional \(S(A;\mathcal P,\pi)\) of a benchmark family \(\mathcal P\) and protocol \(\pi\), where \(\pi\) fixes instance weights, targets, budgets, costs, randomness, and aggregation. Values \(S(A;\mathcal P,\pi_1)\) and \(S(B;\mathcal P,\pi_2)\) with \(\pi_1\ne\pi_2\) do not define a controlled solver comparison unless an explicit transformation establishes equivalence of the protocols.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solver results from different benchmark protocols are not directly comparable without a justified equivalence transformation.
assumptions_latex: The performance functional depends on at least one protocol component.
No equivalence transformation between \(\pi_1\) and \(\pi_2\) is supplied.
review_flags: methodological claim requiring explicit protocol declaration
knowledge_statements.title: Protocol-Change Comparability Boundary
Benchmark Representativeness Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary on generalizing solver rankings beyond the benchmarked instance class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P_0\) be the tested family and let \(M(A,P)\) be a solver-performance metric. If no relationship is assumed between \(\mathcal P_0\) and an untested family \(\mathcal P_1\), observations on \(\mathcal P_0\) do not determine rankings on \(\mathcal P_1\). Indeed, performance mappings can agree with all measured values on \(\mathcal P_0\) while satisfying either \[M(A,P)<M(B,P)\] or \[M(B,P)<M(A,P)\] on instances \(P\in\mathcal P_1\). Thus empirical superiority is supported only for the sampled population, weighting, targets, budgets, and metric actually used.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without assumptions linking tested and untested problems, a benchmark ranking cannot establish the same ranking outside the sampled protocol.
assumptions_latex: No distributional or structural link between tested and untested families is imposed.
Lower values of \(M\) represent better performance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Rankings measured on \(\mathcal P_0\) need not extend to \(\mathcal P_1\).

notation.meaning: Performance of solver A on problem P.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: empirical rankings are conditional on the sampled population and protocol

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and limited conclusion are mathematically plausible, but the record has no benchmark-methodology source supporting the population, weighting, target, budget, and metric qualifications. Source support is required for this empirical-generalization formulation.

children.title: Evaluation-Budget Profiles
children.top_down_role: Comparative outcomes indexed by black-box evaluation consumption.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized inverse of the empirical evaluation-budget profile.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q\in(0,1]\), define \[B_s(q)=\inf\{b\geq0:E_s(b)\geq q\},\qquad \inf\varnothing=+\infty.\] Then \(B_s(q)\) is the least evaluation budget at which solver \(s\) has solved at least fraction \(q\) of the benchmark set. It is finite exactly when the empirical success fraction is at least \(q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The generalized inverse is the smallest charged-evaluation budget needed to solve a prescribed benchmark fraction.
assumptions_latex: The benchmark set is finite and nonempty.
\(E_s\) uses fixed success and evaluation-charging conventions.
knowledge_statements.title: Evaluation-Budget Quantile Representation
Evaluation-Budget Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empirical success profile indexed by charged black-box evaluation budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite problem set \(\mathcal P\), solver \(s\), and fixed success predicate, let \(N_{p,s}\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{+\infty\}\) be the number of charged evaluations first required to solve problem \(p\). The evaluation-budget profile is the empirical distribution function \[E_s(b)=\frac{1}{\lvert\mathcal P\rvert}\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}\mathbf 1\{N_{p,s}\le b
e},
eqquad b\ge0.\] Therefore \(E_s(b)\) is the fraction of test problems solved within budget \(b\). Unsuccessful runs contribute zero at every finite budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The evaluation-budget profile gives, for each budget, the fraction of benchmark problems first solved within that many charged evaluations.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\) is finite and every solver uses the same success predicate.
Evaluation charging and unsuccessful-run conventions are identical across solvers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_s(b)\) equals the empirical fraction of problems solved by solver \(s\) within \(b\) charged evaluations.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: this is the empirical cumulative success fraction under an evaluation resource

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A representation is the correct role, and the intended empirical cumulative success fraction is clear. However, the displayed formula contains corrupted TeX commands after the budget variable and before the domain qualifier, and no source establishes that this exact object is conventionally an evaluation-budget profile.

children.title: Wall-Clock Profiles
children.top_down_role: Comparative outcomes indexed by elapsed execution time.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized inverse of the empirical wall-clock profile under a fixed execution protocol.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q\in(0,1]\), define \[Q_s(q)=\inf\{t\geq0:W_s(t)\geq q\},\qquad \inf\varnothing=+\infty.\] Then \(Q_s(q)\) is the least elapsed-time threshold by which solver \(s\) has solved at least fraction \(q\) of the benchmark set. It is finite exactly when the empirical success fraction is at least \(q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The generalized inverse is the shortest elapsed time by which a prescribed benchmark fraction has been solved.
assumptions_latex: The benchmark set is finite and nonempty.
Hardware, concurrency, timing boundaries, success criteria, and preprocessing conventions are fixed.

notation.meaning: Elapsed time required to solve fraction \(q\).

knowledge_statements.title: Wall-Clock Quantile Representation
Wall-Clock Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empirical success profile indexed by elapsed wall-clock time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite problem set \(\mathcal P\), solver \(s\), and fixed success predicate, let \(T_{p,s}\in[0,+\infty]\) be the elapsed wall-clock time to first success on problem \(p\). The wall-clock profile is \[W_s(t)=\frac{1}{\lvert\mathcal P\rvert}\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}\mathbf 1\{T_{p,s}\le t\u0002
e},
eqquad t\ge0.\] Hence \(W_s(t)\) is the fraction solved by time \(t\). Hardware, concurrency, initialization, compilation, communication, and timing boundaries must be fixed because they affect \(T_{p,s}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The wall-clock profile gives the fraction of problems solved by each elapsed-time threshold under a fixed timing and hardware protocol.
assumptions_latex: All runs use the same success predicate and declared timing boundaries.
Hardware, concurrency, and preprocessing conventions are controlled or reported.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W_s(t)\) equals the empirical fraction of problems solved by solver \(s\) within time \(t\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: this is the empirical cumulative success fraction under elapsed time

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A representation is appropriate, but the formula contains both corrupted TeX commands and an embedded control character. The timing protocol qualifications are sensible, yet no authoritative source is supplied for the exact profile definition or its required timing controls.

children.title: Cost-Metric Divergence
children.top_down_role: Cases where evaluation-based rankings differ materially from time-based rankings.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common-Rate Agreement of Count and Time Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient regime in which absolute evaluation-budget and wall-clock profiles differ only by a common change of units.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every successful run satisfies \(T_{p,s}=cN_{p,s}\) for one constant \(c>0\) common to every problem and solver, and failures are infinite under both metrics. Then \[W_s(cb)=E_s(b)\] for every solver \(s\) and budget \(b\geq0\). Consequently the two profile families induce identical solver comparisons after rescaling the horizontal axis. Problem-dependent or solver-dependent evaluation times, unequal overhead, and concurrency remove this guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every charged evaluation takes the same time and there is no unequal overhead, count and time profiles agree after a single unit conversion.
assumptions_latex: Both profiles use the same problem set, success predicate, and failure convention.

notation.meaning: Charged evaluations to the common target.
Elapsed time to the common target.
Common elapsed time per charged evaluation.

review_flags: revised_builder_claim: a problem-dependent factor preserves relative performance ratios but does not identify the absolute sibling profiles by one common axis rescaling
knowledge_statements.title: Common-Rate Agreement of Count and Time Profiles
Cost-Metric Divergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete reversal between evaluation-count and wall-clock rankings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider one problem solved by algorithms \(A\) and \(B\). Suppose \(A\) uses \(N_A=10\) evaluations costing \(c_A=2\) seconds each, whereas \(B\) uses \(N_B=15\) evaluations costing \(c_B=1\) second each, with negligible common overhead. Then \[N_A<N_B
eqquad\text{but}\qquad T_A=N_Ac_A=20>15=N_Bc_B=T_B.\] Thus evaluation-budget performance ranks \(A\) ahead of \(B\), while wall-clock performance ranks \(B\) ahead of \(A\). Count and time profiles need not induce the same ordering when per-evaluation or algorithmic overhead costs differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solver may use fewer evaluations yet take longer, so evaluation-budget and wall-clock profiles can rank solvers oppositely.
assumptions_latex: Both algorithms satisfy the same success predicate.
Per-evaluation costs are constant in this example and common overhead is negligible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Evaluation-count ordering does not imply wall-clock ordering.

notation.meaning: Evaluation counts of algorithms A and B.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit arithmetic counterexample establishes the claimed ranking reversal
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind exactly fits Cost-Metric Divergence, and the arithmetic correctly demonstrates a ranking reversal. Nevertheless, the displayed comparison contains corrupted TeX commands, and the record has no cited source despite being normalized to needs_source; an inspectable benchmarking reference is required.

children.title: Data Profiles
children.top_down_role: Solver progress comparisons relative to problem-specific accuracy targets and budgets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Empirical-Distribution Structure of a Data Profile
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural properties of a dimension-normalized evaluation-budget data profile.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B_{p,s}=t_{p,s}/(n_p+1)\in[0,+\infty]\) and \(d_s(\alpha)=|\mathcal P|^{-1}\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}\mathbf 1\{B_{p,s}\leq\alpha\}\). Then \(d_s\) is a nondecreasing, right-continuous step function whose finite jump points are attained values of \(B_{p,s}\). Moreover, \(\lim_{\alpha\to\infty}d_s(\alpha)=|\{p:t_{p,s}<+\infty\}|/|\mathcal P|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A data profile is the empirical distribution function of dimension-normalized evaluation counts, and its limiting height is the empirical success fraction.
assumptions_latex: The target, evaluation charging, and normalization conventions are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_s\) is the empirical cumulative distribution of finite normalized solution costs, with failures contributing no finite mass.

notation.meaning: Dimension-normalized evaluations to first target attainment.

knowledge_statements.title: Empirical-Distribution Structure of a Data Profile
Data Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension-normalized DFO data profile based on evaluations required to reach a fixed objective reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal P\) be finite, let problem \(p\) have dimension \(n_p\), initial value \(f_p^0\), and reference value \(f_p^L<f_p^0\). For \(\tau\in(0,1)\), define \(t_{p,s}\) as the first charged evaluation count at which solver \(s\) obtains \[f_p(x)\le f_p^L+
tau(f_p^0-f_p^L),\] with \(t_{p,s}=+\infty\) on failure. The data profile is \[d_s(
alpha)=\frac{1}{\lvert\mathcal P\rvert}\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}\mathbf 1\!\left\{\frac{t_{p,s}}{n_p+1}\le
alpha\right\},
eqquad
alpha\ge0.\] It reports the fraction solved within \(\alpha\) simplex-gradient-equivalent evaluation units.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A data profile reports the fraction of problems solved within a dimension-normalized evaluation budget using a fixed objective-reduction target.
assumptions_latex: All solvers use the same \(\tau\), charging convention, and problem set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(d_s(
alpha)\) is the fraction solved using at most \(\alpha(n_p+1)\) charged evaluations on each problem \(p\).

notation.meaning: Evaluations to first attainment of the target.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard dimension-normalized DFO data-profile formula

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role and intended dimension-normalized data-profile formula fit the leaf. Multiple parameters and spacing commands are corrupted in the TeX, however, and no primary citation supports the target convention, normalization by \(n_p+1\), or the simplex-gradient-equivalent interpretation.

children.title: Performance Profiles
children.top_down_role: Relative solver performance comparisons across a benchmark collection.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariance of performance ratios under common positive rescaling on each problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(t'_{p,s}=c_p t_{p,s}\), where \(c_p>0\) is independent of solver \(s\), and preserve infinite failures. Whenever problem \(p\) has a finite best cost, \[\frac{t'_{p,s}}{\min_{u\in S}t'_{p,u}}=\frac{t_{p,s}}{\min_{u\in S}t_{p,u}}.\] Hence all resulting performance profiles are unchanged. Solver-dependent scaling or a nonmultiplicative transformation need not preserve them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplying every solver's cost on one problem by the same positive factor leaves performance profiles unchanged; solver-dependent transformations need not.
assumptions_latex: \(c_p>0\) depends on the problem but not the solver.
The solver set, success criterion, and failure convention remain fixed.

notation.meaning: Common positive cost scale for problem \(p\).

knowledge_statements.title: Problemwise Scale Invariance
Performance Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dolan–Moré performance profile using a fixed problem set and a common performance measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a finite nonempty set of test problems and \(S\) a finite set of solvers. For each \(p\in P\) and \(s\in S\), let \(t_{p,s}\in(0,\infty]\) be the measured cost, with failure represented by \(+\infty\). Define \(r_{p,s}=t_{p,s}/\min_{u\in S}t_{p,u}\) when at least one solver succeeds on \(p\), and \(r_{p,s}=+\infty\) otherwise. The performance profile of solver \(s\) is \[\rho_s(\tau)=\frac{1}{|P|}\left|\{p\in P:r_{p,s}\leq\tau\}\right|,\qquad \tau\geq1.\] Thus \(\rho_s(1)\) is the fraction of problems on which \(s\) attains the best observed cost, while \(\lim_{\tau\to\infty}\rho_s(\tau)\) is its empirical success fraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solver’s performance profile is the fraction of test problems solved within a factor τ of the best observed solver cost.
assumptions_latex: All solvers use the same success criterion and performance measure.
At least one solver succeeds on any problem included in finite-ratio comparisons.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_s:[1,\infty)\to[0,1]\) is nondecreasing and summarizes relative efficiency and empirical robustness.

notation.meaning: Measured cost of solver s on problem p; infinity denotes failure.
Cost ratio relative to the best observed solver on problem p.
Performance profile of solver s at factor τ.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the Performance Profiles leaf and are mathematically coherent, but no citation supports the Dolan–Moré normalization, tie handling, or infinite-cost failure convention.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative function-evaluation performance over a finite benchmark set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty finite test set \(\mathcal P\), an algorithm \(a\in\mathcal A\), and performance ratios \(r_{a,p}\), the performance profile is the function \(\rho_a:[1,\infty)\to[0,1]\) defined by
\[
\rho_a(\alpha)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal P|}\left|\{p\in\mathcal P:r_{a,p}\leq\alpha\}\right|.
\]
Thus, \(\rho_a(\alpha)\) is the proportion of test problems that algorithm \(a\) solves using at most \(\alpha\) times the function evaluations used by the best solver for the respective problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a factor alpha, the performance profile gives the fraction of benchmark problems that an algorithm solves using no more than alpha times the function evaluations of the best solver for each problem.
assumptions_latex: \(r_{a,p}\) is the solver-to-best performance ratio for algorithm \(a\) on problem \(p\)

children.title: Profile Interpretation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of profile conclusions to baselines, tolerances, failures, and problem selection.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Profile Crossing Prevents a Total Solver Ranking
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite counterexample showing that performance-profile curves need not induce a total ranking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider three problems with ratios \((r_{1,A},r_{2,A},r_{3,A})=(1,1,10)\) and \((r_{1,B},r_{2,B},r_{3,B})=(2,2,1)\). Then \(\rho_A(1)=2/3>1/3=\rho_B(1)\), whereas \(\rho_A(2)=2/3<1=\rho_B(2)\). Neither profile dominates on \([1,\infty)\), so selecting one winner requires an externally chosen range or scalar summary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Performance profiles can cross, so one solver may be more often best while another solves more problems within a larger factor.
assumptions_latex: All ratios use one fixed benchmark, solver set, cost measure, and success protocol.
Ties use the common weak-inequality convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pointwise performance-profile comparison need not define a total order on solvers.

notation.meaning: Performance ratio for problem \(p\) and solver \(s\).

knowledge_statements.title: Profile Crossing Prevents a Total Solver Ranking
Profile Interpretation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits on causal or population-level conclusions from empirical benchmark profiles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be the sampled problem set, \(S\) the compared solver set, and \(m\) the chosen cost and success convention. A profile value \(\rho_s(\tau)\) is an empirical statistic conditional on \((P,S,m)\). It does not, without a specified sampling model, imply the probability that \(s\) will solve a new problem within factor \(\tau\) of an absolute optimum. Moreover, adding or removing a solver can change \(\min_{u\in S}t_{p,u}\), hence every ratio \(r_{p,s}\); changing tolerances, budgets, failure penalties, aggregation, or random seeds can likewise change the profile. Therefore profile dominance supports comparison only under the fixed benchmark protocol and competitor set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Profiles compare solvers only under the sampled problems, competitors, costs, tolerances, budgets, and randomness; they do not establish universal or causal superiority.
assumptions_latex: \(\rho_s\) is computed from a finite benchmark set.
Ratios are normalized by the best observed solver in the compared set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any inference beyond the fixed tuple \((P,S,m)\) requires an explicit sampling model and uncertainty analysis.

notation.meaning: Complete measurement, success, and failure protocol.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits the leaf, and the stated protocol dependence is plausible. A benchmarking or statistical source is required for the limits on population-level inference and profile interpretation.

children.title: Stochastic Replicate Design
children.top_down_role: Selection of seeds, repeated runs, blocking factors, and replicate coverage.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matched replicate design for comparing two stochastic solver configurations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each replicate \(i\), generate a random input \(U_i\), run configurations \(A\) and \(B\) with that same input, and record \(D_i=Y_{A,i}-Y_{B,i}\). If the pairs are iid, then \(\bar D_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nD_i\) is unbiased for \(\mathbb E[Y_A-Y_B]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar D_n)=\operatorname{Var}(D_1)/n\), where \(\operatorname{Var}(D_1)=\operatorname{Var}(Y_A)+\operatorname{Var}(Y_B)-2\operatorname{Cov}(Y_A,Y_B)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use the same random input for both configurations within each independent pair and analyze the paired differences; positive within-pair covariance reduces comparison variance.
assumptions_latex: Both members of each pair use the same declared random input and compatible evaluation protocols.
The paired responses have finite second moments.
knowledge_statements.title: Paired Common-Random-Numbers Replicate Design

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes statistical independence from collision-free seed labeling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replicate responses \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\) are independent when \(\mathbb P_{(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)}=\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mathbb P_{Y_i}\). Distinct seed labels, \(U_i\ne U_j\) for \(i\ne j\), neither imply nor are required for this factorization; independent draws from a discrete seed distribution may collide with positive probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent replication concerns the joint response law, whereas distinct seed labels are a separate design constraint.
assumptions_latex: \(Y_i\) is the response produced by replicate \(i\).
All randomness affecting a replicate is included in its declared random input.

notation.meaning: Seed label used by replicate i.

knowledge_statements.title: Independent Replication and Seed Distinctness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Precision boundary for dependent repeated runs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\) have common variance \(\sigma^2\) and common pairwise correlation \(\rho\), then \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_n)=\sigma^2[1+(n-1)\rho]/n\). The variance-equivalent independent-replicate count is therefore \(n_{\mathrm{eff}}=n/[1+(n-1)\rho]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive dependence can make many nominal replicates carry the information of far fewer independent runs.
assumptions_latex: The responses have a valid equicorrelation covariance matrix.
knowledge_statements.title: Correlation Reduces Effective Replication

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic benchmark replicate design without conflating independence and seed uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each fixed solver-problem configuration, prespecify \(n\geq2\) independent complete random inputs \(U_1,\ldots,U_n\), a response map, common initialization, budget and stopping rules, and a failure-recording rule. Execute every scheduled replicate once, record \(Y_i\) or its declared failure outcome, and do not stop or add replicates in response to observed performance unless a valid sequential design was fixed in advance. Report \(n\), the random-input identifiers, all outcomes, and the protocol.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Schedule independent random inputs before observing outcomes, keep run conditions fixed, retain failures consistently, and avoid outcome-dependent replication unless prespecified.
assumptions_latex: U_1,\ldots,U_n\text{ are independent under the declared randomization mechanism}.
Run conditions and the response definition are fixed before outcomes are observed.
Every scheduled run is retained under a prespecified success or failure convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (U_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n\text{ is an auditable replicate sample under the declared protocol}.

notation.meaning: complete random input for replicate i

knowledge_statements.title: Prescheduled Independent-Replication Protocol
Stochastic Replicate Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent-replicate design for estimating a solver’s mean benchmark response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each fixed solver–problem pair, choose a replicate count \(n\geq2\), a seed-generation rule fixed before observing outcomes, and a scalar response \(Y\) such as evaluation count, terminal objective value, or success indicator. Generate distinct seeds \(U_1,\ldots,U_n\) independently from the declared seed distribution; run the solver once with each seed under identical budgets and stopping rules; and record \(Y_i=Y(U_i)\), including failures according to a prespecified censoring or penalty convention. Report \(\bar Y_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i\), \(s_n^2=(n-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\bar Y_n)^2\), the seed list, and \(n\). Stop only at the fixed \(n\) or under a prespecified sequential rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run independent, prespecified random seeds under one protocol, retain failures consistently, and report the replicate count, seeds, sample mean, and sample variance.
assumptions_latex: Replicate seeds are independent draws from the declared seed distribution.
Budget, stopping, initialization, and failure conventions are fixed across replicates.
The reported response is scalar and finite after applying the declared failure convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is \((n,\{U_i,Y_i\}_{i=1}^n,\bar Y_n,s_n^2)\), suitable for protocol-specific uncertainty assessment.
